SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Statutory Authority

    This proposed regulation is being issued under the authority 
granted to the Secretary of Health and Human Services by the Native 
American Programs Act of 1974, as amended (42 U.S.C. 2991 et seq.), 
hereafter referred to as the ``Act.''

II. Background

    The Native American Programs Act of 1974 (NAPA), as amended (42 
U.S.C. 2991 et seq.), authorizes the Administration for Native 
Americans (ANA) to promote social development and economic self-
sufficiency in Native communities through competitive grant funding. 
Under Section 803 of NAPA (42 U.S.C. 2991b), ANA provides financial 
assistance on a single-year or multi-year basis to public and nonprofit 
private agencies, including governing bodies of Indian Tribes on 
federal and state reservations, Alaska Native villages and regional 
corporations established under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act 
(43 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.), and public and nonprofit agencies serving 
Native Hawaiians and Indian and Alaska Native organizations in urban or 
rural areas that are not reservations or Alaska Native villages. ANA 
implements its mission through competitive discretionary grants that 
support Native-led, community-based projects aimed at strengthening 
families and communities and reducing long-term dependency through 
social and economic development, Native language preservation, and 
environmental regulatory enhancement. ANA typically provides short-term 
``seed'' funding ranging from 12 to 60 months to help communities 
launch or expand sustainable efforts. In Federal Fiscal Year (FFY) 
2025, ANA awarded a total of $50,738,495, which included new awards and 
continued funding for previously awarded projects. The regulations that 
implement the NAPA, 45 CFR part 1336, were last amended in 2026 by 91 
FR 36756.

III. Executive Summary

    This would follow a final rule that was published in June 2026 (see 
91 FR 36756) that repealed all of Part 1336 except for five sections. 
Those five sections now are fragmented and could be streamlined to ease 
readability and understanding. The five sections that currently remain 
in regulation are titled: Definitions, Notice of ineligibility, Appeal 
of ineligibility, Financial and administrative requirements, and 
Appeals. Many of these sections have language that is duplicative of 
statute, yet components of the section are not duplicative. Therefore, 
this rulemaking proposes to remove the language that is duplicative and 
streamline the remaining text.

Severability

    The provisions of this NPRM, if finalized, are intended to be 
severable, such that, in the event a court were to invalidate any 
particular provision or deem it to be unenforceable, the remaining 
provisions would continue to be valid. The changes address a variety of 
issues relevant to the Administration for Native Americans. None of the 
provisions contained herein are central to an overall intent of the 
proposed rule, nor are any provisions dependent on the validity of 
other, separate provisions.

IV. Discussion of Proposed Changes

Subpart A--Definitions

Sec.  1336.10 Definitions
    Section 1336.10 identifies the definitions that are applicable to 
part 1336, unless context otherwise requires. This proposal removes the 
definition for ``Economic and social self-sufficiency'' as the term is 
not used in the proposed new part. Further, this NPRM seeks to update 
the definition of ``ANA'' as the Administration for Native Americans is 
no longer under the Office of Human Development Services. Therefore, 
this proposal would remove that reference while maintaining the 
remainder of the definition. This rule proposes to also redesignate 
this section from Sec.  1336.10 to Sec.  1336.1 in accordance with the 
proposed streamlining of the part. There are no other proposed changes 
to definitions in this section.

Subpart C--Native American Projects

Sec.  1336.34 Notice of Ineligibility
    Section 1336.34 states the process of notice for an organization if 
the Commissioner determines them to be ineligible for funding, or the 
activities proposed by the organization are ineligible. This NPRM 
proposes to streamline this section by maintaining the requirement that 
if an organization or activities proposed by an organization are 
determined to be ineligible for funding, the Commissioner must inform 
the applicant of this decision and must state the legal and factual 
grounds for which this decision was made. This NPRM seeks to remove the 
detailed requirements that state that a copy of part 1336 must be 
included in that letter, as well as requiring the letter to include the 
template paragraph that currently exists in regulation. The reason for 
this proposal is in part to simplify the regulatory text, which does 
not benefit from including template paragraphs, but also to recognize 
the fact that the address listed in the current section is no longer 
the appropriate office of ANA. This rule proposes to also redesignate 
this section from Sec.  1336.34 to Sec.  1336.2 and retitle it 
``Notices of ineligibility and appeals'' in accordance with the 
proposed streamlining of the part.
Sec.  1336.35 Appeal of Ineligibility
    Section 1336.35 currently identifies the process that must be 
followed to appeal a finding of ineligibility for funding. This section 
is proposed to be removed as the language detailing this appeals 
process conflicts with the Departmental Appeals Board (DAB) procedures 
which are identified in 45 CFR part 16. To simplify the appeals process 
and ensure consistency among other ACF programs, we propose to add a 
new paragraph to proposed section 1336.2 entitled ``appeals'' (proposed 
1336.2(b)) describing that an applicant who has had their application 
rejected because it has been found ineligible for funding or because 
the activities it is proposing are ineligible for funding by the 
Commissioner may appeal the Commissioner's ruling to the DAB following 
the process identified in 45 CFR part 16.

Subpart E--Financial Assistance Provisions

Sec.  1336.50 Financial and Administrative Requirements
    Section 1336.50 currently describes financial and administrative 
requirements applicable to grantees. This section is proposed to be 
streamlined and renumbered as section 1336.3 under the same name. This 
NPRM seeks to remove current Sec.  1336.50(a) as the regulations 
identified in this subpart apply regardless of being cited here. HHS 
accepts that this list may be helpful for grantees to identify which 
requirements are applicable to them, and if this proposed rule is 
finalized, intends to provide training



and technical assistance to ensure grantees are still aware of 
applicable regulatory requirements.
    Current section 1336.50(b)(1) details that recipients of financial 
assistance under sections 803, 804, and 805 of the Act must provide a 
matching share of 20 percent of the approved cost of the assisted 
project, unless a waiver is attained. This proposed rule removes this 
section because it is duplicative of 42 U.S.C. 2991b(c). We propose to 
streamline current section 1336.50(b)(2) by removing unnecessary 
language while preserving the all core aspects of the regulation and 
renumbering as Sec.  1336.3(a)(1).
    We propose to renumber current section 1336.50(b)(3) as 
1336.3(a)(2) and retain in part. The language proposed for deletion is 
in paragraph (i) which was an overly wordy explanation for why an 
applicant could request a waiver for the non-Federal matching 
requirement and is proposed to be replaced with the proper statutory 
reference. Paragraph (ii) is proposed to be retained, but this NPRM 
seeks to remove the last two sentences of the paragraph which provide 
examples of allowable documentation, as opposed to requirements imposed 
on grantees. Current section 1336.50(b)(4) is proposed to be renumbered 
to 1336.3(a)(3) with no changes.
    We propose to remove current section 1336.50(c)(1) as it does not 
contain any requirements but rather restates language from section 
803(c) of the Act and other parts of the regulation. Paragraph (2) is 
then proposed to be renumbered as paragraph (1) with a minor edit to 
add a statutory reference. There are no other proposed changes to the 
rest of current section 1336.50, other than to renumber as appropriate.
Sec.  1336.52 Appeals
    Section 1336.52 currently identifies the right to appeal decisions 
to suspend, terminate, or deny funding pursuant to the remedies for 
noncompliance under 2 CFR 200.339-200.343 and the process for which to 
do so. We propose to remove this section as the language detailing this 
appeals and hearing process is duplicative of the DAB procedures which 
are identified in 45 CFR part 16. To ensure that grantees are still 
aware of the appeals process, without having to rewrite part 16 in this 
section, we propose to add a new paragraph to proposed section 1336.2 
entitled ``appeals'' (proposed 1336.2(b)) which describes that a 
recipient who has had their financial assistance suspended or 
terminated, or whose non-competing continuation applications for 
refunding have denied under 2 CFR 200.339 and 200.340 may appeal the 
ruling to the DAB following the process identified in 45 CFR part 16.

V. Regulatory Process Matters

Paperwork Reduction Act

    Under the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq., as 
amended) (PRA), all Departments are required to submit to the Office of 
Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval any new or modified 
reporting or recordkeeping requirements inherent in a proposed or final 
rule. This NPRM does not contain any information collections requiring 
OMB approval under the PRA and, therefore, will not create any new 
paperwork burdens or modify existing burdens subject to OMB review.

Executive Order 13132

    Executive Order 13132 requires federal agencies to consult with 
State and local government officials if they develop regulatory 
policies with federalism implications. Federalism is rooted in the 
belief that issues that are not national in scope or significance are 
most appropriately addressed by the level of government close to the 
people. This proposed rule would not have substantial direct impact on 
the States, on the relationship between the federal government and the 
States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the 
various levels of government. This NPRM would not pre-empt State law. 
The changes proposed in the NPRM are removing unnecessary and obsolete 
regulations from the Native American Program rules. Therefore, in 
accordance with Section 6 of Executive Order 13132, it is determined 
that this action does not have sufficient federalism implications to 
warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement.

Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families

    Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families Section 
654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act of 1999 
(Pub. L. 105-277) requires federal agencies to determine whether a 
policy or regulation may negatively affect family well-being. If the 
agency determines a policy or regulation negatively affects family 
well-being, then the agency must prepare an impact assessment 
addressing seven criteria specified in the law. HHS believes it is not 
necessary to prepare a family policymaking assessment because the 
actions proposed in this NPRM will not have any impact on the autonomy 
or integrity of the family as an institution.

VI. Regulatory Impact Analysis

    We have examined the impacts of the proposed rule under Executive 
Order 12866, Executive Order 13563, Executive Order 14192, the 
Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601-612), and the Unfunded 
Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (Pub. L. 104-4).
    Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct us to assess all benefits 
and costs of available regulatory alternatives and, when regulation is 
necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. 
Executive Order 14192 requires that any new incremental costs 
associated with significant new regulations ``shall, to the extent 
permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs 
associated with at least ten prior regulations.'' The Office of 
Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has determined that this 
proposed rule is a significant action under Executive Order 12866 
Section 3(f).
    The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires agencies to consider 
the impact of their regulatory proposals on small entities. Because 
this action would simply repeal obsolete and unnecessary language, we 
propose to certify that the proposed rule would not have a significant 
economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
    The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) generally requires 
that each agency conduct a cost-benefit analysis; identify and consider 
a reasonable number of regulatory alternatives; and select the least 
costly, most cost effective, or least burdensome alternative that 
achieves the objectives of the rule before promulgating any proposed or 
final rule that includes a Federal mandate that may result in 
expenditures of more than $100 million (adjusted for inflation) in at 
least one year by State, local, and tribal governments, in the 
aggregate, or by the private sector. Each agency issuing a rule with 
relevant effects over that threshold must also seek input from State, 
local, and tribal governments. The current threshold after adjustment 
for inflation is $193 million, using the most current (2025) Implicit 
Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product. This proposed rule would 
not result in an expenditure in any year that meets or exceeds this 
amount.

VII. Tribal Consultation Statement

    Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian 
Tribal Governments, requires agencies to consult with Indian Tribes 
when



regulations have ``substantial direct effects on one or more Indian 
Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian 
Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between 
the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.'' Similarly, ACF's Tribal 
Consultation Policy says that consultation is triggered for any 
legislative proposal, new rule adoption, or other policy change that 
significantly affects Tribes, meaning there exists a reasonable 
presumption that it has or may have substantial direct effects on one 
or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal 
Government and Indian tribes, on the amount or duration of ACF program 
funding, on the delivery of ACF programs or services to one or more 
Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities 
between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.
    ACF conducted a Tribal consultation in August 2026, in which a 
panel on ``Reducing Administrative Burden'' was hosted. Commenters 
expressed general support for de-regulation and simplifying of 
regulatory text. This proposed rule begins another comment period by 
which we are requesting further input from Tribes on the proposed 
changes.

    Administrative practice and procedure, American Samoa, Grant

requirements.

CFR part 1336 as follows:

PART 1336--NATIVE AMERICAN PROGRAMS

0
1. The authority citation for part 1336 continues to read:

    Authority:  42 U.S.C. 618, 9858 et seq.


Sec.  1336.1  Definitions.

    For the purposes of this part, unless the context otherwise 
requires:
    Act means the Native American Programs Act of 1974, as amended (42 
U.S.C. 2991 et seq.).
    Alaskan Native means a person who is an Alaskan Indian, Eskimo, or 
Aleut, or any combination thereof. The term also includes any person 
who is regarded as an Alaskan Native by the Alaskan Native Village or 
group of which he or she claims to be a member and whose father or 
mother is (or, if deceased, was) regarded as an Alaskan Native by an 
Alaskan Native Village or group. The term includes any Alaskan Native 
as so defined, either or both of whose adoptive parents are not Alaskan 
Natives.
    American Indian or Indian means any individual who is a member or a 
descendant of a member of a North American tribe, band, Pueblo or other 
organized group of native people who are indigenous to the Continental 
United States, or who otherwise have a special relationship with the 
United States or a State through treaty, agreement, or some other form 
of recognition. This includes any individual who claims to be an Indian 
and who is regarded as such by the Indian tribe, group, band, or 
community of which he or she claims to be a member.
    ANA means the Administration for Native Americans
    Applicant means an organization which has applied for financial 
assistance from ANA.
    Budget period means the interval of time into which a project 
period is divided for budgetary and funding purposes, and for which a 
grant is made. A budget period usually lasts one year in a multi-year 
project period.
    Indian tribe means a distinct political community of Indians which 
exercises powers of self-government.
    Native American means American Indian, Indian, Native Hawaiian, and 
Alaskan Native, as defined in the Act, or in this section.
    Project period means, for discretionary grants and cooperative 
agreements, the total time for which the recipient's project or program 
is approved for support, including any extension, subject to the 
availability of funds, satisfactory progress, and a determination by 
HHS that continued funding is in the best interest of the Government.
    Recipient means an organization which has applied for financial 
assistance, and to which financial assistance is awarded under this 
Act. The term includes grantees and recipients of cooperative 
agreements.


Sec.  1336.2  Notice of ineligibility and appeals.

    (a) Notices of ineligibility. Upon a finding by the Commissioner 
that an organization that has applied for funding is ineligible or that 
the activities proposed by an organization are ineligible, the 
Commissioner shall inform the applicant of the decision stating the 
legal and factual grounds for the Commissioner's finding of 
ineligibility.
    (b) Appeals. An applicant that has had its application rejected 
either because it has been found ineligible or because the activities 
it proposes are ineligible for funding by the Commissioner of ANA, and 
recipients whose financial assistance has been suspended or terminated, 
or whose non-competing continuation applications for refunding have 
been denied, pursuant to the remedies for noncompliance at 2 CFR 
200.339-200.343, may appeal the Commissioner's ruling to the HHS 
Departmental Appeals Board through the process at 45 CFR part 16.


Sec.  1336.3   Financial and administrative requirements.

    (a) Cost sharing or matching.
    (1) Application. If an applicant or recipient wishes to request a 
waiver of the requirement for a 20 percent non-Federal matching share 
for financial assistance under sections 803, 804, and 805 of the Act, 
the following conditions must be met:
    (i) If an applicant for an initial award or an applicant for a non-
competing continuation award anticipates that it will be unable to meet 
the cost-sharing or matching requirement, the applicant may request a 
waiver of the 20 percent non-Federal matching share. It must include 
with its application for funding, the submission of a revised SF424A, a 
written justification that clearly explains why the applicant cannot 
provide the matching share including the amount of non-Federal share to 
be waived, and how it meets the criteria indicated in paragraph (a)(2) 
of this section. For an applicant for an initial award, or an applicant 
seeking a non-competing continuation award, a request for a waiver must 
be submitted at the time of the initial application or non-competing 
continuation (NCC) application.
    (ii) If a recipient is unable to contribute part or all of the 
required non-Federal matching share during a budget period due to an 
emergency situation the recipient may request a waiver of all or part 
of the requirement for a 20 percent non-Federal matching share. Any 
requests for an emergency waiver may be submitted at any time during a 
budget period as soon as the adverse effect is known to the recipient 
and must be submitted in accordance with the requirements specified in 
paragraph (a)(2) of this section.
    (2) Criteria. Both of the following criteria must be met for an 
applicant or recipient to be eligible for a waiver of the non-Federal 
matching requirement:
    (i) Applicant or recipient documents an inability to meet 
requirements of 42 U.S.C. 2991b(c) through an institutional audit if 
available, or a full disclosure of applicant's or recipient's total 
assets and liabilities.



    (ii) Applicants or recipients can document that reasonable efforts 
to obtain cash or in-kind contributions for the purposes of the project 
from third parties have been unsuccessful, including evidence and the 
results of such attempts.
    (3) Approval. For a waiver to be approved, ANA must determine that 
it will not prevent the award of other grants at levels it believes are 
desirable for the purposes of the program. Waiver of all or part of the 
non-Federal share shall apply only to the budget period for which 
application was made.
    (b) Maintenance of effort.
    (1) To be eligible for a waiver from the requirements of 42 U.S.C. 
2991b(d)(1), the applicant must demonstrate to ANA that the 
organization whose funds previously supported the project discontinued 
its support:
    (i) As a result of funding limitations; and
    (ii) Not as a result of an adverse evaluation of the project's 
purpose or the manner in which it was conducted; and
    (iii) Not because it anticipated that Federal funds would replace 
the original source of project funding.
    (2) In addition, the applicant must demonstrate in the request for 
a waiver that the maintenance of effort requirement would result in 
insurmountable hardship for the recipient or would otherwise be 
inconsistent with the purposes of this part.
    (c) Delegation of project operations.
    (1) Each subgrant awarded to a delegate agency must have specific 
prior approval by ANA. Such delegation must be formalized by written 
agreement.
    (2) The agreement must specify the activities to be performed by 
the delegate agency, the time schedule, the policies and procedures to 
be followed, the dollar limitations, and the costs allowed. The 
applicant must submit a budget for each delegate agency as part of its 
application.
    (d) Unallowable costs. ANA funds may not be used by recipients to 
purchase real property.
    (e) Office of the Chief Executive. The costs of salaries and 
expenses of the Office of Chief Executive of a federally recognized 
Indian tribal government (as defined in Sec.  75.2 of this title) are 
allowable, provided that such costs exclude any portion of salaries and 
expenses of the Office of Chief Executive that are a cost of general 
government and provided they are related to a project assisted under 
this part.

summary:
Notice is hereby given that a complaint was filed with the 
U.S. International Trade Commission on September 9, 2026, under section 
337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, on behalf of Vicor 
Corporation of Andover, Massachusetts. A supplement to the complaint 
was filed on September 10, 2026. The complaint, as supplemented, 
alleges violations of section 337 based



upon the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, 
and the sale within the United States after importation of certain 
vertical power delivery systems, components thereof, and computing 
systems containing the same by reason of the infringement of certain 
claims of U.S. Patent No. 10,903,734 (``the '734 patent''). The 
complaint further alleges that an industry in the United States exists 
as required by the applicable Federal Statute. The complainant requests 
that the Commission institute an investigation and, after the 
investigation, issue a limited exclusion order and cease and desist 
orders.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Authority for This Rulemaking

    The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is 
found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 
describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, 
Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's 
authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described 
in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, 
the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of 
the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the 
efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that 
authority as it amends the route structure to maintain the efficient 
flow of air traffic within the National Airspace System (NAS).

History

    This action is due to the decommissioning of the Charlotte, NC 
(CLT), VOR/DME; Foothills, SC (ODF), VOR/DME; Holston Mountain, TN 
(HMV), VORTAC; and the relocation of the Spartanburg, SC (SPA), VORTAC 
on December 24, 2026. The Charlotte VOR/DME, Foothills VOR/DME, and 
Holston Mountain VORTAC were candidate navigational aids (NAVAID) 
identified for discontinuance by the FAA's VOR MON program and listed 
in the Final Policy Statement, ``Provision of Navigation Services for 
the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen) Transition to 
Performance-Based Navigation (PBN) (Plan for Establishing a VOR Minimum 
Operational Network),'' published in the Federal Register on July 26, 
2016 (81 FR 48694), under Docket No. FAA-2011-1082.
    The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-2452 in the 
Federal Register (91 FR 10979; March 6, 2026), proposing to amend VOR 
Federal Airways V-16, V-35, V-37, V-53, V-133, V-136, V-143, V-259, V-
310, V-364, V-409, V-415, V-454, and V-605 in the eastern United 
States. Interested parties were invited to participate in this 
rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the 
FAA. Two public comments were received. One comment was in support of 
the proposal. The second comment objected generally to the 
decommissioning of VORs and NAVAIDs. However, that topic is outside the 
scope of this action, which does not itself direct the decommissioning 
of any NAVAIDs, but rather responds to decommissionings by making 
necessary modifications to affected routes.
    Subsequently, the FAA published a supplemental notice of proposed 
rulemaking (SNPRM) for Docket No. FAA-2026-2452 in the Federal Register 
(91 FR 46023; July 22, 2026), proposing additional amendments to VOR 
Federal Airways V-53, V-364, V-415, and V-605 in the eastern United 
States. Interested parties were invited to participate in this 
rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the 
FAA. One comment was received, but it was outside the scope of this 
action as it pertained generally to the decommissioning of VORs. As 
explained, this action does not direct any decommissionings, but only 
responds to them as necessary.

Differences From the NPRM and SNPRM

    In both the NPRM and SNPRM, the proposed amended legal description 
of VOR Federal Airway V-16 stated that the airspace within Restricted 
Areas R-5002A, R-5002C, R-5002D, and R-5002F is excluded ``during their 
times of use.'' To maintain consistency with the legal description 
language preexisting this rule, the FAA amended the legal description 
to state that the airspace within Restricted Areas R-5002A, R-5002C, R-
5002D, and R-5002F is excluded ``when active.'' This does not represent 
a substantive change to the proposed amendments. Accordingly, the FAA 
finds good cause that recirculating the proposal for additional notice 
and comment is unnecessary.

Incorporation by Reference

    Domestic VOR Federal Airways are published in paragraph 6010(a) of 
FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which 
is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This 
document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 
7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These 
updates will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. 
FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace 
areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly 
available as listed in the ADDRESSES section of this document.

of the Spartanburg, SC (SPA), VORTAC.

Regulatory Notices and Analyses

    The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an 
established body of technical regulations for which frequent and 
routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. 
It, therefore: (1) is not a ``significant regulatory action'' under 
Executive Order 12866; (2) is not a ``significant rule'' under DOT 
Order 2100.6B, ``Rulemaking and Guidance Procedure'' (March 10, 2025); 
and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from 
compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight 
rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled 
airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to 
operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when 
promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a 
substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the 
Regulatory Flexibility Act.

Environmental Review

    The FAA has determined that this rulemaking action of amending 
domestic VOR Federal Airways V-16, V-35, V-37, V-53, V-133, V-136, V-
143, V-259, V-310, V-364, V-409, V-415, V-454, and V-605 due to the

(ODF), VOR/DME; Holston Mountain, TN (HMV), VORTAC; and the relocation 
of the Spartanburg, SC (SPA), VORTAC qualifies for categorical 
exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act (42 U.S.C. 4321 
et seq.) and in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, FAA National 
Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures, paragraph B-2.5(a), 
which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review 
rulemaking actions that designate or modify classes of airspace areas, 
airways, routes, and reporting points (see 14 CFR part 71, Designation 
of Class A, B, C, D, and E Airspace Areas; Air Traffic Service Routes; 
and Reporting Points); and paragraph B-2.5(b), which categorically 
excludes from further environmental impact review ``Actions regarding 
establishment of jet routes and Federal airways (see 14 CFR 71.15, 
Designation of jet routes and VOR Federal airways) . . .'' As such, 
this action is not expected to result in any potentially significant 
environmental impacts. In accordance with the FAA's NEPA implementation 
policy and procedures regarding extraordinary circumstances, the FAA 
has reviewed this action for factors and circumstances in which a 
normally categorically excluded action may have a significant 
environmental impact requiring further analysis. The FAA has determined 
that no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of 
an



environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.

I. General Information

A. Executive Summary

    The Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP, codified at 40 CFR 
part 98) applies to certain industrial facilities that emit greenhouse 
gases (GHG) (primarily facilities emitting at least 25,000 metric tons 
of carbon dioxide equivalents (MTCO2e)), upstream suppliers 
of fossil fuels and industrial GHGs (such as carbon dioxide 
(CO2) and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs)), and industries that 
capture and sequester CO2 as a means of reducing 
CO2 emissions. Under the GHGRP, approximately 8,200 
facilities, suppliers, and CO2 injection sites submit data 
each year. Facilities calculate emissions using methodologies that are 
specified under the regulations and report data to the EPA using the 
electronic Greenhouse Gas Reporting Tool (e-GGRT). Annual reports 
covering emissions from the prior calendar year are due to the EPA by 
March 31st of each year. Once data are submitted, the EPA conducts a 
multi-step verification process to ensure reported data are accurate, 
complete, and consistent. If potential errors are identified, the EPA 
will notify the reporter, who can resolve the issue either by providing 
an acceptable response describing why the flagged issue is not an error 
or by correcting the flagged issue and resubmitting their annual GHG 
report.
    On September 16, 2025, the EPA issued a proposed rule that 
reconsidered the GHGRP (90 FR 44591, here in after referred to as the 
``GHGRP Reconsideration Proposal''). Among other things, the EPA 
proposed that no industries would need to submit annual GHG reports for 
calendar year 2025. The EPA also proposed to extend the deadline for 
submitting the calendar year 2025 report (i.e., the reporting year 2025 
reporting deadline) from March 31, 2026, to June 10, 2026. The EPA 
subsequently received over 50,000 comments on the GHGRP Reconsideration 
Proposal. On February 27, 2026, the EPA issued a final rule that 
extended the reporting deadline (hereinafter ``deadline'') for the 
GHGRP for reporting year 2025 from March 31, 2026, to October 30, 2026 
(91 FR 9712). In this action, the EPA is further extending the deadline 
for reporting year 2025 to March 10, 2027, to allow the EPA additional 
time to consider comments on the GHGRP Reconsideration Proposal and to 
take any final action before the further extended reporting year 2025 
deadline.

GHG reports pursuant to the GHGRP (40 CFR part 98). Entities affected 
by this action are owners or operators of facilities that are direct 
emitters or suppliers of GHGs or that sequester CO2 
underground. Regulated categories and entities include, but are not 
limited to, those listed in Table 1 of this preamble:

II. Background

A. What is the statutory authority for this action?

    The EPA is extending the regulatory deadline of the GHGRP for 
reporting year 2025, which was promulgated pursuant to Clean Air Act 
(CAA) section 114 and under the authority provided in CAA section 136 
for certain segments of the petroleum and natural gas source category 
(subpart W).
    The EPA's authority for the rulemaking procedures followed in this 
interim final rule is provided by Administrative Procedure Act (APA) 
section 553(b)(B), 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), which allows an agency to forego 
prior notice and comment ``when the agency for good cause finds (and 
incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefore in 
the rule issued) that notice and public procedure thereon are 
impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.'' This 
interim final rule is being issued without prior notice or opportunity 
for public comment because the EPA finds that prior notice and comment 
would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest under the 
current circumstances.
    As discussed in section II.B of this preamble, this interim final 
rule amends the GHGRP to extend the reporting year 2025 deadline from 
October 30, 2026, to March 10, 2027, to allow the EPA additional time 
to consider comments on the GHGRP Reconsideration Proposal and to take 
any final action on that proposal. The EPA finds that it is 
impracticable and contrary to the public interest for the Agency to 
provide notice and comment prior to issuing this interim final rule 
because there is not adequate time for the notice-and-comment process 
prior to the October 30, 2026 deadline that this interim final rule 
extends.
    Additionally, in a typical reporting year the Agency allows six 
weeks for reporters to work within the e-GGRT system to prepare and 
submit reports. Should the EPA later take final action on the GHGRP 
Reconsideration Proposal by retaining all or many existing reporting 
obligations, this revised deadline would allow regulated entities 
sufficient time to react to that final decision and work in the e-GGRT 
system to prepare and submit reports. Conversely, should the EPA later 
take final action on the GHGRP Reconsideration Proposal by finalizing 
all or most of the proposed rescissions and revisions, this revised 
deadline would allow regulated entities sufficient time to adjust their 
compliance efforts and avoid wasted time and effort.
    As previously stated, the EPA notes that extending the reporting 
deadline will also allow the Agency time if needed to prepare and 
release the e-GGRT system in advance of the revised



RY2025 reporting deadline. In addition, the EPA notes that the GHGRP 
requires facilities to submit reports electronically in a format 
specified by the Administrator.\1\ The EPA developed the e-GGRT for 
facilities to use to prepare and submit reports in accordance with this 
requirement. The e-GGRT system performs thousands of internal 
electronic validation and consistency checks, and appropriately 
safeguards information, including controlled unclassified information 
such as protects sensitive business information/confidential business 
information (SBI/CBI). Typically, the EPA would release e-GGRT six 
weeks in advance of the deadline so that facilities would have ample 
time to prepare and electronically submit reports prior to the 
deadline. As there is not adequate time for the EPA to have the 
electronic reporting tool prepared in time for the October 30, 2026, 
reporting year 2025 deadline that this rule extends, this also supports 
EPA's finding that it is impracticable and contrary to the public 
interest for the Agency to provide notice and comment prior to issuing 
this interim final rule.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ 40 CFR 98.5.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Furthermore, this action serves the public benefit by reducing risk 
of harm to regulated entities from inadvertently or hastily reporting 
erroneous or unnecessary information that could later be made public. 
This extension also ensures that entities subject to the GHGRP could 
benefit from any burden reduction revisions that the EPA may make for 
the 2025 reporting year in any separate final action following the 
GHGRP Reconsideration Proposal and/or have adequate time to prepare and 
submit reporting year 2025 reports.
    This final rule is effective immediately upon publication. Section 
553(d)(1) of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1), 
provides that final rules shall not become effective until 30 days 
after publication in the Federal Register ``except . . . a substantive 
rule which grants or recognizes an exemption or relieves a 
restriction.'' The purpose of this provision is to ``give affected 
parties a reasonable time to adjust their behavior before the final 
rule takes effect.'' Omnipoint Corp. v. Fed. Commc'n Comm'n, 78 F.3d 
620, 630 (D.C. Cir. 1996); see also United States v. Gavrilovic, 551 
F.2d 1099, 1104 (8th Cir. 1977). However, when the agency grants or 
recognizes an exemption or relieves a restriction, affected parties do 
not need a reasonable time to adjust because the effect is not adverse. 
Absent this action, regulated entities would have insufficient time to 
prepare and submit annual reports in the e-GGRT system, and by 
extending the deadline, this action relieves that restriction. 
Therefore, the normal 30-day minimum period between this action's dates 
of publication and effectiveness is not required. Accordingly, the EPA 
is making this rule effective immediately upon publication.

B. Description of Final Regulatory Amendments and Rationale

    In this final action, the EPA is amending subpart A (General 
Provisions) at 40 CFR 98.3(b)(6) to extend the reporting year 2025 
deadline to March 10, 2027. As explained in the GHGRP Reconsideration 
Proposal, the deadline is set in the regulation, and the only way that 
the EPA can alter the deadline for any year is through a regulatory 
amendment. This extension only applies to the reporting year 2025 
deadline. This action will further extend the reporting year 2025 
deadline to allow the EPA additional time to consider comments on the 
GHGRP Reconsideration Proposal and to take any final action before the 
further extended reporting year 2025 deadline of March 10, 2027. This 
extension ensures that entities subject to the GHGRP could benefit from 
any burden reduction revisions that the EPA may make for the 2025 
reporting year in any separate final actions following the GHGRP 
Reconsideration Proposal and/or have adequate time to prepare and 
submit reporting year 2025 reports. Additionally, at this point the EPA 
cannot have the electronic reporting tool prepared in time for the 
October 30, 2026, reporting year 2025 deadline, consistent with the 
GHGRP requirements that facilities submit reports electronically in a 
format specified by the Administrator.\2\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ 40 CFR 98.5.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

III. Request for Comment

    As explained in section II.A of this preamble, the EPA finds good 
cause to issue this interim final rule without prior notice or 
opportunity for public comment. However, the EPA is providing an 
opportunity for the public to comment on the EPA's action to extend the 
deadline under the GHGRP for reporting year 2025 data from October 30, 
2026, to March 10, 2027. The EPA intends to review comments received 
and consider whether this action should be revised, if appropriate, in 
response to comments received. If the EPA takes additional action on 
this interim final rule, as described in Section IV.L of this preamble, 
the Administrator has determined that subsequent final action will be 
subject to the requirements of CAA section 307(d), pursuant to section 
307(d)(1)(V).

IV. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews

    Additional information about these statutes and Executive Orders 
can be found at www.epa.gov/laws-regulations/laws-and-executive-orders.

A. Executive Order 12866: Regulatory Planning and Review and Executive 
Order 13563: Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review

B. Executive Order 14192: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation

C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)

    This action does not impose any new information collection burden 
under the PRA. OMB has previously approved the information collection 
requirements contained in the existing regulation and has assigned OMB 
control number 2060-0629, OMB control number 2060-0748, and OMB control 
number 2060-0751. This interim final rule extends the deadline for 
submitting annual GHG reports for reporting year 2025 data from October 
30, 2026, to March 10, 2027.

D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)

    I certify that this final action will not have a significant 
economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the 
RFA. In making this determination, the EPA concludes that the impact of

have therefore concluded that this action will relieve regulatory

E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)

    This action does not contain an unfunded mandate as described in 
UMRA, 2 U.S.C. 1531-1538 and does not significantly or uniquely affect 
small governments. This action imposes no enforceable duty on any 
state, local, or Tribal governments. Requirements for the private

F. Executive Order 13132: Federalism

    This action does not have federalism implications. It will not have

    The EPA interprets Executive Order 13045 as applying only to those

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: 

Authority for this Rulemaking

    The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is 
found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 
describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, 
Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's 
authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described 
in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, 
the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of 
the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the 
efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that 
authority as it amends the coordinates for restricted areas R-5301, R-
5302B, and R-5302C in North Carolina to close small gaps and eliminate 
overlaps between the restricted areas.

Background

    The FAA recently conducted a review of restricted areas R-5301, R-
5302B, and R-5302C, revealing minor discrepancies in the points 
defining the areas. The FAA identified small gaps and overlap points 
based on the coordinates used in the boundary descriptions, which 
necessitates this amendment to accurately align the restricted areas. 
Moreover, the U.S. Marine Corps, the using agency, requested that the 
FAA amend the coordinates to eliminate these gaps and overlaps.

Good Cause for Bypassing Notice and Comment

    Under 5 U.S.C. 553, federal agencies engaged in informal rulemaking 
must provide the public with a notice of proposed rulemaking and an 
opportunity for public participation. However, 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) 
exempts a rule from these requirements ``when the agency for good cause 
finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons 
therefor in the rules issued) that notice and public procedure thereon 
are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.'' 
Courts have construed these exceptions narrowly, but have nonetheless 
accepted determinations of good cause that notice and comment is 
unnecessary in ``those situations in which the administrative rule is a 
routine determination, insignificant in nature and impact, and 
inconsequential to the industry and to the public.'' See Mack Trucks, 
Inc. v. EPA, 682 F.3d 87, 94 (D.C. Cir. 2012). This action consists of 
minor technical amendments only. It does not affect the external 
boundaries or change the altitudes, time of designation, operating 
requirements, or activities conducted in the restricted areas. 
Therefore, the FAA finds good cause that notice and public procedure 
under 5 U.S.C. 553(b) are unnecessary.

The Rule

    This action amends 14 CFR part 73 by updating the coordinates used 
in the boundary descriptions to accurately align restricted areas R-
5301, R-5302B, and R-5302C, eliminating gaps and overlaps. The first 
coordinate listed in R-5301 is changed from ``lat. 36[deg]04'56'' N, 
long. 76[deg]16'47'' W'' to ``lat. 36[deg]04'56'' N, long. 
76[deg]16'48'' W''. Two tie-in coordinates are added to R-5302B, ``lat. 
36[deg]04'23'' N, long. 076[deg]20'59'' W'' to ``lat. 36[deg]04'56'' N, 
long. 076[deg]16'48'' W'', to eliminate overlap and provide coincidence 
with R-5301. Finally, an additional tie-in coordinate is added to R-
5302B and R-5302C, ``lat. 36[deg]00'01'' N, long. 76[deg]14'29'' W'', 
to eliminate overlap and provide coincidence with R-5302A.

Regulatory Notices and Analyses

    The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an 
established body of technical regulations for which frequent and 
routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. 
It, therefore: (1) is not a ``significant regulatory action'' under 
Executive Order 12866; (2) is not a ``significant rule'' under DOT 
Order 2100.6B, ``Rulemaking and Guidance Procedures'' (March 10, 2025); 
and (3) is anticipated to have a minimal economic impact, as it only 
affects air traffic procedures and air navigation, resulting in at most 
de minimis costs from minor rerouting of flights. Since this is a 
routine matter that only affects air traffic procedures with de minimis 
impact on operators, it is certified that this rule, when promulgated, 
does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of 
small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

Environmental Review

    The FAA has determined that this action of making an administrative 
change of updating the coordinates used in the boundary descriptions to 
accurately align restricted areas R-5301, R-5302B, and R-5302C, NC, 
eliminating gaps and overlaps, qualifies for categorical exclusion 
under the National Environmental Policy Act (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.) 
and in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, FAA National Environmental 
Policy Act Implementing Procedures, paragraph B-2.5 (d) Modification of 
the technical description of special use airspace (SUA) that does not 
alter the dimensions, altitudes, or times of designation of the 
airspace (such as changes in designation of the controlling or using 
agency, or correction of typographical errors). As such, this action is 
not expected to result in any potentially significant environmental 
impacts. In accordance with Appendix B, paragraph B-1 of FAA Order 
1050.1G regarding Extraordinary Circumstances, the FAA has reviewed 
this action for factors and circumstances in which a normally 
categorically excluded action may have a significant environmental 
impact requiring further analysis. Accordingly, the FAA has determined 
that no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of 
an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.

    Title: Use of Prenotification Negative Option Plans, 16 CFR part 
425.
    OMB Control Number: 3084-0104.
    Type of Review: Reinstatement of and extension of a previously 
approved collection.

Background

    On February 13, 2024, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) 
approved an extension of the information collections associated with 
the version of the Negative Option Rule effective at the time.\1\ On 
November 15, 2024, the Commission published a final rule (``2024 
Rule'') amending the Negative Option Rule.\2\ On November 18, 2024, the 
OMB approved the additional information collections associated with the 
final rule amendments through November 30, 2027.\3\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ Extension without change of a currently approved collection, 
ICR Ref. No. 202307-3084-005, OMB Control Number 3084-0104, 02/13/
2024, available at https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202307-3084-005.
    \2\ FTC, Final Rule: Negative Option Rule, 89 FR 90476 (Nov. 15, 
2024).
    \3\ Revision of a currently approved collection, ICR Ref. No. 
202411-3084-002, OMB Control Number 3084-0104, 11/18/2024, available 
at https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202411-3084-002.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    On July 8, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit 
vacated the 2024 Rule.\4\ On February 12, 2026, the Commission issued a 
final rule revising the Negative Option Rule to restore it in the form 
it existed before the 2024 Rule became effective.\5\ Thus, only the 
information collections associated with the OMB's February 13, 2024 
approval of an extension for information collections are now in effect 
and need to be extended for three additional years.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \4\ Custom Commc'ns, Inc. v. FTC, 142 F.4th 1060, 1074 (8th Cir. 
2025).
    \5\ 91 FR 6507 (Feb. 12, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The Negative Option Rule, as now restored, governs the operation of 
prenotification subscription plans. Under these types of plans--which 
can include things such as a book-of-the-month club, food-of-the-month 
club, or clothing-items-of-the-month club--a seller provides a consumer 
with automatic shipments of merchandise unless the consumer 
affirmatively notifies the seller they do not want the shipment. The 
Rule requires that a seller notify a member that they will 
automatically ship merchandise to the member and bill the member for 
the merchandise if the subscriber fails to expressly reject the 
merchandise beforehand within a prescribed time. The Rule protects 
consumers by: (1) requiring that promotional materials disclose the 
terms of membership clearly and conspicuously; and (2) establishing 
procedures for the administration of such ``negative option'' plans.
    Affected Public: Sellers of prenotification subscription plans.
    Estimated Annual Burden Hours: 2,500 hours.
    Estimated Annual Labor Costs: $160,755 (solely related to labor 
costs).
    Estimated Annual Non-Labor Costs: $0 or de minimis.
    As required by section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA, 44 U.S.C. 
3506(c)(2)(A), the FTC is providing this opportunity for public comment 
before requesting that OMB reinstate and extend the clearance for the 
information collection requirements contained in the Negative Option 
Rule.

Burden Statement

    Estimated Annual Burden Hours: 2,500.
    Based on industry input, FTC staff estimates that no more than 25 
sellers are subject to the disclosure requirements contained in the 
Rule.\6\ FTC staff further estimates that each seller will require 
annually about 100 hours to comply with the Rule's disclosure 
requirements. This yields a total annual burden of 2,500 hours (25 
sellers x 100 hours).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \6\ In 2023, FTC staff estimated 25 sellers were subject to the 
Rule's disclosure requirements based on industry input. 88 FR 59922 
(Aug. 30, 2023). That estimate reflected a severe decline from 75 
sellers estimated in 2020. 85 FR 46628 (Aug. 3, 2020). FTC staff 
anticipates that the number of sellers subject to the Rule's 
requirements continues to decline as firms offering prenotification 
negative option plans exit the market and other firms increasingly 
adopt a subscription-based approach without a prenotification 
feature. See, e.g., Sam Spratford, Subscription Addiction, 
Publishers Weekly (May 8, 2026), https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/by-topic/industry-news/publisher-news/article/100363-subscription-addiction.html (last visited Sept. 15, 2026) (noting 
book-of-the-month sellers offering monthly subscription without 
prenotification negative option feature); Jordan Valinsky, Columbia 
House--yes, it still exists--is going out of business, CNN (Aug. 19, 
2026), https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/19/media/columbia-house-shut-down 
(last visited Sept. 9, 2026) (reporting that Columbia House, a 
pioneer of product-of-the-month plans with prenotification negative 
option feature, is ceasing operations).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Estimated Annual Cost Burden: $160,755 (solely related to labor 
costs).
    Based on recent data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the mean 
hourly wage for advertising and promotion managers is approximately 
$74.18 per hour; \7\ compensation for office and administrative support 
personnel is approximately $24.79 per hour.\8\ Assuming that managers 
perform the bulk of the work, and clerical personnel perform associated 
tasks (e.g., placing advertisements and responding to inquiries about 
offerings or prices), the total cost to the industry for the Rule's 
information collection requirements would be approximately $160,755 
[(80 hours managerial time x 25 sellers x $74.18 per hour) + (20 hours 
clerical time x 25 sellers x $24.79 per hour)].
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \7\ See Occupational Employment and Wages--May 2025, Table 1, at 
https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm (mean hourly wage 
rate for advertising and promotion managers).
    \8\ See id. (mean hourly wage rate for office and administrative 
support occupations).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Because the Rule has been in effect since 1974, the vast majority 
of the negative option sellers have no current start-up costs. For new 
sellers entering the market, the costs associated with the Rule's 
disclosure requirements, beyond the additional labor costs discussed 
above, are de minimis. Negative option sellers already have access to 
the ordinary office equipment necessary to comply with the Rule. 
Similarly, the Rule imposes few, if any, printing and distribution 
costs. The required disclosures generally constitute only a small 
addition to the advertising for negative option plans. Because printing 
and distribution expenditures are incurred to market the product 
regardless of the Rule, adding the required disclosures results in 
marginal incremental expense.



Request for Comment

    Pursuant to section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA, the FTC invites 
comments on: (1) whether the proposed collection of information is 
necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, 
including whether the information will be practically useful; (2) the 
accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed 
collection of information, including whether the methodology and 
assumptions used are valid; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, 
and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to 
minimize the burden of the collection of information.
    For the FTC to consider a comment, we must receive it on or before
