Non-Adversarial Interview (Dec. 13, 2024).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    USCIS further instructed its adjudicators that it was no longer 
necessary to ask additional detailed questions to identify and explore 
inadmissibility grounds, including security-related inadmissibility 
grounds, absent a clear indication of a concern. For example, per 
internal guidance, if an alien was transported across a border by 
smugglers, or an alien's home was attacked by an armed group, absent 
additional information in the record or in country conditions 
information indicating possible security-related concerns with respect 
to these incidents (e.g., material support to a terrorist 
organization), officers were not required to follow up or explore if 
the individual was potentially inadmissible, or if these interactions 
raised other concerns. Officers were discouraged from investigating 
potential concerns or delving into an applicant's background or past 
experiences unless referral documents, such as the U.N. High 
Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Resettlement Registration Form (RRF), 
explicitly noted concerns. In other words, officers were discouraged 
from seeking or obtaining additional information beyond what was 
provided in the record, already provided by non-U.S. government 
entities, such as UNHCR or the Resettlement Support Center.
    With respect to country of origin information (COI), rather than 
using COI to inform their interviews and adjudications, USCIS, under 
the Biden administration, trained refugee officers that for certain 
populations, they could rely on COI ``profiles'' (e.g., ``Venezuelans 
who oppose the government of Venezuela'') to establish various elements 
of refugee eligibility once an alien indicated they were part of a 
group of individuals for which COI supported a finding of well-founded 
fear. Officers shifted from individualized, more detailed assessments 
of refugee eligibility to confining interviews to review of the Form I-
590 and an alien's affirmation of belonging to a designated group 
(e.g., Rohingya), rather than exploring and evaluating an alien's 
unique experiences of past persecution or fears. In doing so, they 
bypassed in-depth interviews exploring an alien's background, 
experiences of past persecution in their home country, affiliations and 
relationships, if the alien in fact had a well-founded fear of future 
persecution in their home country, and other relevant details.
    In 2017, President Trump issued Executive Order 13769, Protecting 
the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States, 
restricting entry to the U.S. by certain foreign nationals and 
temporarily suspending the USRAP.\35\ During this suspension of refugee 
processing agencies were directed to review and strengthen vetting 
procedures. As a result of the review, USCIS clarified and confirmed 
that as a matter of policy, officers interviewing refugee applicants 
were required to elicit sufficient information to make a determination 
on both the past persecution and well-founded fear of future 
persecution claims. Gathering testimony on both past persecution and 
well-founded fear ensures a thorough and accurate evaluation of the 
applicant's eligibility and prevents overlooking critical facts that 
could substantiate, or call into question, their claim. For example, 
thorough elicitation of testimony regarding past and future harm may 
help identify inconsistencies and potential fraud by allowing 
adjudicators to probe the alien's narrative for credibility by ensuring 
it is internally consistent and consistent with statements the alien 
may have provided to processing partners prior to interview. Most 
importantly, it requires officers to probe more thoroughly into an 
applicant's background and experiences, helping to establish his or her 
identity, and further ensure that the correct decision is made in his 
or her case. Although eliciting testimony about both past persecution 
and well-founded fear helps develop a fuller picture of the alien and 
better assess eligibility--ensuring that protection is granted to those 
who genuinely qualify under the law--during the Biden administration 
this policy was rescinded. Refugee officers were no longer required to 
elicit testimony on both past persecution and well-founded fear claims, 
and were instead instructed to only pursue one or the other, once one 
had been established, precluding opportunities to identify critical 
information and concerns related to an alien's eligibility.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35 \ Protecting the Nation From Foreign Terrorist Entry Into 
the United States, 82 FR 8977 (Feb. 1, 2017).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition to the relaxed requirements for principal refugee 
applicants, USCIS changed policies regarding derivative applicants. The 
first Trump administration issued guidance emphasizing the importance 
of eliciting testimony from derivative I-590 applicants apart from the 
principal refugee applicant to further explore potential national 
security, identity, inadmissibility, and credibility issues. However, 
USCIS subsequently rescinded this guidance under the Biden 
administration and provided refugee officers the sole discretion on 
when to interview derivative applicants separately. The purpose of this 
change was to reduce the amount of questions and time spent with 
derivatives in an interview, thus not thoroughly vetting and 
identifying potential issues of all members of a case who, upon case 
approval, were eligible to travel to the United States as refugees 
along with the principal applicant.
    Compounding the issue, marriage guidance under the previous 
administration relaxed the criteria for adding a derivative spouse to a 
case. Although intended to accommodate couples who genuinely acted as 
spouses but could not formalize their union due to local restrictions, 
the standards were misapplied, allowing individuals with minimal or 
short-term connections to be classified as spouses and included on 
cases. This practice, combined with lowered interview standards and 
increasingly brief, less detailed case reviews in the name of 
streamlining, increased the risk of approving applicants with only 
tenuous relationships with the principal applicant.
    In parallel with this minimized focus on eliciting substantive 
information to comprehensively understand an alien's background and 
identify potential issues of concern, the increased interview quotas 
made it more difficult for officers to explore important issues, fully 
probe the alien's credibility, and still meet their productivity 
expectations. During the first Trump administration, USCIS reduced the 
number of refugee interviews conducted per day per officer for certain 
cases to allow for further exploration of potential national security, 
inadmissibility, and credibility issues at interviews for refugee 
adjudications. Notwithstanding, USCIS under the Biden administration, 
in their effort to streamline interviews and increase the volume of 
refugee cases that could be processed, increased the number of cases an 
officer was expected to interview and adjudicate in a day for certain 
cases, again pressuring officers to at times scale back interviews to 
comply with the expectations.
    This shift away from in-depth, thorough interviews in order to 
streamline and expedite admission of aliens to the United States as 
refugees shut down important lines of questioning to identify potential 
national security, public safety, and other concerns to accurately 
assess eligibility, illustrating the program's emphasis on the volume 
of refugee case completions rather than the quality of interviews or 
the integrity of



adjudications. Refugee officers potentially missed vital information 
that could impact an applicant's eligibility, including issues related 
to fraud, public safety, and national security, and discretionary 
factors. USCIS, under the Biden administration, failed to fulfill its 
responsibility to ensure that its officers thoroughly assessed 
applicants, potentially resulting in an influx of ineligible aliens 
into the country that may pose a risk to the national interests of the 
United States.
    Moreover, USCIS under the Biden administration decreased 
requirements for supervisory review of refugee cases by only requiring 
review of the assessment in lieu of reviewing the entire case contents. 
This limited supervisor oversight to ensure cases were thoroughly and 
accurately adjudicated, increased the risk that important information 
about an alien was overlooked.
    An overarching desire to approve as many refugee cases as possible 
to meet the refugee ceiling set by the Biden administration contributed 
to a culture in which the expectation appeared to be to approve cases, 
even where egregious concerns may have existed. For instance, in one 
processing location, a number of aliens identified as having defrauded 
the U.S. government or submitting fraudulent documentation were found 
inadmissible pursuant to the INA provisions related to fraud and 
misrepresentation. Despite clear evidence of misrepresentation, 
including falsification of identity and key information relevant to 
their access to the USRAP, USCIS almost universally approved waivers of 
the misrepresentation or fraud. This pattern demonstrates a troubling 
disregard for the integrity of the refugee program, as individuals who 
had already demonstrated a willingness to engage in fraud and 
misrepresentation of their identities to U.S. government officials, 
were nonetheless permitted to proceed with resettlement to the United 
States, undermining both the security and credibility of the admissions 
process.
    The persistent presence of individuals, both in the United States 
and overseas, attempting to exploit and defraud the U.S. humanitarian 
programs, poses risks to national security, public safety, and the 
integrity of the U.S. immigration system. Historically, DHS and State 
have identified, through investigations, fraud concerns among the 
special humanitarian access categories. For example, in January 2021, 
DHS and State suspended the Iraqi Direct Access P-2 Program, following 
an extensive investigation carried out by the State Diplomatic Security 
Service and the DHS Office of the Inspector General, which uncovered a 
fraud scheme related to the program.\36\ According to the indictment 
and statement of facts agreed to by one of the three defendants in the 
criminal case against the individuals:

IV. Discussion of Interim Final Rule

    Previous administrations' prioritization of the admissions of large 
numbers of refugees over homeland



security blatantly overlooked essential components of eligibility and 
put at risk the national security, public safety and other interests of 
the U.S. citizenry. Safeguarding national security and public safety 
remains the foremost priority of the country's immigration programs, 
taking precedence over numerical admission targets. The agency stands 
committed to conducting rigorous vetting of all aliens and to the 
detection and prevention of fraud and other serious threats, ensuring 
the safety of all Americans prior to admission of an alien to the 
United States.
    Accordingly, this IFR shortens the amount of time that refugees are 
provided to respond to a NOIT in order to ensure that terminations of 
refugee status can occur as expeditiously as possible to protect 
national security and public safety, given the risks created by the 
deficient vetting described above in Section III.C. Under this IFR, 
refugees will continue to receive a NOIT, which will specify DHS's 
intent to terminate their refugee status based on a determination that 
they did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission. DHS 
will provide the specific reason or reasons why USCIS found the refugee 
failed to meet the refugee definition at the time of admission (e.g., 
failure to establish that past harm experienced was serious enough to 
rise to the level of persecution, a determination that the alien's harm 
was not on account of a protected ground, failure to provide credible 
testimony as to any or all of the elements of the refugee definition, 
etc.). However, this rule will provide such aliens with ten days 
(rather than 30 days) to respond (provide documentary evidence or 
indicate a desire to provide oral evidence) if they choose. If the 
deadline to reply to the NOIT passes without a response, the refugee is 
considered to have forfeited his or her right to rebut the allegations 
in the NOIT, and DHS will terminate his or her refugee status.
    By regulation, the response period begins either upon personal 
service of the NOIT directly to the alien or, if sent by mail, upon 
mailing of the NOIT.\52\ When calculating the response deadline, all 
days, including Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays, are 
counted.\53\ However, if the final day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or 
federal holiday, the deadline is extended to the next business day.\54\ 
Per 8 CFR 103.8(b), if the notice is served by mail, three days are 
added to the response period, with service considered complete on the 
date the notice is mailed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \52\ 8 CFR 103.8.
    \53\ See 8 CFR 1.2 (definition of ``day'').
    \54\ Id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS's foremost priority is the safety and security of American 
citizens and residents. At the same time, DHS is committed to ensuring 
that refugees who receive a NOIT are afforded a meaningful opportunity 
to respond or provide a rebuttal. To enhance mail service reliability 
and afford refugees the full response period, DHS will utilize express 
delivery service providers, which guarantee a three-day delivery window 
and offer tracking and confirmation of both the NOIT's departure from 
DHS custody and its delivery to the recipient.\55\ This approach 
ensures that refugees receive their NOIT promptly and can exercise 
their right to respond. The NOIT will be dated on the day it is mailed, 
and the 10-day response period for the refugee will begin from that 
date. If the refugee wishes to request an opportunity to provide oral 
testimony in lieu of responding to each point or points in the NOIT, 
such a request would be considered a timely response by DHS. As 
explained above, in accordance with 8 CFR 103.8(b), when a notice is 
served by mail, three additional days are added to the response period, 
with service considered complete on the date the notice is mailed. 
Therefore, applicants who are mailed notices are afforded a total of 13 
days to respond, accounting for this regulatory provision.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \55\ See, e.g., https://www.fedex.com/en-us/shipping/3-day-express-saver-shipping.html.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Reducing the 30-day response timeframe for NOITs issued in refugee 
terminations to a 10-day response timeframe allows DHS to take swifter 
action in cases where aliens did not meet the definition of a refugee 
when admitted to the United States. USCIS needs the ability to 
terminate refugee status in such cases in order to more quickly begin 
the removal process for aliens who should never have been admitted to 
the United States as refugees in the first place, including aliens 
similarly situated to those discussed above in Section III.C, who also 
pose a national security or public safety risk. While termination of 
refugee status is not a precondition for initiation of removal 
proceedings, the termination of refugee status gives DHS a statutory 
basis for removal, and in some cases, no other removal grounds apply, 
so this termination is needed.\56\ Accordingly, promptly terminating 
refugee status in cases where the alien was clearly ineligible at the 
time of admission facilitates DHS's ability to process the alien for 
removal under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the INA, and to remove the 
alien if they do not qualify for relief from removal.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \56\ In Matter of Smriko, 23 I&N Dec. 836 (BIA 2005), the Board 
of Immigration Appeals held that termination of an alien's refugee 
status under section 207 of the INA is not a precondition to the 
initiation of section 240 removal proceedings, but only because the 
alien in that case was removable on the basis of certain criminal 
conduct that independently qualified him for removal irrespective of 
refugee status. See id. at 837-838; compare Matter of D-K-, 25 I&N 
Dec. 761 (BIA 2012) (affirming that DHS need not terminate refugee 
status prior to commencing section 240 removal proceedings but 
determining that the alien was not removable under the grounds 
charged by DHS). On January 21, 2026, the DHS Secretary formally 
referred the BIA's decision in Matter of D-K- to the Attorney 
General for review. In that referral, DHS asked the Attorney General 
to vacate the BIA's decision insofar as it erroneously holds that 
aliens admitted as refugees may not be taken back into DHS custody 
under section 209(a)(l) of the INA, charged with inadmissibility 
under section 212(a) of the INA, and promptly removed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    More broadly, timely termination of their refugee status is 
critical to the integrity of the country's immigration programs, 
considering the risks they may pose to the United States. As USCIS 
continues to encounter aliens admitted as refugees who did not meet the 
definition of refugee at the time of admission, termination of refugee 
status in as prompt and efficient manner as possible ensures USCIS can 
best protect the safety and security of Americans and continue 
complying with E.O.s 14161 and 14163. By shortening the 30-day period 
for an alien to respond to a NOIT to 10 days, USCIS is exercising its 
authority to expeditiously terminate the status of refugees who did not 
meet the refugee definition at the time of their admission to the 
United States. Streamlining the termination process additionally 
ensures that ineligible aliens who were erroneously allowed to enter 
the United States as refugees lose their authorization to work in as 
timely a manner as possible since termination of refugee status also 
results in termination of employment authorization.
    DHS believes that reducing the NOIT response period from 30 days to 
10 days maintains adequate procedural safeguards for aliens by 
affording them an opportunity to respond to the NOIT while also 
balancing the government's interests in national security and public 
safety and in protecting the integrity of the refugee program. The NOIT 
will inform the alien the basis for termination and explain that they 
may submit evidence to contest termination, and/or request an 
interview. An alien does not need to submit evidence or a full response 
within the 10 days, and may instead opt for an interview, but must make 
the interview request to USCIS within the response period.



Aliens who receive a NOIT under the proposed process therefore will 
continue to receive a meaningful opportunity to respond to the 
allegations in the notice--the alien can submit a written response to 
the NOIT within the deadline and/or request an interview with USCIS 
where their refugee claim can be heard. The abbreviated time period to 
respond to the NOIT will in turn allow the government to more 
efficiently process cases where aliens did not meet the refugee 
definition at the time of admission to the United States, and who were 
from the outset, never eligible for the benefit they received. Instead 
of waiting 30 days for an alien to respond to a NOIT before scheduling 
an interview if requested by the alien or taking other action, this 
rule will allow USCIS to act as soon as 10 days after service of the 
NOIT. For aliens who do not respond timely, the 10-day response period 
will allow USCIS to finalize termination much more quickly. 
Furthermore, each alien whose refugee status is terminated will be 
processed under INA sections 235, 240, or 241 and may seek other forms 
of relief or protection from removal as permitted in those proceedings. 
For example, aliens in section 240 removal proceedings may seek other 
forms of relief in a hearing before an immigration judge where the 
interests of the U.S. Government are properly represented by an 
attorney from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Office 
of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA).
    The regulatory amendment being made in this IFR is clearly 
authorized by INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4), which gives 
discretion to the Secretary to ``prescribe'' regulations governing 
termination of aliens who were ``not in fact a refugee within the 
meaning of section 101(a)(42) . . . at the time of the alien's 
admission.''

V. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements

A. Administrative Procedures Act (APA)

    DHS is issuing this IFR without prior notice or public procedure 
because DHS is invoking the ``good cause'' and foreign affairs 
exceptions of the APA. See 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1), (b)(B). For the same 
reasons, a delayed effective date of no less than 30 days is not 
required under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3). DHS has also considered potential 
reliance interests and discusses them below.
a. Good Cause
    An agency may forgo notice-and-comment rulemaking and a delayed 
effective date when the agency ``for good cause finds . . . that notice 
and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or 
contrary to the public interest.'' See 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). Likewise, 
section 553(d)'s requirement of 30-day advance publication may be 
waived by the agency for good cause found and published with the rule. 
See 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3).
    The ``impracticable'' prong of the good cause exception excuses 
notice and comment in emergency situations, or where the delay caused 
by the APA's notice-and-comment procedures would result in serious harm 
to life, property, or an immediate threat to public safety.\57\ 
Although the good cause exception is ``narrowly construed and only 
reluctantly countenanced,'' \58\ it is an important safety valve to be 
used where delay caused by notice and comment would do real harm (even 
absent an emergency situation).\59\ An agency may find that advance 
notice and comment or a delayed effective date is ``impracticable'' 
when undertaking such procedure would impede due and timely execution 
of an important agency function.\60\ For example, courts have explained 
that notice-and-comment rulemaking may be impracticable where, for 
instance, air travel security would be unable to address threats posing 
a ``possible imminent hazard to aircraft, persons and property within 
the United States;'' \61\ if a rule was of life-saving importance to 
mine workers in the event of a mine explosion; \62\ if public safety is 
jeopardized; \63\ or in case of an urgency related to an international 
crisis and national security.\64\ Impracticability is inevitably a 
fact-or-context dependent inquiry.\65\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \57\ See Nat. Res. Def. Council v. Nat'l Highway Traffic Safety 
Admin, 894 F.3d 95, 114 (2d Cir. 2018); see Jifry v. FAA, 370 F.3d 
1174, 1179 (D.C. Cir. 2004) (finding good cause for the promulgation 
of security rules in the aftermath of 9/11 terrorist attacks); see 
also Util. Solid Waste Activities Grp. v. EPA, 236 F.3d 749 (D.C. 
Cir. 2001).
    \58\ See State of New Jersey v. EPA, 626 F.2d 1038, 1045 (D.C.

    The good cause exception may also apply when affording prior notice 
and comment would be contrary to the public interest. See 5 U.S.C. 
553(b)(B). The question is not whether dispensing with notice and 
comment would be contrary to the public interest, but whether providing 
notice and comment would be contrary to the public interest.\66\ This 
prong is met when the ordinary procedures under the APA--generally 
presumed to serve in the public interest--would in fact harm the 
interest of the public.\67\ The exception is appropriately invoked when 
the timing and the disclosure requirement of the usual procedures would 
defeat the purpose of the proposal and harm the public interest.\68\ 
This prong of the good cause exception is closely related to the 
impracticable prong.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \66\ Mack Trucks, Inc. v. EPA, 682 F.3d 87, 95 (D.C. Cir. 2012).
    \67\ Id.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For the reasons explained below, DHS believes that, based on the 
totality of the circumstances, it has good cause to bypass ordinary 
notice-and-comment procedures because following these public procedures 
is impracticable and moving expeditiously is in the best interest of 
the public. As discussed in the preamble, streamlining the process to 
terminate refugee status in cases where the alien is determined to not 
have met the refugee definition at the time of admission to the United 
States is consistent with DHS's mission and responsibilities to ensure 
national security and public safety, and to



protect the immigration system from fraud and exploitation. DHS is 
immediately taking measures to implement a process that changes the 30-
day response timeframe in refugee termination cases to 10 days, thereby 
expediting terminations in a manner that averts harm to the public.
    Engaging in the APA's notice-and-comment requirement under 5 U.S.C. 
553(b) would impede DHS's duties as outlined in E.O. 14161, requiring 
that sufficient safeguards are in place to prevent any refugee from 
being admitted to the United States without undergoing stringent 
vetting, and E.O. 14163, permitting admission of refugees on a case-by-
case basis only so long as it is determined to be in the national 
interest and the alien does not pose a threat to the security and 
welfare of the United States.
    Thus, in accordance with President Trump's policy determinations 
related to foreign nationals, DHS is taking, without delay, immediate 
action to ensure that aliens who did not meet the refugee definition at 
the time of admission to the United States are vetted and screened to 
the maximum degree possible to ensure they do not receive significant 
benefits, including employment authorization, permanent legal status, 
and other federal, state, and local benefits. Furthermore, unless DHS 
acts immediately, there is a risk that aliens who were not eligible for 
admission as refugees could present harm to the public interest.
    As explained in detail in Section IV of this preamble, DHS 
reasonably believes, based on a review of prior refugee approvals and 
internal procedures, policies, and directives, that the lack of 
detailed refugee interviews and insufficient inquiry into critical 
matters such as inadmissibilities or terrorism-related grounds, coupled 
with the prioritization of admission numbers over legally sufficient 
decisions and other programmatic issues like over-reliance on COI, have 
resulted in aliens receiving refugee status when they were not 
eligible. These practices have compromised the integrity of the refugee 
program.
    In Operation PARRIS, DHS has further identified similar issues 
regarding the quality of refugee interviews after reviewing a subset of 
cases, where in some instances populations from specific countries were 
processed and approved with minimal lines of questioning. This rule 
amends the 30-day period to 10 days for aliens to respond to a NOIT so 
that the agency can expeditiously issue terminations in cases where, 
after a thorough review of the case and comprehensive vetting, USCIS 
determines that the alien did not meet the refugee definition at the 
time of admission. In such cases, an alien will not maintain valid 
refugee status a day longer than legally required. This IFR would 
accordingly more quickly eliminate a pathway to permanent status used 
by aliens with falsified claims or malevolent intent, including those 
who may pose an ongoing and imminent threat to public safety and 
national security such as the refugee cases reviewed and terminated by 
the USCIS Vetting Center outlined above.
    Therefore, if DHS had to engage in advance notice-and-comment 
procedures, it would continue to allow aliens who should have never 
been admitted to the United States as refugees to remain present longer 
than necessary, potentially putting at risk the safety and security of 
the United States and compromising the integrity of the U.S. 
immigration system. For example, in one case, after admission to the 
U.S. it was later discovered that the refugee was a war criminal who 
should have been subject to the persecutor bar and not allowed into the 
country. In another case listed above, the refugee was not admissible 
due to a lack of credibility with regard to both participation in and 
sending money to the OLF (a Tier III terrorist organization at the time 
of the alien's involvement) as well as his father's status as a well-
known OLF member. In these circumstances, providing advance notice-and-
comment procedures is impracticable and not in the public interest.
    Finally, DHS finds that it is unnecessary to delay this final 
rule's effective date under 5 U.S.C. 553(d). There is no need to give 
affected parties additional time to adjust their behavior before this 
final rule takes effect because DHS believes there are likely no 
behavioral adjustments to make. The aliens who would be affected by 
this rule have already entered the United States.\69\ In other words, a 
delay in the rule's effective date would be unlikely to have an impact 
on an alien's choice to seek to enter the United States as a refugee or 
not and would not impact whether or not they were eligible for such 
status at the time of admission. A delayed effective date would serve 
no purpose but create further harm to the public, as exemplified by the 
cases that, upon review and additional vetting, have resulted in the 
issuance of NOITs because the record indicated the alien was not a 
refugee at the time of admission.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \69\ DHS recognizes that there are some ongoing case-by-case 
admissions of refugees and that, as a result, there may be a small 
number of aliens admitted as refugees during what would have been 
the 30-day delayed effective date period. DHS does not believe, 
however, that these aliens would likely be subject to a later 
termination of their refugee status and subject to this rule given 
the actions taken as discussed above to strengthen refugee vetting 
and processing.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For the reasons outlined above, DHS believes that bypassing the 
ordinary notice-and-comment procedures and the delayed effective date 
requirement is justified, under the totality of circumstances, and 
given that immediate action is necessary, is consistent with DHS's 
statutory mission to take regulatory action to administer the refugee 
program effectively, as well as the President's directives in E.O. 
14161 and E.O. 14163. Nevertheless, recognizing the value of public 
comments, DHS is publishing this rule as an IFR with a request for 
public comment.
b. Foreign Affairs Exception
    Agencies may forgo notice-and-comment rulemaking and a delayed 
effective date when the rulemaking involves a ``military or foreign 
affairs function of the United States.'' 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1). The 
Secretary of State, on February 21, 2025, determined that:

    all efforts, conducted by any agency of the federal government, 
to control the status, entry, and exit of people and the transfer of 
goods, services, data, technology, and any other items across the 
borders of the United States, constitutes a foreign affairs function 
of the United States under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 
U.S.C. 553, 554.\70\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \70\ Determination: Foreign Affairs Functions of the United 
States, 90 FR 12200 (Mar. 14, 2025).

    This rulemaking is connected to an alien's status as a refugee 
admitted into the United States, which directly stems from the conduct 
of international relations of the United States. Therefore, it 
constitutes a foreign affairs function. U.S. refugee law is rooted in 
international law. In 1968, the United States acceded to the 1967 
United Nations Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees (Refugee 
Protocol) \71\, which incorporates the 1951 United Nations Convention 
Relating to the Status of Refugees (Refugee Convention). The Refugee 
Convention sets out the rights of refugees and establishes the 
standards for their treatment in the countries that receive them, 
providing the most comprehensive codification of refugee rights at the 
international level. State



signatories to the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol are bound by 
international obligations to provide for the protection of refugees 
whether such States are countries of first asylum or of resettlement. 
Refugee status is a product of statutorily mandated foreign affairs 
considerations and U.S. foreign policy commitments. With respect to 
refugee admissions, the relevant Departments must consider conditions 
within the specific countries, ``the extent to which other countries 
will admit and assist'' in resettlement, and ``the impact of the 
participation of the United States in the resettlement of such refugees 
on the foreign policy interests of the United States''. INA sec. 207; 8 
U.S.C. 1157(e). Refugee determinations require diplomatic relationships 
with countries of origin, transit, and habituation as well as ongoing 
assessments of foreign governments' conduct, stability, and human 
rights practices.\72\ The United States' management of its refugee 
program and immigration enforcement strategies is predicated on the 
belief that migration is a shared responsibility among all countries 
with which the United States has ongoing diplomatic relations and 
negotiations. The common thread in these engagements is the United 
States' commitment to provide protection to refugees who clearly 
qualify, while enforcing national immigration laws, and that addressing 
this challenge requires a multinational response. As such, this is a 
function of foreign affairs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \71\ United Nations General Assembly, Protocol Relating to the 
Status of Refugees, 31 January 1967, United Nation Treaty Series, 
vol. 606, p. 267, also found in the United Nations High Commissioner 
for Refugees, Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining 
Refugee Status under the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol 
relating to the Status of Refugees, (Geneva 1979, re-issued 1992 and 
2019), Annex III.
    \72\ USCIS, ``The United States Refugee Admissions Program 
(USRAP) Consultation and Worldwide Processing Priorities'' (last 
updated Sept. 17, 2025), https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/refugees-and-asylum/usrap.; see also U.S. Department of State, 
``About Refugee Admissions'' (last accessed Jan. 23, 2026), https://2017-2021.state.gov/refugee-admissions/about/.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under this IFR, changing the 30-day response period to NOITs to 10 
days in refugee termination cases allows DHS to expeditiously terminate 
cases where applicable, and process aliens for removal as soon as 
possible. Thus, this rulemaking is also related to the control of the 
entry and exit of aliens across the borders of the United States and 
falls within the Secretary's foreign affairs determination.\73\ Because 
this rule implicates the foreign affairs policy of the United States, 
DHS is issuing this rule without pre-publication notice and comment 
procedures and with an immediate effective date.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \73\ The Secretary of State's determination references and 
implements numerous Presidential actions reflecting the President's 
top foreign policy priorities, including E.O. 14161. See 
Determination: Foreign Affairs Functions of the United States, 90 FR 
12200 (Mar. 14, 2025). See, e.g., Yassini v. Crosland, 618 F.2d. 
1356, 1361 (9th Cir. 1980) (because an immigration directive ``was 
implementing the President's foreign policy,'' the action ``fell 
within the foreign affairs function and good cause exceptions to the 
notice and comment requirements of the APA'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

c. Reliance Interests
    DHS has considered potential reliance interests regarding this IFR. 
DHS recognizes the difficulty aliens may face if their refugee status 
is terminated, but DHS believes the significant public safety, national 
security, and integrity benefits described in detail above heavily 
outweigh any potential reliance interest and adverse impacts. DHS 
notes, however, that aliens will continue to receive an opportunity to 
respond to the NOIT and overcome the reasons for termination, if 
merited. With this IFR, DHS is merely ensuring that aliens who were 
never eligible for refugee status do not receive the attendant benefits 
of being a refugee admitted into the United States for as long as they 
could have without this rule. This IFR does not remove the ability of 
aliens who legitimately qualify for refugee status to obtain employment 
authorization, permanent residency, and any other available benefits. 
Aliens whose refugee status is terminated may be able to seek 
protection or other relief in proceedings under sections 235, 240, or 
241 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1225, 1229a, or 1231, which would mitigate any 
potential reliance interests.\74\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \74\ See, e.g., Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244, 274 
(1994) (``Application of a new jurisdictional rule usually takes 
away no substantive right but simply changes the tribunal that is to 
hear the case.'' (cleaned up)).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), 13563 
(Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and 14192 (``Unleashing 
Prosperity Through Deregulation'')

    E.O.s 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess the costs and 
benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if a regulation is 
necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. 
E.O. 13563 emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and 
benefits, of reducing costs, of harmonizing rules, and of promoting 
flexibility. E.O. 14192 directs agencies to significantly reduce the 
private expenditures required to comply with Federal regulations and 
provides that ``any new incremental costs associated with the new 
regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law be offset by the 
elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior 
regulations.''
    The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has designated this IFR a 
``significant regulatory action'' under section 3(f) of E.O. 12866, 
although not economically significant under section 3(f)(1), because 
its annual effects on the economy do not exceed $100 million in any 
year of the analysis. Accordingly, the rule has been reviewed by the 
Office of Management and Budget.
    This rule is not an E.O. 14192 regulatory action because it is 
being issued with respect to an immigration-related function of the 
United States. The rule's primary direct purpose is to implement or 
interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as described in 
INA101(a)(17), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17), or any other function performed by 
the U.S. Federal Government with respect to aliens. See OMB Memorandum 
M-25-20, ``Guidance Implementing Section 3 of Executive Order 14192, 
titled ``Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation'' (Mar. 26, 2025).
    In this section, DHS discusses several types of impacts that could 
accrue from this IFR. They are described qualitatively as DHS cannot 
make quantitative or monetized estimates of potential impacts. DHS 
welcomes public comment on the cost and benefit impacts described 
herein.
    DHS typically reviews an alien's underlying refugee determination 
prior to the final adjudication of their adjustment of status to 
permanent residence and initiates termination when warranted.\75\ 
Therefore, the impacted population are aliens with refugee status who 
entered the U.S. and have not yet adjusted status or had their 
determination reviewed. DHS has identified about 186,000 cases of 
refugees that entered the U.S. from Fiscal Year (FY) 2015 through FY 
2025 that have not adjusted status.\76\ This figure could represent the 
maximum population that could be subject to the IFR, as USCIS and ICE 
are currently working to identify particular subsets and aliens for 
requisite vetting. As it relates to potential impacts, foremost, there 
will be a change in the earnings (labor compensation) to the applicable 
aliens when their refugee status is terminated, as their work 
authorization would also be terminated immediately, which is at least 
20 days sooner than without this rule.\77\ Refugees are granted



work authorization incident to status but can file a Form I-765, 
``Application for Employment Authorization,'' under primarily the (A3) 
category, with a small number under the (A4) category applicable to 
paroled refugees. In FY 2024, for example, USCIS approved approximately 
125,000 (A3) initial employment authorization documents, which was a 
sharp increase from about 49,000 in FY 2023.\78\ This IFR shortens the 
time for a refugee to respond to a NOIT from 30 days to 10 days. 
Accordingly, this rule would shorten the amount of time that an alien 
has refugee status prior to termination, and the gap (duration, in 
working days) in earnings time due to earlier employment termination 
under the IFR would pose a change in earnings ability to the 
aliens.\79\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \75\ U.S. immigration law requires refugees to apply for lawful 
permanent resident status after they have been physically present in 
the United States for at least one year. See Green Card for Refugees 
at https://www.uscis.gov/green-card/green-card-eligibility/green-card-for-refugees.
    \76\ Source, USCIS, Chief Data and Analytics Office (CDAO) 
formerly Office of Performance and Quality (OPQ), CLAIMS, ELIS, 
CIS2, PAER0019303 (Jan. 21, 2026).
    \77\ USCIS is unable to provide analysis on past cases in which 
NOITs have been issued but the alien's refugee status was not 
subsequently terminated because USCIS terminated so few cases.
    \78\ Source: USCIS CDAO, CLAIMS, ELIS, PAER0020264 (Feb. 13, 
2026). A small number of approximately 190 refugees received a (C9) 
employment authorization document when they adjusted status, from FY 
2021 through FY 2025. There are currently about 113,000 refugees 
with approved (A3) initial work authorizations who have an I-485 
pending with USCIS. Since refugees are authorized to work via 
status, those filing for an (A3) authorization probably do so for 
documentation and identification purposes, or other reasons.
    \79\ Since refugees do not have to file an employment 
authorization request with USCIS, we do not attribute sunk costs to 
the opportunity costs of time if their status is terminated, for 
which the current public reporting burden is 4.38 hours. If, 
however, under another category of relief, the aliens would need to 
file for employment authorization, they would incur costs applicable 
to the burden, as well as, if applicable, direct filing fees and 
biometrics submission charges.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For those aliens in the labor force and employed at the time of 
their employment authorization termination, the earnings impact could 
create both potential distributional effects (which are transfers) and 
costs. The extent depends on labor market factors and the individual 
characteristics of aliens and potential substitute workers. The 
distributional impacts (transfers) would be in the form of forgone 
compensation (wages and benefits). However, a portion or all of this 
forgone compensation to aliens might comprise beneficial transfers to 
U.S. citizens and others lawfully allowed to work in the United States.
    In addition, if employers are able to hire American workers to fill 
the jobs that refugees held, with relatively little labor market 
friction, the beneficial wage and benefit transfers to American workers 
would potentially pose no productivity loss or costs to employers. 
While it is possible that aliens without work authorization could 
require assistance from their social and support networks, which could 
include public entities, there could be a counterbalance; if the IFR 
process results in, or contributes to, faster removal of aliens who 
were ineligible for refugee status, there could be less of an economic 
strain on states, local government, and non-governmental organizations, 
in terms of any public assistance and resources that are currently 
provided to refugees.
    As it relates to earnings impacts, there could be tax impacts. 
Aliens who sustain earnings changes because their employment 
authorization is terminated under the IFR may generate forgone federal 
and state taxes. However, any tax losses could be partially or fully 
recovered if employers are able to easily substitute others into the 
positions the alien held. In addition, aliens can pose fiscal strains 
that could be mitigated due to the effects of this rule as a 
counterbalance of some or all of the tax losses, if there are any.
    DHS assesses that there could be labor turnover costs incurred by 
businesses employing aliens who would lose employment authorization 
under the IFR whom would not otherwise lose the authorization (i.e., if 
currently they could reaffirm their status in 30 days but not in 10 
days under this rule). Employment separations can comprise direct or 
``hard'' costs applicable to separation and replacement charges.\80\ 
The separation costs include exit interviews, severance pay, and costs 
of temporarily covering the employee's duties and functions with other 
employees, which may require overtime or temporary staffing. The 
replacement costs typically include expenses of advertising positions, 
search and agency fees, screening applicants, interviews, background 
verification, employment testing, hiring bonuses, and possible travel 
and relocation costs. Once hired, employers face additional training, 
orientation, and assessment costs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \80\ For a description of these costs, see ``Employee Retention: 
The Real Cost of Losing an Employee,'' by Holly Bengfort, PeopleKeep 
(updated Dec. 15, 2025), at: https://www.peoplekeep.com/blog/Employee-Retention-The-Real-Cost-of-Losing-an-Employee. See also, 
``This Fixable Problem Costs U.S. Businesses $1 Trillion,'' by Shane 
McFeely and Ben Wigert, Gallup Workplace (Mar. 13, 2019) at: https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Second, there can be costs for productivity and possibly 
profitability due to operational and production disruptions, which can 
include errors from other employees that may temporally fill the 
position. A third cost segment, which is a type of indirect cost, can 
encompass loss of institutional knowledge, networking, and impacts to 
work culture, morale, and interpersonal relationships.
    DHS is providing a 10-day, as opposed to the current 30-day, 
timeframe to contest applicable NOITs. The NOIT will inform the alien 
the basis for termination and explain that they may submit evidence to 
contest termination, and/or request an interview. Aliens who would 
currently respond to a NOIT to attempt to reaffirm their status would 
sustain some direct costs and also opportunity costs of time applicable 
to generating and preparing responses, organizing documents and 
evidence, and participating in interviews. Under the 10-day timeframe, 
such resourcing and expenditure would likely still be incurred, but the 
timeframe would be contracted. There could be impacts and costs to 
aliens applicable to having less time to collect evidence, prepare 
documentation, and prepare their response.
    As is pertinent to the public sector, planned extensive vetting, 
case review, and reinterviews, as well as enforcement operations for 
the Federal Bureau of Investigation and ICE, in support directly or 
indirectly of this IFR, could require an increase in public resources. 
As is applicable to mailing the NOITs, DHS will utilize express 
delivery service providers, which guarantee delivery within the IFR 
timeframe, and offers tracking and confirmation of both the package's 
departure from DHS custody and its delivery to the recipient. This is 
not a significant change from current practice and DHS does not expect 
that this IFR will generate additional costs applicable to mailing the 
NOITs. USCIS will continue to expend resources on processing and review 
of the responses. However, the revised timeline may generate 
efficiencies as USCIS will be able to schedule interviews or take 
action more quickly. DHS cannot predict in advance the net effect to 
public resources and welcomes public input concerning public sector 
resources.
    DHS, however, does not and cannot assert that it knows and has 
considered every policy change that may occur at all levels and 
agencies of the U.S. government that may directly or indirectly affect 
this IFR. Therefore, there could be other impacts not currently 
described in this discussion.
    DHS cannot quantify the benefits of this IFR but believes that 
increased national security, public safety, credibility, and reduced 
fraud or misrepresentation by applicable aliens, among other concerns, 
will contribute to the safety of the American people and integrity of 
the lawful United States immigration system to the extent that the 
benefits will outweigh any costs.



Streamlining the process to terminate refugee status in cases where the 
alien is determined to not have been a refugee at the time of admission 
to the United States is consistent with the DHS mission and 
responsibilities to ensure national security and public safety and 
beneficially protects the immigration system from fraud and 
exploitation.

C. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)

    The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.), as 
amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 
1996, requires federal agencies to consider the potential impact of 
regulations on small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, and 
small organizations during the development of their rules. The term 
``small entities'' comprises small businesses, not-for-profit 
organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not 
dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with 
populations of less than 50,000. The RFA's regulatory flexibility 
analysis requirements apply only to those rules for which an agency is 
required to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to 
5 U.S.C. 553 or any other law.\81\ DHS did not issue a notice of 
proposed rulemaking for this action.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \81\ See 5 U.S.C. 604(a).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA)

    The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) is intended, among 
other things, to curb the practice of imposing unfunded federal 
mandates on State, local, and Tribal governments.\82\ Title II of UMRA 
requires each Federal agency to prepare a written statement assessing 
the effects of any Federal mandate in a proposed rule, or final rule 
for which USCIS published a proposed rule, which includes any Federal 
mandate that may result in a $100 million or more expenditure (adjusted 
annually for inflation) in any one year by State, local, and Tribal 
governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector. See 2 U.S.C. 
1532(a). This rule is exempt from the written-statement requirement, 
because DHS did not publish a notice of proposed rulemaking for this 
rule.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \82\ The term ``Federal mandate'' means a Federal 
intergovernmental mandate or a Federal private sector mandate. See 2 
U.S.C. 1502(1) and 658(5) and (6).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition, this rule does not exceed the $100 million expenditure 
in any one year when adjusted for inflation ($211 million in 2025 based 
on the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) \83\), and 
this rulemaking does not contain such a federal mandate as the term is 
defined under UMRA. The requirements of title II of UMRA therefore do 
not apply, thus DHS has not prepared a statement under UMRA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \83\ See BLS, ``Historical Consumer Price Index for All Urban 
Consumers (CPI-U): U.S. city average, allitems, by month,'' https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/supplemental-files/historical-cpi-u-202512.pdf (last visited Aug. 18, 2026). Calculation of inflation: 
(1) calculate the average monthly CPI-U for the reference year 
(1995) and the current year (2025); (2) subtract reference year CPI-
U from current year CPI-U; (3) divide the difference of the 
reference year CPI-U and current year CPI-U by the reference year 
CPI-U; (4) multiply by 100 = [(average monthly CPI-U for 2025-
average monthly CPI-U for 1995) / (average monthly CPI-U for 1995)] 
x 100 = [(321.943-152.383) / 152.383] = (169.560/152.383) = 1.113 x 
100 = 111.3 percent = 111 percent (rounded). Calculation of 
inflation-adjusted value: $100 million in 1995 dollars x 2.11 = $211 
million in 2025 dollars.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

E. Congressional Review Act (CRA)

    The Congressional Review Act (CRA) was included as Subtitle E of 
the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 
(SBREFA), Public Law 104-121, 110 Stat. 847 (Mar. 29, 1996). Based on 
DHS's assessment, the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has 
determined that this IFR is not a major rule as defined under the CRA 
in 5 U.S.C. 804(2). This rule will not result in an annual effect on 
the economy of $100 million or more; a major increase in costs or 
prices; or significant adverse effects on competition, employment, 
investment, productivity, innovation, or an ability of the United 
States-based companies to compete with foreign-based companies in 
domestic and export markets. See 5 U.S.C. 804(2). However, even if this 
IFR did meet the criteria at 5 U.S.C. 804(2), as stated in the 
preamble, DHS has good cause to forgo the APA's requirements for notice 
and public comment (and delayed effective date) pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 
553. Therefore, DHS also has good cause to forgo the CRA's 60-day 
delayed effective date requirement, pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 808(2). This 
rule is effective upon publication. DHS has complied with the CRA's 
reporting requirements and has sent this rule to Congress and to the 
Comptroller General as required by 5 U.S.C. 801(a)(1).

F. Executive Order 13132 (Federalism)

    This IFR does not have substantial direct effects on the States, on 
the relationship between the National Government and the States, or on 
the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels 
of government. Therefore, in accordance with section 6 of E. O. 13132, 
64 FR 43255 (Aug. 4, 1999), this IFR does not have sufficient 
federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism 
summary impact statement.

G. Executive Order 12988 (Civil Justice Reform)

    DHS drafted and reviewed this IFR in accordance with E.O. 12988, 
Civil Justice Reform. DHS wrote this IFR to provide a clear legal 
standard for affected conduct and reviewed it carefully to eliminate 
drafting errors and ambiguities, so as to minimize litigation and undue 
burden on the Federal Court system. DHS determined that this rule meets 
the applicable standards provided in section 3(a) and 3(b)(2) of E.O. 
12988, 61 FR 4729 (Feb. 5, 1996).

H. Family Assessment

    DHS reviewed this rule in line with the requirements of section 654 
of the Treasury General Appropriations Act, 1999, Public Law 105-277, 
112 Stat. 2681 (1998). DHS systematically reviewed the criteria 
specified in section 654(c)(1), by evaluating whether this regulatory 
action: (1) impacts the stability or safety of the family, particularly 
in terms of marital commitment; (2) impacts the authority of parents in 
the education, nurture, and supervision of their children; (3) helps 
the family perform its functions; (4) affects disposable income or 
poverty of families and children; (5) only financially impacts 
families, if at all, to the extent such impacts are justified; (6) may 
be carried out by State or local government or by the family; or (7) 
establishes a policy concerning the relationship between the behavior 
and personal responsibility of youth and the norms of society. If the 
agency determines a regulation may negatively affect family well-being, 
then the agency must provide an adequate rationale for its 
implementation.
    DHS has no data that indicates this rule will have any impact on 
family well-being. DHS has determined that the implementation of this 
regulation will not negatively affect family well-being and will not 
have any impact on the autonomy and integrity of the family as an 
institution.

I. Executive Order 13175 (Consultation and Coordination With Indian 
Tribal Governments)

    This IFR will not have Tribal implications under E.O. 13175, 
Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because 
it will not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian 
Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian 
Tribes, or on



the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal 
Government and Indian Tribes.

J. National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)

    DHS and its components analyze final actions to determine whether 
the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq., 
applies and, if so, what degree of analysis is required. DHS Directive 
023-01, Rev. 01``Implementing the National Environmental Policy Act'' 
(Directive 023-01) and Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01 Revision 01, 
``Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act'' 
(Instruction Manual) \84\ established the policies and procedures that 
DHS and its components use to comply with NEPA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \84\ The Instruction Manual contains DHS' procedures for 
implementing NEPA and was issued Nov. 6, 2014. See DHS, Office of 
the Chief Readiness Support Officer, National Environmental Policy 
Act Compliance, https://www.dhs.gov/ocrso/eed/epb/nepa (last updated 
Apr. 14, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish, in their NEPA 
implementing procedures, categories of actions (``categorical 
exclusions'') that experience has shown do not, individually or 
cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human environment and, 
therefore, do not require an environmental assessment or environmental 
impact statement.\85\ The Instruction Manual, Appendix A lists the DHS 
Categorical Exclusions.\86\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \85\ See 42 U.S.C. 4336(a)(2), 4336e(1).
    \86\ See Instruction Manual, Appendix A, Table 1.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under DHS NEPA implementing procedures, for an action to be 
categorically excluded, it must satisfy each of the following three 
conditions: (1) the entire action clearly fits within one or more of 
the categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger 
action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the 
potential for a significant environmental effect.\87\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \87\ Instruction Manual 023-01 at V.B(2)(a)-(c).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This IFR is strictly administrative and procedural because it is 
only amending an existing DHS regulation governing the termination of 
refugee status. DHS has reviewed this IFR and finds that no significant 
impact on the environment, or any change in environmental effect will 
result from the amendments being promulgated in this rule.
    Accordingly, DHS finds that the promulgation of this IFR's 
amendments to a current regulation clearly fits within the categorical 
exclusion A3 established in DHS's NEPA implementing procedures as an 
administrative change with no change in environmental effect, is not 
part of a larger Federal action, and does not present extraordinary 
circumstances that create the potential for a significant environmental 
effect. Therefore, these regulatory amendments are categorically 
excluded from further NEPA review.

K. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)

    Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, Public Law 104-13, all 
agencies are required to submit to OMB, for review and approval, any 
reporting requirements inherent in a rule. This rule does not impose 
any reporting or recordkeeping requirements under the Paperwork 
Reduction Act.

    Administrative practice and procedure, Refugees, Reporting and 
recordkeeping requirements.

    Accordingly, for the reasons set forth in the preamble, DHS amends 
8 CFR part 207 as follows:

PART 207--ADMISSION OF REFUGEES

0
1. The authority citation for part 207 continues to read as follows:

    Authority:  8 U.S.C. 1101, 1103, 1151, 1157, 1159, 1182; 8 CFR 
part 2.


0
2. Revise Sec.  207.9 to read as follows:


Sec.  207.9  Termination of refugee status.

    The refugee status of any alien (and of the spouse or child of the 
alien) admitted to the United States under section 207 of the Act will 
be terminated by USCIS if the alien was not a refugee within the 
meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the Act at the time of admission. 
USCIS will notify the alien in writing of its intent to terminate the 
alien's refugee status. The alien will have 10 days from the date 
notice is served upon him or her in accordance with 8 CFR 103.8 to 
present written or oral evidence to show why the alien's refugee status 
should not be terminated. There is no appeal under this chapter from 
the termination of refugee status by USCIS. Upon termination of refugee 
status, USCIS will process the alien under sections 235, 240, and 241 
of the Act.

Markwayne Mullin,

I. Executive Summary

A. Basis and Purpose

    DHS's mission is to safeguard the American people, our homeland, 
and our values with honor and integrity. In service of that mission, 
DHS protects the United States from threats by terrorists, criminals, 
smugglers, transnational criminal organizations, failed-state actors, 
and unpredictable lone offenders that constitute present and future 
threats to public safety and national security.
    USCIS issues EADs to certain classes of aliens. These documents are 
valid for a specified period. Aliens who intend to continue their 
employment beyond the date specified on their EAD must generally file 
an application to renew their employment authorization and/or EAD.
    The automatic extension of the validity of an EAD grants the alien 
the benefit of extending his or her expired employment authorization 
and/or EAD merely by filing a timely renewal EAD application and 
without first completing adjudicative review and related vetting, 
including resolution of any derogatory information identified during 
the vetting process. That is, the automatic extension allows for the 
granting of the benefit without USCIS first performing the following 
actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening 
checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in 
connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment 
authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if 
applicable.
    On October 30, 2025, DHS issued an IFR titled, ``Removal of the 
Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization Documents,'' with a 
request for comment. See 90 FR 48799 (Oct. 30, 2025). The IFR amended 
DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the 
validity of EADs for aliens in certain employment authorization 
categories who timely filed an application to renew their EAD. After 
careful consideration of the public comments submitted in connection 
with the IFR, DHS is reaffirming and finalizing the IFR without 
changes. The rationale and reasoning provided in the preamble for the 
IFR remains unchanged with respect to the regulatory amendments, and 
DHS, therefore, adopts such reasoning also to support this final rule.
    In reaffirming and finalizing the changes made in the IFR, the 
purpose of this rule remains the same as articulated in the IFR: to 
prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure 
continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment 
authorization and/or a new EAD by ending the practice of automatically 
extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for 
certain employment authorization categories.
    Ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of EADs is 
consistent with Section 16 of President Trump's directive in Executive 
Order (E.O.) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion, 
which directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with 
the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, to take all 
appropriate action to align any departmental activities with the 
policies set out by the President and to ensure, among others, ``that 
employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with 
section 274A of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1324a), 
and that employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized 
alien in the United States.'' \1\ It is also consistent with Section 2 
of E.O. 14161, Protecting the United States From Foreign Terrorists and 
Other National Security and Public Safety Threats, which directs the 
Secretary of State, in coordination with the Secretary of Homeland 
Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National 
Intelligence to ``identify all resources that may be used to ensure 
that all aliens seeking admission to the United States, or who are 
already in the United States, are vetted and screened to the maximum 
degree possible.'' \2\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ See E.O. 14159, Protecting the American People Against 
Invasion (Jan. 20, 2025), 90 FR 8443, 8446 (Jan. 29, 2025).
    \2\ See E.O. 14161, Protecting the United States from Foreign 
Terrorists and Other National Security and Public Safety Threats 
(Jan. 20, 2025), 90 FR 8451, 8451 (Jan. 30, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Legal Authority

    The legal basis of this rulemaking is found in section 103(a) of 
the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a), which 
authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and 
nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems 
necessary for carrying out such authority, and section 101(b)(1)(F) of 
the Homeland Security Act (HSA), 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F), which 
establishes as a primary mission of DHS the duty to ``ensure that the 
overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by 
efforts, activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland.''

C. Summary of the Major Provisions of the Regulatory Action

    This final rule adopts the IFR as final, without any changes, after 
careful consideration of the comments received. Accordingly, DHS is 
adopting as final the following changes that the IFR has made:
     Revised the heading of 8 CFR 274a.13(d) to clearly 
indicate that the up-to-540-day automatic extension period only applies 
to renewal EAD applications filed before October 30, 2025.
     Added new 8 CFR 274a.13(e). The new provision explains 
that, unless otherwise provided in 8 CFR 274a.13(d), by law, or through 
a Federal Register notice for Temporary Protected Status (TPS)-related 
employment documentation, the validity period of an expired or expiring 
Employment Authorization Document and/or employment authorization will 
not be automatically extended by a renewal EAD application filed on or 
after October 30, 2025.
    DHS explained in the IFR that the IFR did not impact the validity 
of EADs that were automatically extended prior to October 30, 2025. It 
also explained that the IFR did not impact automatic extensions of EADs 
and/or employment authorization provided by law or Federal Register 
notices, such as those for TPS applicants pursuant to section 244 of 
the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1254a, and 8 CFR part 244.\3\ This final rule 
similarly does not impact these provisions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \3\ However, on July 4, 2025, Congress passed and the President 
signed into law sections 100003(c) and 100012(a) of the One Big 
Beautiful Bill Act, Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat.72 (July 4, 2025) 
(H.R 1), which limit the validity period of any employment 
authorization for aliens granted TPS under section 244 of the INA, 8 
U.S.C. 1254a, to a period of one year or for the duration of the 
designation of TPS, whichever is shorter.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

D. Costs and Benefits

    This final rule has been designated a ``significant regulatory 
action'' and economically significant as defined under section 3(f)(1) 
of E.O. 12866, because its annual effects on the economy may exceed 
$100 million in any year of the analysis. Accordingly, this rule has 
been reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).



    This final rule reaffirms and finalizes changes made by the IFR to 
DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the 
validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I-766 or EADs) 
for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in 
certain employment authorization categories. The purpose of this change 
is to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure 
continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment 
authorization and/or a new EAD. This final rule does not affect the 
validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to the IFR. In 
previous rules providing for the automatic extension of EADs based on 
the timely filing of a renewal EAD application, DHS attempted to 
stabilize aliens' earnings and avoid labor turnover costs of employers. 
However, as explained in the IFR, the Department has shifted focus to 
prioritizing public safety and national security, and ensuring that 
aliens continue to be eligible and merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, as applicable, before being granted continued employment 
authorization. See 90 FR 48799, 48816 (Oct. 30, 2025).
    DHS has prepared two types of quantified estimates of the impacts 
generated by this final rule. For a single 18-month window (starting in 
May 2027) from about 20,000 to 33,000 EADs are estimated to lapse, 
based on several assumptions. This rule may result in some EAD holders 
incurring a loss of earnings (``reduced earnings'') because of USCIS 
process delays for renewal EAD applications, as under this rule there 
could be disruption to their earnings due to a lapsed EAD. Such 
earnings loss to aliens could comprise beneficial transfers to other 
U.S. workers if the substitution of the latter for the former is 
relatively frictionless. Additionally, to the extent this rule affects 
EAD holders' jobs going unfilled, there will be impacts to tax 
transfers from businesses and employees to the Federal Government.\4\ 
This rule will also generate labor turnover costs to businesses that 
employ the affected-lapsed EAD holders, as under this rule there would 
be a disruption to the EAD holders' employment authorization and/or 
document validity. In conducting these estimates DHS emphasizes that 
variation in factors involved in the impact, including impact 
processing times, filing volumes, the timing of renewal filings, and 
underlying benefit requests, will cause variation in the impacts.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \4\ This rule could also result in a reduction in State and 
local tax revenue, but this impact is not quantified in this 
analysis due to variations in state and local tax laws and 
individual's tax scenarios.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Due to variation in future populations and process times, there is 
likely to be substantial variation in the impact estimates. For this 
reason, DHS develops wide ranges capturing a high and low bound for the 
estimates, in terms of the means (expected value). This rule is 
estimated to result in $138.1 million in lost productivity costs to 
employers that are not able to easily replace aliens with lapsed EADs, 
costs of $312.1 million to U.S. employers from potential labor 
turnover, transfers due to earnings changes worth $138.1 million from 
employment-authorized aliens to replacement workers and is expected to 
generate tax reduction impacts of $14.5 million over an 18-month 
period. Approximately 1,700 and 2,800 employers are estimated to be 
impacted.
    Section V.B. provides an A-4 accounting statement supporting the 
analysis and the accompanying economic analysis details the data and 
methodology supporting the impact estimates.
