B. Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization and Documentation

    Before November 2016, 8 CFR 274a.13(d) stated that USCIS would 
adjudicate an EAD application within 90 days of receipt. If USCIS did 
not adjudicate the EAD application within that timeframe, the alien was 
eligible to request an interim EAD with a validity period not to exceed 
240 days.\7\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \7\ See 8 CFR 274a.13(d) (2016).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    On November 18, 2016, as part of DHS's efforts to implement the 
American Competitiveness in the



Twenty-first Century Act of 2000 (AC21), DHS published a final rule 
that eliminated Interim EADs and replaced them with a maximum 180-day 
automatic extension period for certain renewal applicants.\8\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \8\ See 81 FR 82398 (Nov. 18, 2016) (AC21 Final Rule).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

C. Increasing the Automatic Extension Period From a Maximum of 180 Days 
to a Maximum of 540 Days

    Since the promulgation of the final rule authorizing up to 180-day 
automatic extension period for certain renewal EAD applicants, USCIS' 
ability to process both initial and renewal EAD applications within 
USCIS' targeted processing times was adversely impacted by a variety of 
temporary circumstances.\9\ In May 2022 \10\ and April 2024,\11\ DHS 
temporarily increased the automatic extension from up to 180 days to up 
to 540 days. The May 2022 and April 2024 temporary final rules were 
intended to reduce the number of renewal EAD applicants eligible for an 
automatic extension of their EAD validity under 8 CFR 274a.13(d) 
experiencing lapses in their employment authorization and/or EAD 
validity because of USCIS processing delays.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \9\ See 87 FR 26614, 26617-26 (May 4, 2022) (identifying USCIS' 
precarious fiscal status, the COVID-19 public health emergency, and 
dramatic increases in Form I-765 filings); see also 89 FR 24628, 
24634-40 (Apr. 8, 2024) (identifying an increase in referrals to 
USCIS for Credible Fear Assessment and an increase in affirmative 
and defensive asylum filings as contributing factors to increased 
EAD processing times).
    \10\ 87 FR 26614 (May 4, 2022) (temporarily increased the 
automatic extension period to up to 540 days).
    \11\ 89 FR 24628 (Apr. 8, 2024) (temporarily increased the 
automatic extension period to up to 540 days).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS also issued a final rule in December 2024 \12\ that 
indefinitely increased the up to 540-day automatic extension for 
certain applications pending on May 4, 2022, or properly filed on or 
after May 4, 2022. That rule was intended to reduce the effects of 
unknown future circumstances that could significantly impact EAD 
renewal processing times.\13\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \12\ See 89 FR 101208 (Dec. 13, 2024) (permanently increased the 
automatic extension period to up to 540 days).
    \13\ See 89 FR 101210 (``When unforeseen future circumstances 
cause processing times to extend beyond 180 days and result in large 
scale lapses in renewal EADs, this permanent adjustment of the 
automatic extension period to 540 days will result in benefits and 
cost savings, such as stabilized earnings and avoided labor turnover 
costs.'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

D. The 2025 Interim Final Rule Removed Automatic Extensions for Certain 
Employment Authorization Documents

    The IFR amended DHS regulations to end the practice of 
automatically extending the validity of certain EADs. See 8 CFR 
274a.13(e). The IFR did not impact the automatic extensions already 
granted to renewal EAD applicants under 8 CFR 274a.13(d)(1), if the 
renewal EAD application was filed before October 30, 2025. See 8 CFR 
274a.13(d). The IFR also did not impact automatic extensions otherwise 
provided by law or in an applicable Federal Register notice regarding 
procedures for renewing TPS-related employment documentation pursuant 
to section 244 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1254a, and 8 CFR part 244.\14\ See 
8 CFR 274a.13(e).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \14\ DHS notes, however, that sections 100003(c) and 100012(a) 
of H.R. 1, Public Law 119-21 (2025), 139 Stat. 221 (2025) (codified 
at 8 U.S.C. 1802-1815), limits the validity period of any employment 
authorization for aliens granted TPS under section 244 of the INA, 8 
U.S.C. 1254a, to a period of 1 year or for the duration of the 
designation of TPS, whichever is shorter.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The IFR made two changes to the regulations governing EAD, as 
discussed below.
1. Added New 8 CFR 274a.13(e)
    The IFR added a new paragraph (e) that went into effect immediately 
with the publication of the IFR on October 30, 2025. With 8 CFR 
274a.13(e), DHS eliminated the practice of providing automatic 
extension periods for employment authorization and/or EAD validity for 
up to 540 days for renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 
2025. Therefore, renewal EAD applicants no longer receive an up to 540-
day automatic extension of their employment authorization and/or EAD 
validity if they file their application on or after October 30, 2025. 
See 8 CFR 274a.13(e).
    Except as otherwise provided by law, in 8 CFR 274a.13(d), or in 
accordance with an applicable Federal Register notice regarding 
procedures for renewing TPS-related employment documentation, an 
alien's employment authorization and/or EAD validity will expire as 
explained in the following paragraphs:
    For those aliens who are employment authorized incident to status 
under 8 CFR 274a.12(a), unless otherwise provided by law, their EAD 
will expire on the day after the end validity date stated on the face 
of the EAD. See 8 CFR 274a.13(e)(1). Because the alien's employment 
authorization is tied to the alien's status in the United States, the 
alien's employment authorization will not expire on the date indicated 
on the EAD. Instead, the alien's employment authorization will expire 
or terminate on the same date the alien's status in the United States 
expires or terminates.
    For example, an alien in L-2 nonimmigrant status as the spouse of 
an L-1 nonimmigrant is employment authorized incident to status. See 
INA sec. 214(c)(2)(E), 8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(2)(E). If the L-2 nonimmigrant 
chooses to apply for an EAD to evidence his or her employment 
authorization, the EAD will expire as of the date indicated on the face 
of the EAD. In some cases that may be the same date as the expiration 
of the L-2's nonimmigrant status. But in other cases, the L-2 status 
expiration date may be after the EAD expiration date, particularly if 
the L-2 nonimmigrant travelled outside of the United States after 
obtaining an EAD and, upon return to the United States, was provided a 
new status expiration date that will expire after the EAD expires.\15\ 
In that scenario, the L-2 nonimmigrant would remain employment 
authorized while in L-2 nonimmigrant status, even after the EAD 
expires, but the expired EAD would no longer be a valid document to 
evidence the L-2 nonimmigrant's employment authorization.\16\ Once the 
alien is no longer in L-2 status (for example, the L-2 nonimmigrant 
status expires), the alien would no longer be employment authorized as 
an L-2 nonimmigrant because such employment authorization is dependent 
on being in L-2 nonimmigrant status.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \15\ In this case, the new status expiration date is the date 
stated on the alien's Form I-94, Arrival Departure document.
    \16\ An L-2 can still have other evidence of documentation of 
employment authorization, such as a Form I-94, Arrival/Departure 
Record, designated with the L-2S classification.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For aliens who are not employment authorized incident to their 
immigration status and who instead must obtain employment authorization 
from USCIS, pursuant to 8 CFR 274a.12(c) before accepting employment in 
the United States, such as adjustment of status applicants or aliens 
with a pending asylum application, USCIS determines the length of the 
period of employment authorization in the exercise of its discretion 
and thereafter issues an EAD reflecting the validity period.\17\ 
Therefore, the EAD will expire and the employment authorization will 
terminate the day after the end validity



date stated on the face of the EAD based upon the situations outlined 
in 8 CFR 274a.14, or for aliens with employment authorization under 8 
CFR 274a.12(c)(19) based on a pending TPS application, pursuant to 
section 244 of the Act and 8 CFR part 244 \18\ See 8 CFR 274a.13(e)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \17\ Employment authorization granted pursuant to 8 CFR 
274a.12(c) is generally granted in the discretion of the Secretary. 
See 8 CFR 274a.13(a)(1) (``The approval of applications filed under 
8 CFR 274a.12(c), except for 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(8), are within the 
discretion of USCIS.'').
    \18\ For example, employment authorization may also end prior to 
the expiration date displayed on the EAD, in accordance with 8 CFR 
274a.14, if exclusion or deportation proceedings are instituted 
against the alien; if a condition upon which the EAD was granted has 
not been met or no longer exists; or upon a showing that the 
information contained in the request for an EAD was not true and 
correct.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For example, an alien with a pending adjustment of status 
application (Form I-485) has an EAD that expires on May 30, 2026. The 
alien's adjustment of status application has not been adjudicated and 
continues to be pending. The alien is eligible to apply for a renewal 
EAD based on the pending adjustment of status application. The alien 
applies for a renewal of the EAD on February 4, 2026, which is after 
the October 30, 2025, effective date of the IFR. The alien will 
maintain continuous employment authorization if his or her renewal 
application is granted before his or her current employment 
authorization expires on May 30, 2026. If the renewal EAD application 
remains unadjudicated on May 31, 2026, the alien cannot continue to 
work for his or her employer on or after May 31, 2026, unless the alien 
is employment authorized on a separate basis. See 8 CFR 274a.13(e). If 
the renewal EAD application is subsequently approved, the alien would 
again be employment authorized and may resume employment during the 
validity period stated on the new EAD. The longer an alien waits to 
file a renewal EAD application, the more likely it is that he or she 
may experience a temporary lapse in his or her employment authorization 
and/or EAD validity.

E. Severability

    In issuing this final rule, like the IFR, DHS continues to intend 
that the rule's various provisions be considered severable from one 
another to the greatest extent possible. For instance, if a court of 
competent jurisdiction were to hold that ending the practice of 
automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or 
EADs for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their 
employment authorization and/or EAD in certain employment categories 
may only be applied to a particular category of renewal EAD applicants 
or in a particular circumstance, DHS would intend for the court to 
leave the remainder of the rule in place with respect to all other 
covered persons and circumstances. DHS's overarching goal is to 
militate against threats to national security and public safety and to 
ensure that employment authorization and/or EADs are provided only 
after USCIS conducts adequate vetting and determines that the alien 
continues to be eligible and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, 
if applicable.

III. Changes in the Final Rule

    This final rule adopts as final, without change, the amendments to 
8 CFR 274a.13(d) and (e) in the IFR, published on October 30, 2025, at 
90 FR 48799.

IV. Response to Public Comments on the Interim Final Rule

A. Summary of Comments

    When issuing the IFR, DHS invited the public to participate in the 
rulemaking by submitting post-promulgation comments on every aspect of 
the rule. DHS provided a 33-day comment period following the 
publication of the IFR. DHS received 653 public comment submissions in 
the Federal eRulemaking Portal site under Docket ID Number USCIS-2025-
0271 \23\ in response to the rulemaking.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \23\ The comments can be viewed by visiting the docket for this 
rule on the Federal eRulemaking Portal site at https://www.regulations.gov/document/USCIS-2025-0271-0001/comment.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comments were submitted by a range of entities and individuals, 
including attorneys and legal service providers, applicants, individual 
commenters, professional organizations, unions, advocacy groups, 
religious organizations, research and community organizations, and 
State and local government agencies or elected officials. Some 
commenters expressed support for the rule or offered suggestions for 
improvement. Some expressed general opposition to the rule, and some 
offered alternatives. For some of the public



comments, DHS could not ascertain whether the commenter supported or 
opposed the IFR. Finally, some commenters addressed topics outside the 
scope of this rulemaking.
    DHS carefully reviewed all the public comments received in response 
to the IFR and addresses relevant comments in this final rule, grouped 
by subject area.

B. Comments in Support of the Rule

    Comment: Several commenters supported the rule based on national 
security concerns, citing the need for proper vetting of nonimmigrant 
workers. Specifically, they stated that the rule would allow for 
thorough vetting of nonimmigrants before DHS extends their 
authorization to work in the United States. Commenters called the rule 
a ``critical'' measure to support the safety and security of the 
public. One commenter emphasized that working in the United States is a 
privilege, not a right, while another said that safety and national 
security should be government's highest priority.
    Several commenters supported the rule based on concerns about fraud 
and abuse in the visa system, stating, for example, that it would help 
deter potential fraud and abuse by preventing aliens from remaining in 
the workforce for extended periods without final adjudication of their 
eligibility.
    Multiple commenters supported the rule based on concerns about 
protecting job opportunities for American citizens. A commenter stated 
that automatic extensions keep nonimmigrant workers employed without 
timely reevaluation, allowing them to compete with American workers for 
positions while requiring renewed authorization before continuing 
employment ensures that only eligible aliens remain in the workforce.
    Response: DHS agrees that this rule safeguards the process to fully 
evaluate the applicants in order to determine continued eligibility, 
identify national security and public safety concerns, and enhance 
fraud prevention through robust vetting and screening processes. This 
administration prioritizes the safety of the American people. Ensuring 
that employment authorization and/or EADs are provided only after USCIS 
conducts adequate vetting and determines that the alien continues to be 
eligible and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable, 
better protects national security, public safety, and the integrity of 
the immigration system. This rule is part of a larger DHS effort to 
reduce frivolous, fraudulent, and otherwise non-meritorious EAD filings 
and focus adjudicatory and other resources on ensuring national 
security and program integrity.

C. Comments in Opposition to the Rule and Mixed Comments

1. DHS Legal Authority
i. DHS Statutory Authority and Congressional Intent
    Comment: Multiple commenters requested that the rule be withdrawn 
stating that the rule contradicts DHS's statutory mandate, including 
the mandate to ensure that ``the overall economic security of the 
United States is not diminished by efforts . . . aimed at securing the 
homeland'' under 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F). Many of these commenters stated 
that, consistent with this statutory mandate, DHS recently concluded 
that a 540-day automatic EAD extension was necessary to protect 
employers and workers from lapses in work authorization due to USCIS 
delays, and DHS previously found that even the 180-day extension 
established under the 2016 Final Rule was not enough time to avoid 
harmful gaps in work authorization.
    Response: DHS disagrees that this rule is inconsistent with DHS's 
statutory mandate, including the mandate under 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F). 
According to 6 U.S.C. 111(b), DHS's primary mission includes preventing 
terrorist attacks within the United States, reducing the vulnerability 
of the United States to terrorism, minimizing the damage, and assisting 
in the recovery, from terrorist attacks that occur within the United 
States, and ensuring that the overall economic security of the United 
States is not diminished by efforts, activities, and programs aimed at 
securing the homeland. See 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(A), (B), (C), and (F). 
While the provision does not specifically define ``economic security,'' 
another provision within 6 U.S.C. Chapter 1 (Homeland Security 
Organization), defines ``economic security'' as the ``condition of 
having secure and resilient domestic production capacity, combined with 
reliable access to the global resources necessary to maintain an 
acceptable standard of living and to protect core national values.'' 
See 6 U.S.C. 474(c)(2).\24\ In addition, DHS is charged with the 
implementation of section 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324a, preventing 
unlawful employment of aliens. This rule, which is part of an effort to 
secure the homeland, supports DHS's mission as provided by Congress in 
6 U.S.C. 111(b) and section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a, ensures 
lawful employment, and supports the overall national and economic 
security of the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \24\ See Sorenson v. Sec'y of Treasury of U.S., 475 U.S. 851, 
860 (1986) (``The normal rule of statutory construction assumes that 
identical words used in different parts of the same act are intended 
to have the same meaning.'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Ending the practice of providing automatic extension of employment 
authorization and/or EADs enhances the benefit integrity in 
adjudications of employment authorization requests and better protects 
public safety and national security by ensuring that aliens are 
properly vetted and determined to be eligible (and merit a favorable 
exercise of discretion, if applicable), for employment authorization 
before such authorization is provided to the alien. The automatic 
extension of an EAD grants the benefit of extending an alien's expired 
employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a timely renewal 
EAD application and without first completing adjudicative review and 
related vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information 
identified during the vetting process. That is, the benefit is granted 
without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility 
determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving 
potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, 
and a determination that the employment authorization should be renewed 
in the exercise of discretion, if applicable. Without the IFR and this 
final rule, aliens could still obtain an automatic extension despite 
derogatory information that could flag them as national security or 
public safety risks. Automatic extensions, therefore, pose a security 
risk.
    DHS is charged with combating unauthorized employment in accordance 
with section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a, which Congress 
implemented, among other reasons, because of the detrimental negative 
effect that unauthorized employment and illegal immigration has on the 
United States and the national economy.\25\ Sections 103 and 274A of



the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 8 U.S.C. 1324a, among other provisions, 
provide DHS and USCIS with considerable flexibility to administer and 
enforce the INA, including granting employment authorization and the 
issuance of an EAD. There is no generally applicable statutory mandate 
that requires DHS to provide an automatic extension. As explained in 
the IFR, the automatic extension carries the risk that employers 
unwittingly continue to employ a worker whose employment authorization 
is in fact no longer valid. See 90 FR at 48810. This includes that 
aliens may no longer be entitled to employment authorization because 
they no longer have an underlying status which entitles them to work. 
Additionally, vetting every alien before granting an immigration 
benefit, including employment authorization, has been one of the key 
considerations of Congress.\26\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \25\ Section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a was codified as 
part of the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, Public Law 
99-603, for the purpose of controlling illegal immigration to the 
United States by, among other things, establishing penalties for 
employers who knowingly hire undocumented aliens and prohibiting the 
employment of aliens who are unauthorized to work in the United 
States either because they entered the country illegally or are in 
an immigration status which does not permit employment. See H. Rep. 
No. 99-682, 46, 1986 U.S.C.C.A.N. 5649, 5649-5650. The legislative 
history reflects that Congress considered, among other things, 
evidence of prior studies demonstrating the adverse impact of 
illegal immigration that warranted legislation to protect U.S. labor 
and the economy. See, e.g., H. Rep. 99-682, 46--52, 1986 
U.S.C.C.A.N. 5649, 5649-5656 [``The need for control is underscored 
by international demographics. Undocumented aliens tend to come from 
countries with high population growth and few employment 
opportunities. The United States is not in a position to redress 
this imbalance by absorbing these workers into our economy and our 
population. U.S. unemployment currently stands at 7%, and is much 
higher among the minority groups with whom undocumented workers 
compete for jobs most directly . . . Extensive investigative and 
legislative hearings on the problem of undocumented aliens were held 
during the 92d Congress beginning in 1971, by the House Judiciary 
Subcommittee with special jurisdiction over immigration matters, 
then under the chairmanship of Representative Peter W. Rodino, Jr. 
Quoting from a 1975 House Judiciary Committee report, `The basic 
conclusion reached by the majority of the members of the 
subcommittee as a result of the hearings was that the adverse impact 
of illegal aliens was substantial, and warranted legislation both to 
protect U.S. labor and the economy, and to assure the orderly entry 
of immigrants into this country.' (H. Rept. 94-506, p. 3)''].
    \26\ For example, the Congressional recommendation to establish 
an organization ``responsible for developing, implementing, 
directing, and overseeing the joint USCIS-Immigration and Customs 
Enforcement (ICE) anti-fraud initiative and conducting law 
enforcement/background checks on every applicant, beneficiary, and 
petitioner prior to granting immigration benefits.'' See Conference 
Report to accompany H.R. 4567 [Report 108-774], ``Making 
Appropriations for the Department of Homeland Security for the 
Fiscal Year Ending September 30, 2005,'' p. 74, https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CRPT-108hrpt774/pdf/CRPT-108hrpt774.pdf [emphasis added]. 
In response to this recommendation, the Fraud and National Security 
Division (FDNS) was established at USCIS. See USCIS, DHS, ``Fraud 
Detection and Nat'l Security Directorate,'' https://www.uscis.gov/about-us/organization/directorates-and-program-offices/fraud-detection-and-national-security-directorate (last updated Apr. 16, 
2026); USCIS, ``Fraud Detection and Nat'l Security Directorate 
(FDNS),'' May 2022, https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/brochures/FDNS_Brochure_Web_V2_508.pdf.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The rule does not eliminate employment authorizations or prevent 
eligible aliens from obtaining EADs for employment purposes or proof of 
identity; or from seeking and maintaining authorized employment. The 
rule does not reduce economic security. To the contrary, the rule 
supports the condition of having secure and resilient domestic 
production capacity, and protects core national values, as directed by 
Congress, with U.S. workers who are legally authorized to work. 
Therefore, the IFR is consistent with DHS's statutory mandate, 
including the mandate at 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F), because it 
appropriately balances the need for security and vetting while 
maintaining overall EAD eligibility practices.
    DHS is cognizant that prior rulemakings stated that DHS believed, 
at the time, that taking immediate action and providing automatic 
extensions of employment authorization supported USCIS' (as a component 
of DHS) statutory mission to administer employment authorization 
effectively, and as a measure to ensure that the overall economic 
security was not diminished by potentially harmful gaps in employment 
authorizations. See, e.g., 89 FR 101208, 101209 (Dec. 13, 2024); 89 FR 
24628, 24629 and 24651(Apr. 8, 2024). As explained in this response, 
and throughout this rule, DHS believes that the factual situation 
underlying prior rules, in particular the Dec. 13, 2024 rule, have 
significantly changed, including that DHS has taken significant steps 
to reduce the flood of filings of EADs that overwhelmed USCIS' 
adjudicative resources.\27\ Furthermore, the 2024 final rule made the 
automatic extension period permanent based on the presumption that 
harmful gaps would occur given the operational realities at the 
time.\28\ Even if the 2024 final rule had taken into account the 
security posture of the United States, it was unclear how the rule 
furthered the economic security given that the rule was based on 
potential harm to individual applicants and their employers, rather 
than the broader national economy. It is thus unclear how removing the 
automatic extension period, which improves the security posture of the 
United States and is consistent with immigration laws, would undermine 
the overall economic security of the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \27\ See 90 FR 48799, 48809 (Oct. 30, 2025).
    \28\ See 89 FR 101208, 101245 (noting ``the purpose of this 
final rule is to provide a long-term solution to mitigate the 
potential for unpredictable circumstances to significantly increase 
renewal EAD application processing times that would require future 
urgent action).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: A commenter asserted that removing the automatic extension 
of employment authorization without ensuring timely adjudication would 
strip lawfully authorized noncitizens \29\ of their ability to work due 
to USCIS processing delays, which, according to the commenter, 
contradicts the intent of the INA and the ``right'' to work in the 
United States. Another commenter stated that the IFR incorrectly states 
that the rule is consistent with section 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 
1324a. Another commenter stated that it seems illegal to deny someone a 
renewal when they have followed the law and have filed the renewal 
application in a timely manner.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \29\ USCIS generally refers to ``aliens'' when discussing 
foreign nationals present in the United States. The term ``alien'' 
is a legal term defined in the INA that is used to describe any 
person who is not a citizen or national of the United States. See 
INA sec. 101(a)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(1). Some commenters 
used ``aliens'', but others may have used different terminology 
(such as person or individual). In general, when describing comments 
in this preamble, DHS has sought to mirror the language used in 
those comments, sometimes with quotation marks for clarity. 
Otherwise, DHS has used alien, or applicant, beneficiary, or 
requestor.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Response: DHS disagrees with these commenters' assertions. This 
final rule and the IFR are consistent with section 274A of the Act, 8 
U.S.C. 1324a, which, among other things, recognizes the Secretary's 
authority to grant employment authorization in his or her discretion. 
DHS disagrees with the commenter's assertion that aliens have a broadly 
applicable ``right'' to work in the United States. Rather, the INA 
makes clear that aliens, to lawfully work in the United States, must be 
so authorized by law or a grant of employment authorization by the 
Secretary. See INA 274A(h)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(3). Contrary to the 
commenters' assertions, this rule does not impact whether DHS will 
renew an alien's employment authorization; it only removes an 
intermediate automatic extension of the EAD period. If DHS determines 
that the alien is eligible for continued employment authorization and 
merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, DHS may grant 
the renewal of employment authorization. This final rule merely ends 
the practice of automatically granting the benefit of continued 
employment authorization without USCIS first performing the following 
actions: eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening 
checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in 
connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment 
authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if 
applicable.
    Comment: A commenter stated that, when providing the ability for 
asylum



seekers to obtain work authorization, Congress could not have intended 
the arbitrary and capricious impact, on both the alien authorized to 
work and the employer who has relied on that alien, of being without 
authorization for an indeterminate amount of time until USCIS 
adjudicates either the asylum application or a new EAD. A commenter 
stated, without pointing to specific provisions, that the IFR should be 
discontinued because its policy changes do not reflect the law or the 
intent of the law or even the will of the people who voted for 
candidates who would make immigration changes.
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertion. Section 
208(d)(2) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2), expressly states that ``[a]n 
applicant for asylum is not entitled to employment authorization,'' 
though it also provides the Secretary with authority to grant 
employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for 
asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum. 
The IFR, and this final rule, clearly outline the legal authority for 
this change, and are consistent with the Secretary's discretionary 
authority regarding the grant of employment authorization for asylum 
applicants and the duration of such authorization.
ii. Constitutional Concerns
    Comment: Multiple commenters expressed that the IFR raises First 
Amendment concerns, because the IFR suggests that USCIS must evaluate 
whether renewal applicants ``bear hostile attitudes'' toward U.S. 
citizens, culture, government, institutions, or founding principles. 
The commenters reasoned that employment authorization may not be 
conditioned on ideological conformity and that agency action on 
unconstitutional factors may not be sustained as it is constitutionally 
questionable and impermissible. Another commenter stated that an 
ideological screening regime for work authorization renewals would 
further entrench USCIS in DHS's ``troubling pattern'' of suppressing 
First Amendment rights in the name of national security and opens the 
door for USCIS to profile individuals.
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters. Citizens and aliens 
may object to various statutes, regulations, and policies and express 
those objections publicly. This rule neither penalizes individuals for 
protected political beliefs or associations nor subjects them to 
activities such as ideological screenings or profiling. This rule does 
not abridge the freedom of speech, of the press, or of association or 
peaceful assembly. Rather, it ends the practice of automatically 
granting the benefit of continued employment authorization without 
USCIS concurrently performing the following actions: eligibility 
determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving 
potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, 
or a determination that the employment authorization should be renewed 
in the exercise of discretion, if applicable.
    DHS notes that freedom of speech for aliens is not absolute. See, 
e.g., INA sec. 212(a)(3)(B)(i)(VII), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(3)(B)(i)(VII) 
(stating that any alien who endorses or espouses terrorist activity, or 
persuades others to endorse or espouse terrorist activity or support a 
terrorist organization, is inadmissible), and INA sec. 
212(a)(6)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(6)(C)(ii) (stating that any alien 
who falsely represents, or has falsely represented, himself or herself 
to be a citizen of the United States for any purpose or benefit under 
Federal or State law is inadmissible). DHS has a compelling interest in 
vetting and screening aliens before granting a benefit request, 
particularly when such request is granted in USCIS' discretion, as 
applicable.
    DHS also notes that a challenge to the First Amendment cannot lie 
unless an individual establishes that he or she faces a ``credible 
threat of prosecution'' specifically for his or her speech, ``under a 
statute [or rule] that appears to render the [individual]'s arguably 
protected speech illegal.'' See, e.g., Am. Library Ass'n v. Barr, 956 
F.2d 1178, 1194 (D.C. Cir. 1992). As indicated above, that is not the 
case in this scenario as neither section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 
1324a, nor the associated regulations, renders any form of speech 
illegal or attempts to directly or indirectly regulate or penalize 
speech. Rather, the IFR and this final rule subject all EAD renewal 
applicants to the same vetting and screening procedures used for 
initial applications or those applicants who were not previously 
eligible for an automatic extension of their renewal employment 
authorization and/or EAD.
    Comment: Several commenters raised concerns related to due process. 
Referencing the Fifth Amendment, a commenter stated that the IFR 
undermines the right to due process and the right to seek asylum by 
eliminating automatic extensions, which will cause large numbers of 
asylum seekers and other immigrants to lose employment authorization 
through no fault of their own. Another commenter said the rule replaces 
due process with guilt by association and abandons any pretense of a 
fair and rational immigration system. Other commenters expressed 
concerns about due process related to the immediate effective date of 
the IFR, stating that implementation of the IFR appears to be designed 
to reflect and further the current administration's policies and 
efforts toward ``creating and enhancing chaos and dysfunction.''
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertions that the 
IFR, and this final rule by virtue of reaffirming and finalizing the 
IFR, undermine due process or the ability of aliens to request asylum, 
or that it will cause large numbers of asylum seekers or other aliens 
to lose employment authorization.
    In general, the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution protects 
due process rights to a government benefit if the alien has an 
entitlement to it, but a benefit is not a protected entitlement if 
government officials may grant or deny it in their discretion. See Town 
of Castle Rock, Colorado v. Gonzales, 545 U.S. 748, 756 (2005). There 
is no generally applicable statutory mandate to grant automatic 
extensions of employment authorizations. DHS and USCIS have been 
provided with considerable flexibility and discretion under section 103 
and 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 8 U.S.C. 1324a, among other 
provisions, to administer and enforce the INA, including granting 
employment authorization. Therefore, there is generally no cognizable 
due process interest in matters related to automatic extensions of 
employment authorizations and/or EADs. Additionally, contrary to the 
commenter's assertion, the rule does not suggest guilt by association 
or that the immigration system is unfair or irrational. A fair and 
rational immigration system ensures that aliens are sufficiently 
vetted, and any background hits are resolved before a determination is 
made that the alien is eligible for an extension of his or her 
employment authorization and/or an EAD and merits a favorable exercise 
of discretion, as applicable. The examples provided in the IFR do not 
suggest guilt by association. Rather, those examples highlight the 
importance and urgency of ensuring that aliens are not granted 
employment authorization until appropriate adjudicative review has been 
completed, and the risks to the national security and public safety if 
such benefits are granted automatically.
    DHS also disagrees with the assertion that immediate implementation 
of the IFR was designed or intended to create chaos or dysfunction. DHS 
explained in the IFR why it was implementing the



rule with immediate effect. DHS concluded that the good cause 
exceptions in 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) and (d)(3) apply to the IFR and that 
delaying the implementation of the IFR until the conclusion of notice 
and comment procedures and the delayed effective date would be 
impracticable and contrary to public interest. See 90 FR 48814 (Oct. 
30, 2025). DHS also explained that the IFR was issued with an immediate 
effective date because the rule clearly implicates the foreign affairs 
policy of the United States, and that notice and comment procedure as 
well as a 30-day delayed effective date would result in undesirable 
international consequences. See 90 FR 48816 (Oct. 30, 2025).
iii. International Law and Refugee Protections
    Comment: Several commenters stated that the IFR violates refugee 
protections, including the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of 
Refugees and the Refugee Act of 1980.\30\ One of these commenters said 
the Refugee Act of 1980 specifically enshrines the right of refugees to 
work, obtain documentation, and access education, and UNHCR Guidance 
makes clear that asylum seekers awaiting adjudication of their cases 
are to be afforded the right to work. The commenter said asylum seekers 
must obtain EADs to work while their cases are pending, and gaps in 
EADs restrict the enjoyment of these rights either by directly 
impacting the right to safe work, or because many services require 
documentation for which an EAD may be the only form of proof available.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \30\ In 1968, the U.S. acceded to the 1967 Protocol Relating to 
the Status of Refugees (``Protocol''), which adopted articles of the 
1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (``Convention'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Another commenter stated that eliminating the automatic extension 
was contrary to Article 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention, because the 
resulting loss of employment and the bar of legal employment impede 
assimilation and naturalization of refugees. The commenter also said 
the IFR was contrary to Article 33's nonrefoulement, and the Refugee 
Convention's and Protocol's mandate to facilitate access to fair and 
efficient refugee status determination procedures that function as a 
safeguard against refoulement. The commenter reasoned that by 
undermining asylum seekers' ability to meet their basic needs through 
legal employment while their claims are pending, the rule obstructs 
access to a fair asylum procedure and risks forcing aliens to abandon 
their claims, potentially resulting in their return to the country of 
persecution.
    A commenter stated that cutting off work authorization from people 
fleeing persecution contradicts our legal obligations and longstanding 
values.
    Response: DHS disagrees that ending the practice of granting 
automatic extensions for EAD renewals is inconsistent with the United 
States' international obligations related to refugee protections, 
including the Refugee Convention and its Protocol and the Refugee Act 
of 1980. Although the United States is party to the 1967 Protocol, 
which incorporates, among others, Articles 17, 33, and 34 of the 1951 
Refugee Convention, the treaty is not self-executing and is not 
directly enforceable in U.S. law. It is the domestic implementing law 
that governs. The Supreme Court and other case law makes clear that the 
Protocol serves only as a useful guide in determining congressional 
intent in enacting the Refugee Act of 1980, because the Act sought to 
bring U.S. law into conformity with the Protocol. See, e.g., INS v. 
Stevic, 467 U.S. 407, 428 n.22 (1984); Khan v. Holder, 584 F.3d 773, 
783 (9th Cir. 2009). The United States Congress implemented U.S. 
obligations with respect to certain provisions of the Refugee 
Convention in the Refugee Act of 1980, including in sections 208, 235, 
and 241 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1158, 1225 and 1231, and DHS regulations, 
including 8 CFR part 208 and 1208. Section 208(d)(2) of the INA, 8 
U.S.C. 1158(d)(2), provides the Secretary with authority to grant 
employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for 
asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum.
    The IFR is limited in scope, merely ending the practice of 
automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or 
EADs for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD 
in certain employment categories. There is no mandate under 
international or United States law that DHS provide an automatic 
extension of employment authorization and/or EAD validity for aliens 
filing renewal EAD applications, and certainly not without adequately 
being vetted for continued eligibility. Aliens with a pending asylum 
application are permitted to still apply for employment authorization 
as nothing in this rule restricts the ability to apply for an EAD.\31\ 
Rather, the IFR, and this final rule, are consistent with the 
Secretary's discretionary authority regarding the grant of employment 
authorization for asylum applicants and the duration of such 
authorization, and with international obligations, including the 
favorable treatment of those seeking refuge from persecution in their 
countries. DHS finally notes that asylees (but not those with pending 
asylum applications), refugees, and certain other aliens are 
``qualified aliens'' for purpose of receiving public benefits to cover 
basic needs under Title IV of the Personal Responsibility and Work 
Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996.\32\ Therefore, even if there 
are gaps in employment on account of adjudication delays, these aliens 
may be able to obtain public benefits.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \31\ On December 4, 2025, USCIS changed the validity periods for 
certain other EAD categories, including pending asylum seeker 
(``C08'') to enhance screening and vetting efforts. See DHS, USCIS, 
Policy Alert, Subject: Updating Certain Employment Authorization 
Document Validity Periods (December 4, 2025), https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/policy-manual-updates/20251204-EmploymentAuthorizationValidity.pdf. Therefore, C08 applicants now 
must seek renewal of their EAD more often than under the previous 5-
year EAD validity period. DHS, however, cannot accurately predict 
whether this policy change will adversely affect EAD renewal 
processing times, as a likely increase in EAD renewals could be 
offset by other recent or future policy changes. For example, on 
February 23, 2026, DHS published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking 
proposing to modify filing and eligibility requirements for aliens 
requesting employment authorization based on a pending asylum 
application and an employment authorization document. See 91 FR 8616 
(Feb. 23, 2026). As of the publication of this final rule, the NPRM 
has not been finalized. If finalized as proposed, changes to 
eligibility for C08 employment authorization could significantly 
reduce the number of initial C08 applications and, by extension, the 
longer-term number of renewal applications.
    \32\ Public Law 104-193, 110 Stat. 2105, 2260 (1996), codified 
at 8 U.S.C. 1601-1646; see 8 U.S.C. 1641(b)(1) and (2) (defining 
asylees and refugees as ``qualified aliens'' eligible for federal 
public benefits); see also 8 U.S.C. 1611(a) (providing that an alien 
who is not defined as a ``qualified alien'' is not eligible for 
federal public benefits).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: A commenter referenced Article 17 of the Refugee 
Convention, which provides that refugees lawfully in the territory of 
the host state (which would include not only asylees and resettled 
refugees, but all aliens pursuing asylum claims who apply for renewal 
EADs), shall be the accorded the ``most favorable treatment accorded to 
nationals of a foreign country in the same circumstances.'' The 
commenter stated that, because the rule does not end all automatic 
extensions of the validity period of EADs for those applying for 
renewal (for example, TPS-based EAD validity extensions through FRN), 
it provides refugees applying to renew their EADs less favorable 
treatment than other foreign nationals. The commenter concluded that 
the rule is therefore issued in violation of Article 17 of the Refugee 
Convention and should be withdrawn.



    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters. The United States 
implemented the ``Wage-earning and Employment'' provision of Article 17 
of the 1951 Refugee Convention (as incorporated through the 1967 
Protocol) through sections 207 and 208 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1157, 1158, 
and implementing regulations at 8 CFR 207, 208 and 274a. Refugees (and 
asylees) \33\ have the right to employment authorization upon arrival, 
with minimal restrictions and are provided a pathway to lawful 
permanent residency because their status in the United States is 
permanent. This approach aligns with Article 17's requirements and 
complies with the U.S. obligation including that these individuals are 
not subject to more restrictive conditions than other foreign nationals 
in similar circumstances. Even if Article 17 were imposing a binding 
obligation, nothing in Article 17 requires DHS to provide employment 
authorization to noncitizens seeking refugee status or asylum before 
DHS or an immigration judge has made a final determination that they 
meet requirements for asylum or refugee status and grant the alien's 
application.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \33\ Asylees are aliens who are physically present in the United 
States or at a U.S. port of entry and who meets the definition of a 
refugee because he or she has a reasonable fear of persecution as 
defined in section 101(a)(42) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42). In 
contrast, a refugee is an alien located outside the United States 
who has been determined to have a fear of persecution. Asylees who 
meet the conditions of section 208 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158 are 
afforded the same treatment as refugees in regard to the wage-
earning and employment requirement of Article 17. Contrary to the 
commenter's assertion, applicants for asylum are not asylees or 
covered by Article 17. Even if they were, the United States 
implemented Article 17 through sections 207 and 208 of the INA, 8 
U.S.C. 1157, 1158.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    TPS applicants do not have the same protections and legal 
definition as refugees and asylees. Aliens granted TPS and TPS 
applicants are only temporarily in the United States on account of the 
Secretary's designation under section 244 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1254a, 
and 8 CFR part 244. As part of the TPS statute, Congress provided 
employment authorization for purposes of the entire designation period. 
See INA sec. 244(a)(1)(B) and (2), 8 U.S.C. 1254a(a)(1)(B) and (2). To 
comply with the law enacted by Congress, DHS is typically extending 
employment authorization via a Federal Register notice. However, TPS 
applicants still must apply for the renewal employment authorization 
document as part of the redesignation to obtain evidence of employment. 
Additionally, TPS may be terminated, and TPS never leads to permanent 
residency. See INA sec. 244(b)(3)(B), (h), 8 U.S.C. 1254a(b)(3)(B), 
(h). Thus, upon termination of TPS, TPS beneficiaries and applicants 
may lose employment authorization in the United States. See 8 CFR 
244.12 and 13. Refugees (and asylees) once granted, do not typically 
lose their refugee status and thus, their right to employment and path 
to lawful permanent residency and eventually citizenship. Therefore, 
the implementation scheme and the termination of automatic extension is 
not contrary to the United States international obligations.
2. DHS Justification and Need for the Rule
i. Security Rationale for the Rule
a. General Security Rationale Comments
    Comment: Multiple commenters said the IFR rests on a single 
asserted justification: the desire to complete vetting and security 
checks before approving an individual's \34\ work permit renewal, and 
DHS offers no other policy rationale for eliminating automatic 
extensions. Commenters stated the IFR is a reversal in policy without 
new evidence or a reasoned explanation and violates the APA. The 
commenters stated that DHS's sole rationale suffers from numerous 
problems and reveals a significant mismatch between the concern 
asserted and the real-world purpose and impact of automatic extensions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \34\ USCIS generally refers to ``aliens'' when discussing 
foreign nationals present in the United States. The term ``alien'' 
is a legal term defined in the INA that is used to describe any 
person who is not a citizen or national of the United States. See 
INA sec. 101(a)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(1). Some commenters 
used ``aliens'', but others may have used different terminology 
(such as person or individual). In general, when describing comments 
in this preamble, DHS has sought to mirror the language used in 
those comments, sometimes with quotation marks for clarity. 
Otherwise, DHS has used alien, or applicant, beneficiary, or 
requestor.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Additional commenters stated that DHS's security rationale for the 
IFR contradicts findings in its own 2024 Final Rule, which did not 
identify any adverse impact of automatic extensions on USCIS' ability 
to conduct security checks. Commenters stated that DHS offers no 
credible rationale for this new finding. Some commenters also stated 
that this rule ignores that DHS narrowly tailored the prior automatic 
extensions to certain applicants who applied for EAD renewals, which 
``reasonably assured'' the agency that the individual remained eligible 
for employment authorization and protected the program from abuse.
    Response: DHS does not agree that the IFR is a ``reversal of policy 
without new evidence or a reasoned explanation,'' that the 
justification for the rule is a ``mismatch between the concern asserted 
and the real-world purpose and impact of automatic extensions,'' or 
that DHS failed to consider important aspects of the program. DHS, in 
the IFR, explained that it is ending the practice of providing 
automatic extensions of employment authorization documents to enhance 
integrity in adjudications of employment authorization requests and 
better protect public safety and national security by ensuring that 
aliens are properly vetted and determined to continue to be eligible 
(and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable), for 
employment authorization before such authorization is provided to the 
alien. The Department also explained the permissibility of the change 
and specifically acknowledged and considered reliance interests that 
applicants could have engendered by the prior policy and explained why 
the policy considerations outweighed these interests. The IFR and this 
final rule reflect a continuation and refinement of DHS's longstanding 
focus on security, fraud prevention, and benefit integrity in the 
employment authorization context.
    In 2016, DHS eliminated the interim EAD and replaced it with the 
180-day automatic extension of employment authorization and explained 
that it would support the Department's vital mission of securing the 
nation from the many threats it faces. Therefore, DHS determined that 
the elimination of both the 90-day EAD processing timeframe and the 
issuance of interim EADs was necessary.\35\ This change in 2016 
reflected DHS's ``continued attention to security and commitment to 
improving adjudication processes, including technological advances in 
document production, to reduce fraud and address threats to national 
security.'' See 81 FR 82398 (Nov. 18, 2016) (AC21 Final Rule). DHS 
implemented the automatic extension of employment authorization to 
avoid gaps in employment without compromising national security and 
public safety given the context at the time. However, the automatic 
extension of employment authorization and/or EADs, whether 180 days or 
540 days, extends employment authorization based solely on the filing 
of a renewal EAD application, before USCIS has completed full vetting, 
resolved any derogatory information, and determined continuing 
eligibility for the benefit. Today, concerns regarding national



security, public safety, and integrity of immigration benefits are at a 
high point, and the President has directed DHS, through Executive 
Orders 14159 and 14161, to vet and screen aliens to the maximum extent 
possible and to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to 
unauthorized aliens.\36\ DHS notes there is no statutory requirement 
for USCIS to automatically extend EADs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35\ On November 18, 2016, as part of DHS's efforts to implement 
the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-first Century Act of 2000 
(AC21), DHS published a final regulation that eliminated interim 
EADs and provided for a 180-day automatic extension period. 81 FR 
82398 (Nov. 18, 2016).
    \36\ See E.O. 14161, Protecting the United States from Foreign 
Terrorists and Other National Security and Public Safety Threats 
(Jan. 20, 2025), 90 FR 8451, 8451 (Jan. 30, 2025); see E.O. 14159, 
Protecting the American People Against Invasion (Jan. 20, 2025), 90 
FR 8443, 8446 (Jan. 29, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS has provided a reasonable explanation for changing its policy, 
namely by giving greater weight to different policy considerations than 
in the past. DHS has concluded that, owing to current conditions and 
presidential directives, the security and program-integrity risks 
inherent in automatic extensions must be given greater weight than the 
benefits and different temporary circumstances that motivated prior 
rules. Given the inherent national security and public safety concerns 
that flow from granting immigration benefits (including EADs) to aliens 
before determining continued eligibility, DHS believes that rescinding 
the automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs is a 
necessary remedy. Ending the practice of providing automatic extensions 
of employment authorization and/or EADs enables DHS to better protect 
the public's safety and enhance benefit integrity.
b. Lack of Evidence Supporting Security Rationale
    Comment: Numerous commenters stated that DHS did not present 
evidence or data supporting the claim that automatic extensions pose 
security risks or that eliminating extensions would meaningfully 
enhance screening. Multiple commenters stated that the absence of any 
such evidence demonstrates that the purported problem does not exist. 
Several commenters wrote that for nearly 10 years, millions of workers 
have worked under automatic extensions, but the IFR provided no 
evidence showing that this system allowed security risks to persist or 
resulted in later security-based denials.
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertions. DHS 
explained in its AC21 Final Rule nearly 10 years ago that it was 
prioritizing national security and fraud concerns by eliminating the 
interim EAD and the mandated EAD 90-day processing timeframe. 
Specifically, DHS noted that ``any reduction in the level of 
eligibility and security vetting before issuing evidence of employment 
authorization, whether on an interim basis or otherwise, would both be 
contrary to its core mission and undermine the security, quality, and 
integrity of the documents issued.'' \37\ Consistent with that 
rationale, and as explained in the IFR, DHS now believes that 
eliminating the automatic extension of employment authorization and/or 
EADs will ensure that all identity verification, public safety and 
security related checks are completed, and that a determination has 
been made that the applicant continues to be eligible and merits a 
favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, before renewing 
employment authorization and/or an EAD. The IFR also clearly explained 
the relevance of the Boulder incident and its connection to the 
automatic extension,\38\ and why the measure was justified. Maintaining 
automatic extensions based upon the filing of an EAD renewal 
application would be inconsistent with DHS's stated benefit integrity, 
security and fraud-prevention objectives.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \37\ See 81 FR 82398 (Nov. 18, 2016) (AC21 Final Rule).
    \38\ See 90 FR 48799, 48808 (Oct. 30, 2025) (explaining that the 
need to fully vet applicants for renewal EADs became clear when an 
alien with an automatically extended EAD perpetrated a terrorist 
attack that injured many people in Boulder, Colorado on June 1, 
2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: Many commenters stated that DHS's reliance on a single 
anecdotal incident involving an individual in Boulder, Colorado, was 
insufficient evidence to justify a policy reversal negatively affecting 
hundreds of thousands of law-abiding workers and their employers. 
Commenters wrote that DHS did not demonstrate that the incident 
involved an automatic extension or how eliminating automatic extensions 
would have prevented this incident.
    Response: DHS disagrees that the IFR relied on insufficient 
evidence to justify the IFR's policy change as alleged by commenters. 
The concern addressed by the IFR and this final rule is that, under the 
automatic extension framework, an alien's employment authorization and/
or EAD validity could be extended for up to 540 days based only on the 
filing of a renewal application and without having fully vetted the 
alien for eligibility, including background and security checks. When 
employment authorization is automatically extended before those checks 
are complete, aliens who may no longer qualify for the benefit, or who 
present public safety or national security concerns, are able to remain 
employment-authorized. This allows aliens who could be public safety or 
national security threats to use associated documentation to 
potentially obtain other credentials, such as driver's licenses, and 
use such document, in turn, to engage in nefarious activities. For 
example, an alien could rent a car by using the driver's license 
obtained with an automatically extended EAD as an identity document and 
subsequently use the car to perpetrate a terrorist attack or other 
criminal activity. As explained in the IFR and throughout this final 
rule, DHS has found that these public safety and national security 
concerns outweigh the interim impacts that may result from a temporary 
lapse in an individual aliens' employment authorization and/or 
documentation while USCIS completes refreshed vetting, evaluates any 
new derogatory information, and determines that the alien remains 
eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if 
applicable.
    The IFR references the attack by an alien against peaceful 
demonstrators in Boulder, Colorado, as a concrete example of an alien 
in possession of an automatic extension that highlighted the urgent 
need to mitigate additional public safety emergencies, as well as the 
importance of ensuring aliens are not granted employment authorization 
until adjudicative review has been completed. The alien responsible for 
the Boulder, Colorado, incident was the beneficiary of an automatic 
extension of his employment authorization, and is thus one example of 
an alien who remained employment authorized without having undergone 
full vetting for eligibility or security concerns. Attacks, such as the 
one in Boulder, Colorado, are tough to predict, but they may not be 
impossible to stop with proper and thorough vetting and intelligence 
sharing among government agencies each time an alien is seeking 
immigration benefits.\39\ DHS is prioritizing the completion of vetting



prior to granting an immigration benefit to ensure public safety and 
national security and to mitigate the immediate risks posed to 
Americans. Ending automatic extensions based on the filing of an EAD 
renewal application alone addresses that systemic vulnerability. It 
ensures that continued employment authorization and its documentation 
is conferred only after USCIS has completed refreshed vetting, 
evaluated any new derogatory information, and determined that the alien 
remains eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, if applicable. As discussed in the Executive Summary, 
President Trump has directed DHS to ``vet and screen to the maximum 
degree possible'' all aliens within the United States and ensure that 
``employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien.'' 
\40\ In line with presidential priorities, DHS is prioritizing program 
integrity, public safety, and national security and believes the 
benefits of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh the risks 
of potential temporary lapses in employment authorization.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \39\ The public, including members from Congress, criticized 
immigration and law enforcement authorities, including DHS, for not 
detecting the alien's activities and not protecting the public. They 
emphasized the urgency to fix security vulnerabilities. See House of 
Representatives Homeland Security Committee, ``Chairman Pfluger, 
Green Request DHS Documents on Suspect in Boulder Terror Attack'' 
(June 4, 2025), https://homeland.house.gov/2025/06/04/chairmen-green-pfluger-request-dhs-documents-on-suspect-in-boulder-terror-attack (``This tragedy is indicative of a heightened terrorism 
threat on U.S. soil, signaling an urgent need for increased homeland

who are unlawfully present in the United States, as Soliman

several major acts of antisemitic terror this year alone, including 
the recent assassination of two Israeli embassy staffers in our 
nation's capital.'').
    \40\ See E.O. 14161, Protecting the United States from Foreign

(Jan. 20, 2025), 90 FR 8451, 8451 (Jan. 30, 2025); see E.O. 14159, 
Protecting the American People Against Invasion (Jan. 20, 2025), 90 
FR 8443, 8446 (Jan. 29, 2025).

c. Prior Vetting of Renewal Applicants and Existing Security Measures
    Comment: One commenter stated that DHS ``offered no credible 
evidence of security risks associated with'' the automatic extension of 
employment authorization and/or EADs, and that the IFR therefore 
``lacks any substantive rationale.'' Other commenters claimed the 
security rationale for the rule is inadequate given that aliens 
applying for EAD renewals have already been vetted. Some commenters 
said many EAD holders are also likely to have other pending 
applications before USCIS with evidentiary submissions, background, and 
identity documents that allow for additional agency vetting.
    Response: DHS disagrees that the IFR lacks a rationale. DHS is 
prioritizing the completion of proper vetting before issuing 
immigration benefits and cannot continue to extend employment 
authorization or EADs without determining that the applicant continues 
to be eligible and, when applicable, merits a favorable exercise of 
discretion, regardless of any prior vetting that may have been 
conducted in connection with past or pending benefit requests. DHS is 
not required by statute to provide an automatic extension of employment 
authorization and/or EADs. Rather, DHS is exercising its authority to 
structure employment authorization processes in a manner that ensures 
the integrity of the immigration benefit provided, and better advances 
national security, public safety, and program integrity.
    Comment: Commenters wrote that the IFR misstates how security 
vetting works, stating that all relevant background check processes 
occur independently of whether a worker has an unexpired EAD. The 
commenter said many security flags require follow up investigation, 
interagency coordination, and a full review of classified or sensitive 
information that can take considerable time to evaluate, and these 
assessments occur within the structured adjudicative framework, not 
during the mechanical, threshold review of an EAD-renewal request.
    Response: DHS disagrees with the premise of these comments. While 
some background checks and security review processes may be ongoing, 
others are initiated when USCIS receives a request and are completed in 
connection with that adjudication. There are no statutory or other 
regulatory limitations on USCIS' authority to conduct background and 
security checks to determine eligibility for employment authorization. 
Additionally, background checks and vetting can be a lengthy process 
that may require additional time to resolve or to make an eligibility 
determination. For USCIS to renew an immigration benefit, the applicant 
must meet the relevant eligibility standards and merit a favorable 
exercise of discretion, if applicable. All individuals who apply for 
immigration benefits, including applications for employment 
authorization, are required to submit and sign the application 
authorizing the release of any information from their records that 
USCIS may need to determine eligibility for the benefit sought. By 
signing and submitting the form to USCIS, the applicant consents to 
verification by USCIS, as well as use of information to determine 
initial or continued benefit eligibility. Given the, at times, lengthy 
vetting process, the previous practice allowed automatic extension of 
EADs to aliens that would otherwise be found ineligible after USCIS 
initiates or resolves background check information.
    The previous practice of automatically extending employment 
authorization for a period of up to 540 days prioritized EAD backlog 
management over program integrity, public safety and national security. 
Requiring completion of adjudicative review before extending employment 
authorization and/or EADs better aligns with DHS's vetting 
responsibilities and the policy priorities of enhancing program 
integrity, public safety, and national security.
    Comment: Multiple commenters stated that USCIS remains free to 
conduct continuous vetting during the renewal process and deny the 
renewal application and terminate employment authorization immediately 
should it identify new information indicating a security concern.
    Some commenters stated that DHS already has the capability to 
perform continuous screening and vetting, such as through ATLAS and the 
Continuous Immigration Vetting (CIV) program, which allow for ongoing 
information sharing and monitoring of individuals in the immigration 
system, stating these systems can identify security concerns at any 
time, not just during the renewal application process.
    Response: DHS continues to implement various strategies to address 
public safety and national security concerns. These efforts include, 
but are not limited to, the use of continuous screening and vetting 
capabilities, interagency information-sharing, and enhancements to 
identity and security verification processes. However, these tools do 
not obviate the need to complete appropriate vetting and screening 
before extending employment authorization. Conducting background 
checks, whether continuously or at certain intervals (for example, when 
an alien again applies for an immigration benefit), is only one part of 
the overall vetting and screening process.
    Furthermore, derogatory information identified during the 
background check process must still be reviewed and resolved.\41\ DHS 
believes that before any immigration benefit is granted, such as an 
extension of employment authorization and/or an EAD, USCIS should 
complete the vetting and screening process and determine that the alien 
continues to be eligible for the benefit and merits a favorable 
exercise of discretion, as applicable.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \41\ Thus, even with CIV, USCIS is required to manually resolve 
derogatory information, which needs time. See DHS/USCIS/PIA-076 
Continuous Immigration Vetting, at 8, https://www.dhs.gov/publication/dhsuscispia-076-continuous-immigration-vetting (last 
updated March 31, 2023) (``Although automation assists with the 
identification of national security concerns, FDNS officers also 
manually review each hit to confirm the validity, relevancy, and 
accuracy of the information and to determine if the information is 
actionable, consistent with DHS authorities. If actionable, USCIS 
FDNS may perform administrative investigations to produce findings 
to sufficiently inform adjudications.'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: A commenter stated that the rule discounts the multiple 
layers of



vetting and monitoring tools that are already being conducted by 
employers to identify potential security threats, including Form I-9 
verification, E-Verify participation, and criminal background checks.
    Response: DHS will not delegate to employers its responsibility to 
enhance program integrity and better protect public safety and national 
security. The varying levels of vetting by different employers are not 
a substitute for the vetting that USCIS conducts. USCIS has 
information-sharing agreements with various agencies within the U.S. 
government and foreign partners. Therefore, vetting from an employer is 
typically not comparable to USCIS access and vetting. In addition, Form 
I-9 and E-Verify are not used for national security and public safety 
vetting. Form I-9 is required for all U.S. employers to document 
identity and employment authorization for every worker hired. E-Verify 
is a voluntary program that electronically compares the information on 
Form I-9 with SSA and DHS records to confirm employment 
eligibility.\42\ Criteria for security checks and vetting depend upon 
the immigration benefit sought as well as various other factors, and 
each benefit request has its own requirements and vulnerabilities. DHS 
does not believe that renewing employment authorization should be an 
exception to the stated policy objectives of better protecting public 
safety and national security and ensuring continued eligibility and 
that the applicant warrants a favorable exercise of discretion (as 
applicable) prior to issuing immigration benefits. USCIS is exercising 
its full authority to investigate immigration benefit requests filed by 
aliens who may pose risks to the national security and public safety of 
the United States while adhering to the provisions of the INA and 
applicable laws, as outlined in DHS Delegation of Authority 0150.1 and 
15006.\43\ The elimination of automatic extensions of employment 
authorization and/or an EAD based on the filing of a renewal 
application is one component of this broader effort to enhance program 
integrity and safeguard the United States.

d. Rule Would Not Strengthen Security
    Comment: One commenter said justifying the rule under ``the guise 
of national security is ironic'' because the rule's likely consequence 
in derailing the livelihoods of aliens may push them to violate the law 
for survival. Another commenter stated that most of the public safety 
and national security risk created by malicious aliens stems from their 
presence in the United States rather than their ability to work and 
encouraged DHS to study how significant the risk associated with income 
generated through lawful employment is compared to the risk associated 
with presence on U.S. soil. A commenter stated that DHS implicitly
