    DHS acknowledges the commenter's view that the primary public 
safety and national security risk posed by malicious actors arises from 
their presence in the United States and not solely from their 
continuing ability to work. Even so, DHS considers it important and 
appropriate to use its authorities to reduce risks associated with both 
presence and employment. Access to lawful employment can provide 
malicious actors with financial resources, routine cover for their 
activities, and access to certain workplaces and facilities. Limiting 
the ability of aliens with potentially malicious intent to retain EADs 
and/or employment authorization, and to lawfully work and generate 
income, without full vetting is therefore a meaningful component of 
DHS's broader efforts to safeguard benefit integrity, national security 
and public safety.
    For these reasons, DHS continues to view measures that reduce the 
likelihood that malicious actors can obtain or rely on employment 
authorization and related secure documentation as worthwhile.
    Comment: Some commenters stated that, if the goal is to strengthen 
vetting integrity, the logical solution is to expedite case processing 
so that all



background checks and reviews are completed more quickly. One commenter 
also stated that workers should be able to maintain their employment 
authorization and support their families while vetting occurs.
    Response: DHS undertakes every effort to complete case processing 
as expeditiously as possible while being conscious of the importance of 
vetting every benefit requestor thoroughly for eligibility, including 
vetting for criminal activity and other security risks. DHS believes 
screening, vetting, and determining continued eligibility before 
granting a renewal of employment authorization and/or documentation is 
essential to enhance program integrity and better protect public safety 
and national security. Such processes, however, especially given the 
volume of initial and renewal EAD applicants that USCIS encounters, 
necessarily take time. Note that expediting a case generally means that 
USCIS would move the benefit request to the front of the processing 
queue to the detriment of those who may have filed earlier but does not 
otherwise change the time needed to properly conduct screening and 
vetting and determine continued eligibility. To the extent that these 
commenters suggest that USCIS should expedite all EAD renewal 
applications and thus put renewal EAD applications in front of other 
applications in the processing queue, DHS maintains that this would not 
be a viable solution and would not enhance program integrity or better 
protect public safety and national security.
    Comment: Multiple commenters stated that the security benefit of 
the rule is incremental because renewal applicants have already been 
robustly vetted and will not be re-vetted until the EAD renewal is 
adjudicated, stating that this second vetting by USCIS occurs even if 
EAD extensions are automatic.
    Response: USCIS must ensure that all aliens who request immigration 
benefits from USCIS are eligible for the benefit sought, merit a 
favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable, and do not pose a 
threat to national security or public safety. It is necessary and 
within USCIS' authority to continue investigating immigration benefit 
requests and to assess whether an applicant has established ongoing 
eligibility and warrants favorable discretion, if applicable, and 
whether they pose a risk to the national security and public safety of 
the United States, before issuing immigration benefits. This includes 
renewal applications for employment authorization and/or EADs, which 
may reveal new derogatory information or changed circumstances that 
were not present at the time of the initial grant.
    Comment: One commenter stated that the IFR would cause DHS 
resources to be spent on EAD processing while people remain in the 
United States without decisions on their ability to stay, stating that 
the rule ``punishes applicants, families, communities, and employers 
for USCIS' failure to timely process applications.'' Another commenter 
similarly stated that the rule ``does not meaningfully improve homeland 
security'' and would divert resources rather than supporting security 
or operational efficiency.
    Response: DHS is dedicated to ensuring that all aliens who enter 
and remain in the United States do not present threats to national 
security or public safety. USCIS plays an instrumental role in 
preventing terrorists and other bad actors from harboring in the United 
States, and screening and vetting should be prioritized over purely 
expedient adjudications to that end. DHS will continue to work to 
reduce frivolous, fraudulent, and meritless EAD filings to free up 
adjudicatory and other resources to better ensure national security and 
program integrity. Therefore, DHS does not agree that focusing 
resources on careful EAD renewal adjudications ``diverts'' resources 
from security; rather, such adjudications are themselves a core 
security function of USCIS.
e. Other Comments on Security Rationale
    Comment: Some commenters expressed concern with DHS's rationale 
that bad actors could benefit from EADs being automatically extended 
and the income generated from working to support ``nefarious 
activities,'' stating that it is speculative, discriminatory, and 
perpetuates anti-immigrant rhetoric. A commenter said this is 
particularly dangerous language for Asian American communities who face 
a persistent narrative as the ``perpetual foreigner'' and will only 
contribute to that ``pernicious stereotype'' and support unfounded 
suspicions that Asians are agents of foreign governments.
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertions. DHS ended 
the practice of providing automatic extension of employment 
authorization and/or EADs based on the filing of a renewal EAD 
application to ensure continued eligibility and prioritizing the proper 
vetting and screening of aliens in furtherance of its mission. This 
rule does not target Asian American communities or any other specific 
group of aliens. Instead, this rule, as written, applies to all aliens 
who were eligible for the automatic extension of their employment 
authorization and/or EADs under former 8 CFR 274a.13(d). As explained 
in the IFR and this final rule, DHS is prioritizing the completion of 
vetting prior to granting an immigration benefit to enhance program 
integrity and better protect public safety and national security. The 
examples provided in the IFR illustrated the broader concern that 
extending employment authorization before completing vetting can allow 
aliens who may present public safety or national security risks to 
retain employment authorization. Ending automatic extensions based on 
the filing of an EAD renewal application ensures that continued 
employment authorization is conferred only after USCIS has completed 
renewed vetting, evaluated any new derogatory information, and 
determined that the alien remains eligible and continues to merit a 
favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. DHS believes that the 
program integrity, public safety, and national security benefits of 
eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh the risks of 
potential temporary lapses in employment authorization.
    Comment: Commenters stated that, while DHS repeatedly cites 
purported national security concerns as justification for the IFR, the 
``underemphasized yet explicit'' motivation for the IFR is a reduction 
in EAD filings overall. They stated that the rule is intended to 
generally deter immigration, specifically for asylum seekers, and that 
DHS ignores that asylees and refugees are authorized employment even if 
the expiration date on their EAD has passed. One commenter stated that, 
while DHS claims it is ending the practice of automatically renewing 
EADs for refugees and asylees to take a ``uniform approach'' and avoid 
``the potential for confusion'' of employers, it does not quantify the 
potential confusion or justify why it cannot at least provide automatic 
renewals for refugees and asylees, who are authorized to work incident 
to their status.
    The commenters concluded that the IFR is meant to undermine and 
frustrate those with legal work authorization and will cause 
unnecessary lapses in work authorization creating unreasonable 
obstacles, citing DHS's referenced goal of providing a ``comprehensive 
policy solution'' and stating the rule is actually intended to 
unnecessarily confuse employers, frustrate immigrants' ability to work, 
and push more into ``dire straits.'' Another commenter questioned 
enhanced security as the true intent of



the rule, suggesting other motives such as intentionally causing aliens 
to fall out of status and lose their jobs.
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters that the goal of this 
rule is to reduce EAD filings overall, generally deter immigration or 
to ``unnecessarily confuse employers'' and ``frustrate immigrants' 
ability to work.'' As previously stated, the purpose of this rule is to 
prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens, to ensure 
continued eligibility, and to confirm that applicants continue to merit 
favorable exercises of discretion, if applicable, before granting new 
periods of employment authorization and/or new EADs by ending the 
practice of automatically extending the validity of employment 
authorization and/or EADs.
    DHS recognizes that aliens who are granted asylum or refugee status 
are authorized employment incident to their asylum or refugee status. 
As explained in the IFR, aliens who are authorized employment incident 
to their status \48\ and are maintaining their respective immigration 
status, such as asylees and refugees, will continue to be employment 
authorized while maintaining their immigration status, regardless of 
the expiration date on their EAD. Aliens who are authorized employment 
incident to status will continue to have the choice to file Form I-765 
to obtain EADs for proof of identity. As stated in the IFR, DHS is 
taking a uniform approach for all aliens by ending the practice of 
providing automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs.

    Comment: One commenter said that eliminating automatic extensions 
does not serve E.O. 14159, Protecting the American People Against 
Invasion, which orders DHS and other agencies to ensure that employment 
authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien in the United

impact on this mandate, as the purpose of such automatic extensions is 
to afford USCIS the time and resources to make a robust determination 
in compliance with its statutory and regulatory obligations in cases 
where aliens were already approved for employment authorization.
    Response: DHS maintains that this rule accomplishes the mandate of 
E.O. 14159. This executive order directs the Secretary of Homeland 
Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Attorney 
General, in Section 16 to take all appropriate action to align any 
departmental activities with the policies set out by the President, to 
ensure that ``employment authorization is not provided to any 
unauthorized alien in the United States.'' As stated in the IFR and 
this rule, ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of 
EADs is consistent with this instruction in E.O. 14159 because a 
previous grant of employment authorization does not mean that an 
applicant remains indefinitely eligible for employment authorization, 
and it is necessary to review eligibility to ensure that an alien's 
circumstances have not changed such that the alien is no longer 
eligible. Granting automatic extensions of employment without proper 
vetting and full adjudication to ensure continued eligibility is not 
consistent with E.O. 14159 or with current priorities.

    USCIS routinely evaluates filing volumes relative to adjudicative 
resources and reallocates workloads to address priorities as 
appropriate and feasible, including between initial and renewal EAD 
filings. The IFR explains that, while USCIS continues to work to 
improve processing times and reduce backlogs, DHS has determined that 
automatic extensions are inconsistent with ensuring continued 
eligibility or with current security and vetting priorities. DHS 
believes that the reasoning provided in the IFR is appropriate and that 
the purpose of the IFR has been adequately justified. Ending automatic 
extensions based on the filing of an EAD renewal application ensures 
that continued employment authorization is conferred only after USCIS 
has completed renewed vetting, evaluated any new derogatory 
information, and determined that the alien remains eligible and 
continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. 
DHS believes that the program integrity, public safety, and national 
security benefits of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh 
the risks of potential temporary lapses in employment authorization.
    As discussed in greater detail in response to a previous comment in 
Section IV.C.2.i.a. of this preamble, the decision to end automatic 
extensions reflects a change in how DHS balances operational efficiency 
and continuity of employment against these security and benefit 
integrity concerns rather than an inconsistency in DHS's underlying 
commitment to timely adjudications.
    DHS expects that overall, EAD filing rates will substantially 
decline and free up adjudicative resources to reduce



renewal EAD processing times. Decreasing processing times would result 
in a reduced need for aliens filing renewal EAD applications to rely on 
an automatic extension of their EAD to avoid potential lapses. Since 
the IFR became effective on October 30, 2025, USCIS has seen a steady 
decrease in overall EAD filings. See Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of 
this preamble. USCIS notes that decreased EAD filing rates support the 
point made in the IFR: that the potential for an alien to have a lapse, 
and in particular the duration of any lapse, is speculative and could 
be outweighed by the harm posed by automatic extensions.

USCIS is primarily a fee-based agency. See sec. 286(m), 8 U.S.C. 
1356(m) that is generally not appropriated by Congress.
    \59\ See, e.g., USCIS Immigration Fees and Related Procedures by 
H-R.1 Reconciliation Bill, 91 FR 22952 (Apr. 29, 2026).

iv. ``Proper Planning'' Rationale
    Comment: Multiple commenters stated that DHS's assertion that 
renewal applicants' ``proper planning'' could avoid lapses in work 
authorization is false and ignores operational realities and backlogs, 
asserting that EAD renewal applicants cannot ``properly plan'' for 
every unforeseen circumstance that may affect USCIS processing times. 
Commenters stated that the 2016 and 2024 Final Rules were issued to 
address unforeseen circumstances that neither the agency nor applicants 
could reasonably anticipate.
    Commenters cited processing backlog figures when stating that 
applicants who follow the agency's recommendation not to file more than 
180 days in advance face unavoidable employment gaps. Multiple 
commenters stated that many EAD applications, including renewals, took 
longer than 180 days to adjudicate.\60\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \60\ See USCIS, Immigration and Citizenship Data, FY 22 
Appropriations Reporting Requirement--Application Processing Data 
for September, 2025, https://www.uscis.gov/tools/reports-and-studies/immigration-and-citizenship-data (last visited Feb. 13, 
2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Response: As previously discussed, DHS has determined that the 
potential impact that some aliens may experience a temporary lapse, of 
unpredictable duration, in the validity of their employment 
authorization and/or EAD is outweighed by the need to better protect 
the safety and security of the American people by ensuring that 
employment authorization and/or an EAD is not granted until USCIS has 
thoroughly vetted and screened the applicant, resolved any derogatory 
hits, and determined that the alien continues to be eligible for the 
immigration benefit and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as 
applicable.
    USCIS provides case processing times for select forms and locations 
to inform the public how long it generally takes to process benefit 
requests.\61\ USCIS updates case processing times on its website 
monthly with the latest available data. The processing times



fluctuate over time and are based on how long it took USCIS to complete 
(meaning issue an approval or denial notice) 80% of adjudicated cases 
over the six months prior to the posted processing times.\62\ Each case 
is unique, and some cases may take longer than others. Processing times 
should be used as a reference point, not an absolute measure of how a 
case will take to be completed. The fact that a particular form type 
and category shows a processing time slightly longer than 6 months at 
the 80th percentile does not mean that a particular application will 
take longer than 6 months to approve or deny. Processing times, because 
they represent a 6-month reporting period, are a lagging indicator as 
it pertains to more recent policy changes and related filing rates. 
Processing times are also based on the time it took USCIS to approve or 
deny applications, which can be skewed by the time needed to request 
additional evidence before an application is approved or denied.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \61\ See USCIS, Case Processing Times, https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times (last visited May 8, 2026).
    \62\ See USCIS, Case Processing Times, https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times/more-info (last visited Apr. 22, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Although USCIS generally recommends that applicants not file 
requests to renew EADs more than 180 days before the expiration of 
their EADs, there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain 
date ahead of expiration. Proper planning by applicants includes filing 
early, rather than close to the expiration of the EAD, and ensuring 
that all evidence needed for USCIS to determine eligibility has been 
submitted with the application at the time of filing. While proper 
planning might not avoid a temporary lapse in employment authorization 
and/or documentation in all cases, it should help to reduce the 
potential of a lapse and shorten the duration if a lapse were to occur.
3. Rationale for Eliminating the Automatic Extension of EADs
    Comment: A couple of commenters opposed the rule without providing 
their rationale. They supported automatic extension of employment 
authorization, and the provision of employment authorization documents, 
without vetting or reviewing aliens' applications. One called the 
regulatory change ``wrong'' and ``inhumane.''
    Response: As discussed in greater detail in response to more 
specific comments elsewhere in this preamble, to the extent that some 
renewal applicants might face a temporary lapse in employment 
authorization and/or documentation, DHS believes this approach is 
nevertheless justified as it will enhance program integrity and better 
protect public safety and national security. Ending automatic 
extensions based on the filing of an EAD renewal application ensures 
that continued employment authorization is conferred only after USCIS 
has completed renewed vetting, evaluated any new derogatory 
information, and determined that the alien remains eligible and 
continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. 
DHS believes that the program integrity, public safety, and national 
security benefits of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh 
the risks of potential temporary lapses in employment authorization and 
or EAD validity.
    In addition to these independent reasons for promulgating this 
rule, DHS is acting in accord with presidential directives. As 
discussed in the Executive Summary, E.O. 14159 instructs the Secretary 
of Homeland Security, alongside the Secretary of State and Attorney 
General, to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to 
unauthorized aliens.\63\ Furthermore, removing automatic extensions of 
employment authorization and/or EADs aligns with Executive Order 14161, 
which requires DHS to vet and screen all aliens within the United 
States ``to the maximum degree possible,'' \64\ and Presidential 
Proclamation 10949, which orders DHS to ensure that aliens already 
within the United States do not support foreign terrorists or bear 
hostile attitudes toward its citizens, culture, government, 
institutions, or founding principles.\65\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \63\ See Executive Order, Protecting the American People Against 
Invasion, 90 FR 8443, 8446 (Jan. 29, 2025).
    \64\ See 90 FR 8451, 8451 (Jan. 31, 2025).
    \65\ Proclamation 10949 (June 4, 2025), 90 FR 24497-98 (June 10, 
2025).

4. Impact on USCIS Processing
i. Administrative Burden and Efficiency
    Comment: Multiple commenters asserted that the IFR would increase 
the administrative burden on the government and further slow the 
adjudication process and USCIS' ability to timely processes EAD 
renewals. A commenter stated that eliminating the automatic extension 
does not speed up adjudications, but simply ``creates a guaranteed 
administrative failure'' and will lead to increases in emergency 
service requests, inquiries, and appeals. Similarly, another commenter 
wrote that the IFR would create unnecessary administrative 
inefficiencies as USCIS would likely face an increase in prematurely 
filed renewal applications, multiple submissions from applicants 
fearing gaps in employment, and additional employer verification 
requests during pending periods. One commenter reasoned it would be 
less burdensome for USCIS to not implement the IFR than to implement 
it.
    Other commenters stated that the Agency has been unable to timely 
adjudicate EAD renewals for several years and the IFR does not resolve 
the current operational reality to avoid gaps in employment 
authorization, because even when applicants file at the earliest 
possible date, their current EADs often expire long before adjudication 
concludes as USCIS processing times are sometimes 8 to 11 months. A 
commenter remarked that backlogs and resulting lapses in employment 
authorization are not the fault of EAD renewal applicants.
    One commenter stated that the IFR does not account for the impact 
of other DHS rules, including the recent Duration of Status proposed 
rule,\66\ which would increase the adjudication workload on USCIS staff 
and jeopardize the Agency's ability to ensure extensions can be 
consistently processed within existing timeframes.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \66\ DHS, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Establishing a 
Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure 
for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and 
Representatives of Foreign Information Media, 90 FR 42070 (proposed 
Aug. 28, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Response: DHS acknowledges that backlogs and operational challenges 
were justifications for the 2022 and 2024 Temporary Final Rules and the 
2024 Final Rule. However, as DHS explained in the IFR, the automatic 
extension of the validity of an EAD grants the benefit of extending an 
alien's expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a 
timely renewal EAD application and without first completing 
adjudicative review and related vetting, including resolution of 
derogatory information identified during the vetting process. That is, 
the benefit is granted without USCIS first performing the following 
actions: an eligibility determination; completing vetting and screening 
checks; resolving potential hits of derogatory information in 
connection with the alien; and a determination that the employment 
authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if 
applicable. The automatic extension, therefore, poses a security 
vulnerability that could allow bad actors to continue to work and 
generate income to potentially finance nefarious activities that pose 
an imminent threat to the American public. Granting benefits without 
proper vetting and full adjudication is contrary to the



mission of DHS and poses a threat to the safety and security of the 
American people.\67\ DHS believes that this concern outweighs concerns 
about potential backlogs and operational challenges that may result in 
temporary lapses of employment authorization and/or EAD validity.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \67\ See, e.g., Conference Report to accompany H.R. 4567 [Report 
108-774], ``Making Appropriations for the Department of Homeland 
Security for the Fiscal Year Ending September 30, 2005,'' p. 74 
(Oct. 9, 2004), https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CRPT-108hrpt774/pdf/CRPT-108hrpt774.pdf (recommending, among other things, the creation 
of an organization to conduct ``law enforcement/background checks on 
every applicant, beneficiary, and petitioner prior to granting 
immigration benefits.'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As DHS stated in the IFR, it is the policy of the Administration 
``to faithfully execute the immigration laws against all inadmissible 
and removable aliens, particularly those aliens who threaten the safety 
or security of the American people.'' \68\ Pursuant to this policy, the 
Secretary of Homeland Security, in collaboration with the Secretary of 
State and the Attorney General, has been directed to ``rescind the 
policy decisions of the previous administration that led to the 
increased or continued presence of illegal aliens in the United States, 
and align any and all departmental activities with the policies set out 
by this order and the immigration laws'' including by ``ensuring that 
the parole authority under section 212(d)(5) of the INA (8 U.S.C. 
1182(d)(5)) is exercised on only a case-by-case basis in accordance 
with the plain language of the statute'' and by ``ensuring that 
designations of TPS are consistent with the provisions of section 244 
of the INA (8 U.S.C. 1254a), and that such designations are 
appropriately limited in scope and made for only so long as may be 
necessary to fulfill the textual requirements of that statute.'' \69\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \68\ See 90 FR 8443, 8446.
    \69\ See 90 FR 8443, 8446.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS has already taken a number of actions in support of the 
directives described in the preceding paragraph.\70\ Thus, in addition 
to the serious concerns relating to automatic EAD extensions discussed 
previously, DHS is taking steps independent of this rule, including 
narrowing the use of parole and to align TPS designations with 
statutory criteria, that are likely to result in lower EAD filing 
volumes and improve renewal EAD application processing times.

    With respect to the comment about the impact of other DHS rules 
that could impact the adjudication workload on USCIS and thus, the 
processing timeframe of EAD renewals: DHS published a final rule 
eliminating duration of status (D/S) on July 17, 2026.\71\ DHS agrees 
with commenters that there will be an increase in the filing volume of

received by USCIS following September 15, 2026, the effective date of

    On December 4, 2025, USCIS changed the validity periods for certain 
other EAD categories, including C08s, to enhance its screening and

ii. Processing Timelines
    Comment: One commenter asserted that early filing routinely leads 
to rejections or denials, and that filing fees are not returned to the 
applicant if they are rejected for early filing. Another commenter 
reasoned that since USCIS' policy only allows service inquiries after 
365 days, this would limit employer and employee's options for 
addressing delays.
    Response: Although USCIS generally recommends that applicants not 
file to renew their EAD more than 180 days before the expiration of 
their current EAD, USCIS will not reject or deny an otherwise eligible 
Form I-765 renewal solely because it was filed sooner. The USCIS 
Contact Center is an available resource and provides specific customer 
service options, including how to obtain assistance if a case is 
rejected or denied.\75\ Further, USCIS does not have a set rule that 
applicants must wait 365 days to submit a service inquiry. Rather, 
USCIS posts processing times on its Case Processing Times web page, 
which includes a tool to help determine whether an applicant can 
request an update on their case. Depending on the applicant's receipt 
date and other factors, USCIS provides an estimated date for when a 
case inquiry may be submitted or a link to submit a case inquiry.\76\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \75\ See USCIS, Contact Us (last visited Feb. 3, 2026), https://www.uscis.gov/about-us/contact-us.
    \76\ See Frequently Asked Questions About Processing Times, 
USCIS, https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times/processing-times-faqs 
(last visited Mar. 23, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS recognizes that an alien who is authorized employment incident 
to their status may still wish to obtain an EAD. Aliens who are 
authorized employment incident to status will continue to have the 
choice to file Form I-765 to obtain an EAD as proof of identity and 
employment authorization. DHS also recognizes that, in the absence of 
automatic extensions, some aliens may experience temporary lapses in 
employment authorization and/or EAD validity if their renewal 
applications are not adjudicated before their current EADs expire. 
However, DHS maintains that the security risks associated with 
automatically extending employment authorization and/or EADs without 
updated vetting and adjudication outweigh the benefits of using 
automatic



extensions to ensure that aliens have uninterrupted employment 
authorization and/or EADs. While DHS cannot guarantee that every 
renewal will be adjudicated before the existing EAD expires, DHS 
believes that proper planning by applicants, combined with reduced 
filing volumes and ongoing operational improvements, may lessen the 
likelihood and duration of lapses.
iii. Procedural Fairness
    Comment: Many commenters expressed concerns about the procedural 
fairness of applicants losing work authorization due to USCIS 
processing times. Specifically, some commenters said that the IFR would 
punish people who are following the law, complying with immigration 
procedures, or, more generally, ``have done everything right,'' losing 
status through ``no fault of their own.'' Likewise, several commenters 
remarked that the current automatic extension policy helps prevent 
nonimmigrants from being punished for delays beyond their control. A 
few commenters said that removing automatic extensions without 
addressing processing delays would be unjust.
    A few other commenters remarked that the IFR would contradict 
administrative equity or fairness. Other commenters said that the rule 
would contradict DHS's own acknowledgement that interruptions in work 
authorization cause ``substantial and unnecessary harm.'' A couple of 
commenters said that the rule would penalize law abiding applicants due 
to an extreme individual case.
    Response: DHS recognizes that many renewal applicants diligently 
comply with filing requirements and that delays in adjudication may not 
be within their control. DHS also acknowledges that prior rulemakings, 
including the 2016 and 2024 rules, sought to mitigate the impact of 
processing delays on workers and employers by providing automatic 
extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs.
    However, as explained in the IFR, DHS has reassessed the balance 
between continuity of employment authorization and the need to ensure 
that immigration benefits are granted only after appropriate vetting 
and eligibility determinations. There is no statutory entitlement to an 
automatic extension of employment authorization. Employment 
authorization in the relevant categories is generally discretionary and 
time-limited, and renewal requires a new adjudication. The IFR and this 
final rule do not deny renewal to eligible applicants; they simply 
require that continued employment authorization be based on an approved 
renewal application rather than on the mere filing of that application.
    DHS has determined that granting automatic extensions without 
updated vetting and adjudication is inconsistent with its mission and 
with E.O.s directing DHS to ensure that employment authorization is not 
provided to unauthorized aliens and that all aliens in the United 
States are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible. While 
DHS is mindful of the hardships that may arise from temporary lapses in 
employment authorization, the need to protect national security and 
public safety, and to enhance the integrity of immigration benefits, 
justifies discontinuing automatic extensions.
iv. General or Mixed Feedback on USCIS Processing
    Comment: Several commenters asked questions about USCIS operational 
metrics, processing times, use of RFEs, and remedial actions for 
applicants who lose their jobs due to adjudication delays. A commenter 
agreed that a 540-day extension was too long because there should be 
thorough vetting before granting EADs and/or employment authorization.
    Response: DHS acknowledges commenters' questions about the rule's 
impact. As discussed in the IFR and earlier in this preamble, the 
department has taken measures to address policies that resulted in the 
historic spike in EAD applications received during the previous 
administration. DHS anticipates a substantial decrease in both initial 
and renewal filings for EADs,\77\ which would allow for a reduction in 
processing times for renewal EADs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \77\ See 90 FR 48814, footnote 157.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    USCIS has the discretion to deny benefit requests for lack of 
required initial evidence or for ineligibility, or to request that 
additional evidence is submitted within a specified period of time.\78\ 
The benefit requestor bears the burden of proof for establishing 
eligibility.\79\ A request for evidence (RFE), though it may add time 
to the adjudication of an application, is an opportunity for the 
applicant to provide additional evidence to USCIS in support of their 
application.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \78\ See 8 CFR 103.2(b)(8)(ii).
    \79\ See INA sec. 291, 8 U.S.C 1361.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS will not be implementing remedial actions in case an alien's 
employment authorization lapses. DHS believes that careful planning by 
applicants includes filing early, rather than close to the expiration 
of the EAD, and ensuring that all evidence needed for USCIS to 
determine eligibility has been submitted with the application at the 
time of filing, may help to reduce the risk of a potential lapse in 
employment authorization. While proper planning might not avoid a 
temporary lapse in employment authorization and/or documentation in all 
cases, it should help to reduce the potential of a lapse and shorten 
the duration if a lapse were to occur. DHS also notes that an applicant 
may request that USCIS expedite the adjudication of an application that 
is under USCIS jurisdiction.\80\ USCIS considers all expedite requests 
on a case-by-case basis and generally requires documentation to support 
such requests.\81\ The decision to expedite is within the sole 
discretion of USCIS.\82\ Expediting a case generally means that USCIS 
would adjudicate a benefit ahead of others, including those who may 
have filed earlier, so USCIS carefully weighs the urgency and merit of 
each expedite request.\83\

https://www.uscis.gov/forms/filing-guidance/expedite-requests.
    \81\ See id.
    \82\ See id.
    \83\ See id.
