    Renewal applicants can further reduce their risk of a temporary 
lapse in employment authorization by filing as early as permitted under 
applicable regulations and form instructions, ensuring that their 
application includes all evidence needed to establish continued 
eligibility so that processing is not delayed by a Request for 
Evidence, and by keeping informed of current processing-time 
information posted by USCIS.\98\ Proper planning by applicants, 
together with anticipated reductions in overall EAD demand, may help 
mitigate the extent of any temporary disruptions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \98\ USCIS publishes case processing times on USCIS.gov that are 
regularly updated. See USCIS, Case Processing Times, https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times (last visited May 8, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As discussed above, DHS believes the public safety, national 
security and benefit-integrity benefits of eliminating automatic 
extensions outweigh the potential macroeconomic and local economic 
costs identified by commenters. Ending the practice of providing 
automatic extension of employment authorization documents enhances the 
benefit integrity in adjudications of employment authorization requests 
and better protects public safety and national security by ensuring 
that aliens are properly vetted and determined to continue to be 
eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable) 
for employment authorization before such authorization is provided to 
the alien.
iii. Relief for Specific Immigration Categories
a. Impact on Refugees, Asylees, Asylum Seekers, Unaccompanied Alien 
Children (UACs), and Other Humanitarian Categories
    Comment: Multiple commenters stated that refugees, asylees, TPS 
beneficiaries, VAWA self-petitioners, and unaccompanied children will 
be disproportionately harmed by gaps in work authorization because of 
their vulnerability, limited access to public benefits, which makes 
work authorization crucial to their wellbeing, and reliance on work to 
support themselves, safety, and integration. A commenter indicated that 
the IFR would not only destabilize the workforce, but would inflict 
unconscionable distress and cause lasting harm to refugees, asylees 
(including those with pending claims) and other humanitarian entrants 
and their families, solely on account of the government's processing 
delay and the impact of lapses in employment on this population.
    Some commenters expressed concern that asylum seekers of specific 
nationalities including Haitians, Ukrainians, Asian Americans and 
Pacific Islanders, and Afghans were disproportionally affected by the 
IFR. Additionally, some of these commenters indicated that these aliens 
did not enter through an unknown or informal process but known, vetted 
and humanitarian programs, and are law-abiding and productive 
individuals that benefited the government and the economy. For that 
reason--while at the same time acknowledging the Department's interest 
in benefit integrity, security vetting, and aligning policies with 
recent executive directives emphasizing enforcement and careful 
screening, a commenter advocated for a narrow, risk-sensitive approach 
that preserves the core logic of the interim final rule while avoiding 
an ``all or nothing'' outcome for the vetted humanitarian population.
    Another commenter remarked that the removal of the automatic 
extension of EADs would have severe consequences for those obtaining 
status through the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), in particular 
Asian American and Pacific Islander women, who are particularly 
vulnerable to these harms, as work interruptions can force them into 
unsafe situations or dependence on abusive partners. Others indicated 
that access to employment authorization offers safety, stability, and a 
better quality of life for survivors of gender-based violence. One 
commenter explained that abusers commonly misuse the immigration 
system, for example, by threatening to withhold, withdraw, or sabotage 
immigration filings, as a means of control and intimidation, and 
predicted the rule would exacerbate this problem. This submission 
called attention to backlogs in adjudicating EAD renewal applications 
and predicted hardships for survivors and families due to lapses in 
employment.
    A commenter expressed concern that unaccompanied children and youth 
would be negatively impacted. The commenter said that young protection 
seekers, even those not yet eligible to work, often rely on EADs as a 
form of government identification to access essential social services 
and care such as psychological, education, and housing services. The 
commenter also said that EADs ``facilitate critical access to jobs and 
training opportunities for older youth.''
    Response: DHS understands that refugees, asylees, asylum 
applicants, TPS beneficiaries, VAWA self-petitioners, unaccompanied 
children, and other humanitarian populations may be particularly 
vulnerable to hardship if they experience lapses in employment 
authorization and/or EAD validity. As recognized in the IFR for 
purposes of all applicants, including those in humanitarian programs, 
DHS is cognizant that a lapse in employment authorization and/or EAD 
validity may impact individual aliens, and their families. Many 
applicants in the United States may have fled persecution, violence, or 
disaster, may have limited access to public benefits, and often rely 
heavily on employment authorization to support themselves and their 
families and to integrate into their communities.
    This rule does not eliminate access to employment authorization for 
any of these categories. Refugees and asylees (not including asylum 
applicants) remain employment authorized incident to their status under 
8 CFR 274a.12(a); they may continue to work so long as they maintain 
that status, regardless of the expiration date on any EAD issued as 
evidence of that authorization. Similarly, aliens with a pending asylum 
application may apply for employment authorization in accordance with 
the regulations provided at 8 CFR part 208 and 8 CFR part 274a. TPS 
beneficiaries likewise receive employment authorization consistent with 
section 244 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1254a, and its implementing 
regulations at 8 CFR 244, and TPS-related extensions of documentation 
may continue to be provided by law or Federal Register notice. This 
rule does not change those underlying eligibility frameworks.
    The IFR and this final rule simply end the practice of 
automatically extending the validity of EADs and, for categories not 
authorized incident to status, attendant employment authorization based 
solely on the filing of a renewal application on or after October 30, 
2025, except where extensions are provided by law or Federal Register 
notice (such as certain TPS-related documents). DHS has determined that 
automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs, even for 
vulnerable populations, present the same underlying concern: they allow 
continued employment authorization and use of secure documentation for 
up to 540 days based solely on a pending renewal application, before 
USCIS has determined continued eligibility and that the applicant 
merits a favorable exercise of discretion (if applicable) in



light of any new information, including potential criminal or other 
derogatory information.
    Consistent with Executive Orders \99\ and the Department's mission, 
DHS does not believe that it is reasonable to maintain a separate 
automatic extension regime for particular categories of applicants, 
while at the same time addressing this core security and benefit 
integrity issue. Even a risk-based approach for humanitarian programs, 
as a commenter suggested, would fail to address the core concern that 
some aliens could continue employment authorization, and potentially 
use associated documents to obtain other benefits, without updated 
vetting and adjudication. The Department has instead chosen a uniform 
approach that applies the same principle across affected categories.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \99\ See Executive Order 14159 ``Protecting the American People 
Against Invasion,'' 90 FR 8443 (Jan. 29, 2025); Executive Order 
14161, ``Protecting the United States from Terrorist and Other 
National Security and Public Safety Threats,'' 90 FR 8451 (Jan. 31, 
2025); Presidential Proclamation 10949, ``Restricting the Entry of 
Foreign Nationals To Protect the United States From Foreign 
Terrorists and Other National Security and Public Safety Threats,'' 
90 FR 24497 (June 10, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS acknowledges that some asylum applicants and other humanitarian 
applicants may experience temporary lapses in employment authorization 
if renewal adjudications are not completed before their current EADs 
expire. Asylum applicants, in particular, may have limited access to 
public benefits under existing statutes, and gaps in income may be 
difficult to absorb. DHS considered these factors but concluded that 
they did not outweigh the need to ensure that each renewal of 
employment authorization and/or an EAD is granted only after USCIS has 
completed appropriate vetting and determined that the applicant 
continues to be eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, if applicable.
    DHS notes that, separate from this rule, asylum and refugee status 
confers or may lead to eligibility for certain public benefits under 
existing law, and certain other vulnerable groups may be eligible for 
specialized support programs.\100\ Those frameworks are not altered by 
this rule.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \100\ See, e.g., U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 
Domestic Violence Fact Sheet (discussing access to HHS funded 
services for immigrant survivors of domestic violence), https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/special-topics/national-origin/domestic-violence/index.html (last revised Aug. 22, 2012).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition, DHS has taken steps to reduce incentives for frivolous 
or non-meritorious filings that might delay adjudications for bona fide 
humanitarian applicants, thereby seeking to improve processing for 
those with meritorious claims. For example, in the past four years, 
USCIS has seen alarming new filing trends, including a 360% overall 
increase in VAWA self-petition filings.\101\ When unqualified aliens 
misuse the VAWA program, it causes significant processing delays, 
harming survivors with legitimate claims.\102\ On December 22, 2025, 
USCIS took steps to address these issues by updating guidance in the 
USCIS Policy Manual to streamline and clarify the expectations of 
submitted evidence and reduce the need for Requests for Evidence and 
Notices of Intent to Deny, among other clarifying changes.\103\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \101\ See USCIS, USCIS Restores Integrity to the VAWA Domestic 
Abuse Program After Finding Rampant Fraud, https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/alerts/uscis-restores-integrity-to-the-vawa-domestic-abuse-program-after-finding-rampant-fraud (last updated Dec. 22, 2025).
    \102\ Id.
    \103\ See USCIS, USCIS Policy Alert: Violence Against Women Act, 
PA-2025-33 (last updated Dec. 22, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to unaccompanied children and youth, this rule does 
not change any statutory protections or procedural safeguards 
applicable to that population.\104\ To the extent that employment-
eligible unaccompanied children and youth seek EADs to participate in 
job training opportunities for valid employment purposes, they remain 
eligible to apply and, if approved, to work consistent with existing 
regulations. The IFR and this final rule do not impact or prevent the 
use of valid EADs as identity documents; they simply end the practice 
of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization 
documents for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew 
their EAD in certain employment authorization categories filed on or 
after October 30, 2025.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \104\ See, e.g., William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims 
Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, Public Law 110-457 (Dec. 23, 
2008).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS recognizes the heightened vulnerability of humanitarian 
populations and will continue to administer those programs consistent 
with statutory protections and humanitarian objectives. However, DHS 
concludes that the core principle underlying this rule, namely that 
renewed employment authorization should not be automatically extended 
without fully completing the adjudicative review and the related 
vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information identified 
during the vetting process--must be applied consistently across 
affected categories to fulfill DHS's national security, public safety, 
and benefit integrity responsibilities. As explained in detail in the 
IFR, granting benefits without fully completing the adjudicative 
review, which includes proper vetting, is contrary to the statutory 
mission of DHS and poses a threat to the safety and security of the 
American people.\105\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \105\ See, e.g., Conference Report to accompany H.R. 4567 
[Report 108-774], ``Making Appropriations for the Department of 
Homeland Security for the Fiscal Year Ending September 30, 2005,'' 
p. 74 (Oct. 9, 2004), https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CRPT-108hrpt774/pdf/CRPT-108hrpt774.pdf (recommending, among other things, the 
creation of an organization to conduct ``law enforcement/background 
checks on every applicant, beneficiary, and petitioner prior to 
granting immigration benefits.'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

b. Impact on Employment-Based Nonimmigrants, Their Dependents, and 
Employment-Based Green Card Applicants
    Comment: Multiple commenters expressed concern about the removal of 
automatic extensions of EADs for H-4 dependent spouses. Some commenters 
said that eliminating automatic EAD renewal disproportionately harms 
women, who make up most H-4 EAD holders. Multiple commenters raised 
concerns that H-4 nonimmigrants are dependent on their spouses' H-1B 
status, creating vulnerabilities.
    A number of commenters remarked that current processing times for 
H-4 EAD applications frequently exceed the recommended filing time of 
180 days prior to the current EAD's expiration and argued the removal 
of automatic extensions would result in many aliens losing employment 
authorization and facing unavoidable work gaps. Commenters said that 
delays in H-1B processing, from either the Department of Labor or DHS, 
could adversely affect an H-4 nonimmigrant's status and application for 
an EAD, complicating timely filing.
    Other commenters suggested that removing the automatic extension 
would significantly reduce the employability of H-4 nonimmigrants and 
will cause adverse effects including family income and savings 
disruption, termination of health insurance for spouses and children, 
possible eviction or inability to meet mortgage obligations, 
psychological stress and medical hardship, administrative burden on 
employers managing I-9 reverifications, and work interruptions.
    Other commenters said that H-4 EAD holders contribute significantly 
to the economy through their specialized work and through taxes; have 
been thoroughly vetted by USCIS; and are actively contributing to their



communities. The commenters indicated that the lack of a reasonable 
extension period for a fully vetted and documented population of legal 
residents is counterproductive to the goals of a stable immigration 
system. Therefore, one commenter urged DHS to reconsider this IFR, or 
revert to the previous duration of the automatic extension or extend it 
to at least 240 days, to align with the current USCIS processing 
timelines or exempt certain categories like C26 and other legal 
resident categories who are already vetted multiple times.
    Other commenters highlighted the effects of the IFR on business as 
they are relying on a stable and authorized workforce to meet client 
commitments, drive innovation, and support U.S. economic growth. This 
commenter concluded that the IFR would primarily affect H-4 and L-2 
dependents whose EAD renewals already face significant processing 
delays, which in turn disrupts projects, increases administrative 
burdens and cause significant financial and emotional distress to the 
employees and their families. Many also believed that they could lose 
their authorization to work, impacting them and the U.S. citizens they 
employ. Many urged USCIS to retain the automatic extensions to reduce 
backlogs and improve adjudication, reduce disruptions to businesses, 
including small-businesses, and increase America's global 
competitiveness.
    Response: This rule does not change the underlying eligibility of 
H-4, L-2, or other employment-based dependents to apply for employment 
authorization and/or EAD. This final rule also does not alter the 
eligibility of employment-based adjustment applicants to seek EADs 
while their Form I-485 applications are pending. For nonimmigrants 
whose employment authorization is incident to status and not 
necessarily evidenced by an EAD (for example, certain L-2 spouses with 
appropriate notation on their Form I-94), that authorization continues 
for so long as the underlying nonimmigrant status remains valid, 
irrespective of any separate EAD. For those whose employment 
authorization is granted under 8 CFR 274a.12(c), renewal of that 
authorization remains discretionary and time limited.
    As is the case for all nonimmigrant classifications who were 
eligible to receive an automatic extension of the validity of 
employment authorization documents prior to the IFR, this rule 
eliminates only the practice of providing an automatic extension of the 
EAD validity and, where applicable, attendant employment authorization 
based solely on a timely filed renewal EAD application on or after 
October 30, 2025. DHS acknowledges that, given current and historical 
processing times for some dependent and employment-based EAD 
categories, as well as the steps needed to fully adjudicate and vet an 
application, there may be a risk that USCIS may not complete 
adjudication of every renewal application before the prior card 
expires. In such cases, affected dependents and adjustment applicants 
may experience temporary lapses in employment authorization and 
associated impacts on income, benefits, and career continuity. 
Employers may also face disruptions if they are unable to retain those 
employees pending renewal.
    DHS has carefully weighed these impacts against its responsibility 
to ensure that renewed employment authorization is granted only after 
USCIS has completed appropriate vetting and determined that the 
applicant continues to be eligible and merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, if applicable. Automatic extensions for H-4, L-2, and 
employment-based adjustment applicants present the same underlying 
security and program integrity concerns as automatic extensions for 
other categories: they allow continued employment authorization and use 
of facially expired secure documentation for up to 540 days based 
solely on a pending application, before USCIS has determined continued 
eligibility in light of any new information, including potential 
ineligibility for employment authorization or potential criminal or 
other derogatory information.
    For these reasons, DHS declines to preserve automatic extensions of 
any length for any subset of renewal EAD applicants, including 
employment-based- dependents or adjustment applicants.\106\ Providing 
carve outs would perpetuate the core concern that some aliens could 
continue employment authorization, and potentially use associated 
documents to obtain other benefits, without updated vetting and 
adjudication. The Department has instead chosen a uniform approach that 
applies the same principle across affected categories.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \106\ See 90 FR 48799, 48810 (discussing DHS consideration of 
alternatives, such as shorter automatic extensions of EADs and 
outlining the security and eligibility concerns underlying rejection 
of alternatives).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS notes that many employment-based EADs are linked to other 
benefit requests (for example, principal nonimmigrant extensions or 
adjustment applications) and that USCIS is engaged in efforts to 
streamline and coordinate processing where operationally feasible. 
USCIS will continue to explore process improvements to further reduce 
the potential for future backlogs, including the potential for expanded 
use of premium processing or other tools where authorized by statute, 
while ensuring that security and integrity are not compromised.
    DHS recognizes the important economic and personal contributions of 
employment-based nonimmigrants, their families, and adjustment 
applicants, and the disruption that lapses in employment authorization 
may cause for these aliens, their employers, or to the businesses that 
these aliens may have opened and operated based on their EAD. 
Nevertheless, DHS concludes that the need to ensure that renewed 
employment authorization is extended only after full adjudicative 
review for continued eligibility (including whether the applicant 
merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable) and vetting, 
consistent with current national security and public safety priorities, 
justifies ending automatic extensions for these categories as well and 
outweighs the potential impacts of temporary lapses in employment 
authorization.
6. Clarification Request
    Comment: A commenter requested that USCIS confirm that the filing 
date governs eligibility for automatic extensions. Specifically, the 
commenter sought to confirm that all timely filers before October 30, 
2025, would receive automatic extensions, regardless of when their 
current EAD expired.
    Response: The IFR,\107\ and this final rule, do not impact the 
validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to October 30, 
2025, or which are otherwise automatically extended by law or Federal 
Register notice. To have received an automatic extension under the 
regulation in effect prior to October 30, 2025, an eligible renewal 
application must have met the following conditions:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \107\ See 90 FR 48799, 48799 (Oct. 30, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     The alien must have timely filed an application to renew 
the employment authorization and/or EAD before the EAD expires. See 8 
CFR 274a.13(d)(1)(i); \108\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \108\ TPS beneficiaries must have filed during the re-
registration period in the Applicable Federal Register notice; see 
81 FR 82398, 82455 (Nov. 18, 2016).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     The alien's application to renew the employment 
authorization and/or EAD must have been properly filed before



October 30, 2025,\109\ irrespective of when the EAD expired;
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \109\ To have been properly filed before October 30, 2025, the 
alien must have submitted their application so that USCIS actually 
received the properly signed application, with required fees, on or 
before October 29, 2025. See 8 CFR 103.2(a)(7)(i). Accordingly, an 
alien whose application was submitted but not yet received before 
October 30, 2025, is ineligible for the automatic extension.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     The renewal EAD application is based on the same 
employment authorization category shown on the front of the expiring 
EAD or, for an alien approved for TPS, whose EAD was issued pursuant to 
either 8 CFR 274a.12(a)(12) or (c)(19); and
     The alien's eligibility to apply for employment 
authorization continued notwithstanding the expiration of the EAD and 
was based on an employment authorization category that does not require 
the adjudication of an underlying application or petition before the 
adjudication of the renewal application, as may have been announced on 
the USCIS website.\110\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \110\ The website entitled ``Automatic Employment Authorization 
Document (EAD) Extension'' has since been archived in light of the 
IFR but the web page is still available for viewing at https://www.uscis.gov/archive/automatic-employment-authorization-document-ead-extension (last updated Oct. 29, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For aliens who meet these requirements, an EAD that appears on its 
face to be expired (``facially expired'') is considered unexpired for 
up to 540 days from the expiration date on the front of the EAD when 
combined with a Notice of Action (Form I-797C) that USCIS mails to an 
applicant, indicating a timely filing (i.e., the receipt notice for the 
Form I-765 issued by USCIS has a receipt date that is prior to the 
expiration date on the EAD and before October 30, 2025) of the renewal 
application based on the same employment eligibility category as stated 
on the facially expired EAD (or in case of an EAD and I-797C notice 
that contains either A12 or C19 category code--the category code need 
not match for these categories. In those cases, the alien's facially 
expired EAD is considered unexpired for up to 540 days from the date of 
the EAD, even if the EAD expires on or after October 30, 2025.
7. Recommendations for the Automatic Extension and EAD Validity Period
    Several commenters encouraged DHS to explore alternative solutions 
that better balance national security, economic stability, and human 
dignity.
i. Maintain the Automatic Extension, Including Various Lengths of the 
Extension Period
    Comment: Many commenters urged DHS to withdraw the IFR and instead 
maintain the automatic extension policy. Some commenters stated that 
keeping the automatic extension policy is necessary to protect workers 
and their families from losing continuity of employment caused by 
processing delays and protecting the economic and strategic interests 
of the United States. Multiple commenters reasoned that the automatic 
extension should be retained until reliable EAD renewal processing 
benchmarks (for example, less than 90 days) are consistently met.
    Numerous commenters said DHS should at a minimum restore the up-to-
180-day automatic extension period. Other commenters recommended 
various extension periods, including up to 120 days, up to 180 days, or 
up to 240 days, rather than removing extension periods entirely to 
better align with the current USCIS processing timelines and ensure 
minimal workforce disruption.
    Response: DHS declines to adopt the commenters' suggestions. 
Keeping a reduced automatic extension period would conflict with DHS's 
overriding concern that granting employment authorization benefits to 
aliens without those aliens being properly vetted and determined to 
continue to be eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, 
if applicable) based on a complete adjudicative review is contrary to 
the DHS mission to enhance benefit integrity and protect public safety 
and national security.\111\ As explained in the IFR,\112\ if DHS 
pursued these options, aliens with derogatory information flagged 
during the background check process would nevertheless still obtain an 
automatic extension of some lengths (such as 180 or 240 days). These 
extensions pose a security vulnerability and undermine benefit 
integrity. As with the up to 540-day automatic extension, any automatic 
extension duration would not eliminate the risk that an alien who 
wished to fund nefarious activities could continue to work lawfully and 
generate money. These same aliens could use their automatically 
extended employment authorization and/or EADs to obtain valid identity 
documents, which would make it easier to commit conduct detrimental to 
the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \111\ See, e.g., Conference Report to accompany H.R. 4567 
[Report 108-774], ``Making Appropriations for the Department of 
Homeland Security for the Fiscal Year Ending September 30, 2005,'' 
p. 74 (Oct. 9, 2004), https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CRPT-108hrpt774/pdf/CRPT-108hrpt774.pdf (recommending, among other things, the 
creation of an organization to conduct ``law enforcement/background 
checks on every applicant, beneficiary, and petitioner prior to 
granting immigration benefits.'').
    \112\ See 90 FR 48810.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

ii. Consecutive EAD Validity Periods
    Comment: Numerous commenters recommended implementing consecutive 
EAD validity periods so that applicants could file early without losing 
work authorization, time, and money. Commenters reasoned that under the 
current system, when aliens file well in advance of expiration, USCIS 
routinely issues overlapping validity periods rather than starting the 
new approval period at the end of the existing authorization period 
resulting in early filers losing usable work authorization time. Some 
commenters concluded that consecutive EAD validity periods would allow 
aliens to apply far in advance, provide USCIS with a longer 
adjudication window, and preserve the full period of authorized 
employment.
    Similarly, another commenter reasoned that EADs should be issued 
for longer validity periods to reduce the frequency of renewals, 
stating that a 1-year EAD is, in practice, effective for only 6 months 
as renewal adjudication typically requires approximately 6 months. The 
commenter wrote that the IFR ignores the operational realities, that, 
although USCIS may accept EAD renewals filed more than 180 days before 
expiration, the agency issues overlapping--not consecutive--validity 
periods, effectively cutting into the card's usable time and forcing 
applicants into an ever earlier renewal cycle.
    Response: DHS considered the alternatives suggested by the 
commenters but will not adopt them. DHS's top priority is the robust 
vetting of all aliens in our country to better protect the safety of 
American workers and the public at large. The IFR, and this final rule, 
will enhance public safety by ensuring proper vetting before issuing 
renewal EADs, which are important benefits, and improve program 
integrity. DHS is enhancing its vetting and screening efforts, 
increasing its ability to detect aliens with potentially harmful 
intent, deter fraud, and place removable aliens into proceedings. USCIS 
uses all provisions under the law, to the extent permissible under the 
law, to deny benefits to those who are a risk to public safety and 
national security. This includes more frequent vetting of aliens, 
including more frequent determinations that an alien granted an EAD 
continues to remain eligible for employment



authorization and, as applicable, continues to merit a favorable 
exercise of discretion. DHS believes that it would be inconsistent with 
these policy goals for USCIS to issue, concurrently or in close 
proximity, multiple EADs to the same alien with consecutive validity 
periods or to issue EADs with longer validity periods, as the 
commenters suggest. Consecutive EADs based on the filing of multiple 
renewal applications, concurrently or in close proximity, would be 
tantamount to one EAD with a longer validity period. The result of 
these alternatives would be less frequent vetting and eligibility 
determinations, which would be directly contrary to DHS's stated policy 
goal of the IFR and this final rule.
iii. Allowing Application Filing Earlier Than 180 days
    Comment: Some commenters recommended extending the filing window 
for EAD renewals beyond the current 180 days prior to expiration to 
mitigate processing risks. A few commenters said USCIS should allow EAD 
renewals to be filed 12 months prior to expiration.
    Response: Although USCIS generally recommends that applicants not 
file requests to renew EADs more than 180 days before the expiration of 
their EADs, there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain 
date ahead of expiration. However, USCIS does not postdate the renewal 
EAD in relation to an applicant's current EAD's validity period. 
Therefore, applicants who file and have their EAD applications 
adjudicated further ahead of the expiration of their current EADs may 
have less of a risk of incurring gaps in their employment authorization 
but may also have a shorter combined employment authorization validity 
period.
    USCIS is committed to continuing to explore processing 
efficiencies, including possible expansion of premium processing for 
some or all affected populations.
iv. Enhanced Vetting
    Comment: Some commenters said DHS should implement enhanced 
vetting, such as ongoing security checks for applicants, without 
eliminating automatic extension of EADs. Other commenters recommended 
DHS maintain the automatic extension of EADs for up to 540 days while 
renewal applications are adjudicated, but conduct vetting on a 
``particularized basis,'' noting that USCIS can use its discretionary 
authority to cancel an extension in individual cases when and if 
derogatory information or other concerns arise.
    Response: In service of the DHS mission, and to ensure that DHS 
grants benefits only after having thoroughly vetted in the context of 
the renewal application and full adjudicative review for continued 
eligibility (including, as applicable, whether the applicant merits a 
favorable exercise of discretion), DHS declines to adopt these 
recommendations. DHS has determined that automatic extensions are not 
compatible with its current security and benefit integrity priorities, 
even in an environment where enhanced vetting tools are used. DHS will 
grant renewed employment authorization only after USCIS has reviewed a 
completed application, conducted the appropriate checks, resolved any 
derogatory information, and determined that the applicant continues to 
be eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, 
if applicable. Even if DHS were to cancel the extension in individual 
cases, as the commenter suggests, the alien would still have had the 
benefit of a renewed EAD, even if for a short time, without proper 
vetting and a full eligibility adjudication, which is contrary to the 
DHS mission to enhance benefit integrity and better protect public 
safety and national security. Any automatic extension of employment 
authorization and/or EAD validity based solely on the filing of a 
renewal application, even if subsequently cancelled or terminated, 
would not eliminate the risk that an alien who wished to fund nefarious 
activities could continue to work lawfully and generate money, even 
though the alien may not be eligible for the renewal EAD in the first 
place. Thus, DHS believes granting a benefit without completely and 
fully finishing the adjudicatory process (including vetting) would make 
it easier for aliens engaged in nefarious activity to commit conduct 
detrimental to the United States and will not adopt the commenter's 
suggestion.
8. Processing Capacity and Timelines
i. Timely Processing of Renewals
    Comment: A few commenters stated support for the IFR but urged 
USCIS to ensure timely processing of renewals, so workers and employers 
do not experience unintended lapses in employment authorization. A 
commenter added that if the process cannot be completed within 180 days 
of application, then the IFR is ``very unfair.'' Many commenters said 
USCIS should be required to adjudicate and process all EAD applications 
more quickly. Multiple commenters recommended a specific timeframe (for 
example, under 90 days or under 6 months/180 days) be set for renewals 
to ensure timely processing. A commenter stated that efficient, timely 
processing is the only measure that genuinely improves both security 
and economic stability.
    Response: DHS remains committed to timely processing applications 
without lowering security and vetting standards or benefit integrity. 
DHS understands the importance of timely processing and strives to 
adjudicate applications as efficiently as possible. However, a variety 
of factors can affect processing times, such as security vetting 
requirements and the total number of applications pending review. USCIS 
continually monitors its resource allocations and makes adjustments, as 
appropriate and feasible to ensure customer service. However, DHS 
cannot commit to a maximum processing time in all cases given the need 
for thorough review of each application to ensure that USCIS only 
grants employment authorization after full vetting and screening of the 
applicant, including resolution of any derogatory information, and 
determining that the alien continues to be eligible for employment 
authorization and/or an EAD and to merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, if applicable.
    DHS notes that we expect overall EAD filing rates (initials and 
renewals) are likely to substantially decline given actions DHS has 
taken to align policy with statutory text. DHS anticipates that this 
decline will free up adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD 
processing times and the need for renewal EAD applicants in the longer 
term to rely on an automatic extension of their EAD to avoid lapses in

eliminate the core security and program-integrity risk inherent in 
granting automatic extensions without a full adjudication of the 
application.

    Comment: A commenter reasoned that DHS resources should prioritize 
initial EAD screenings, where new entrants are evaluated, rather than 
duplicating



review efforts for previously cleared renewal applicants.
    Response: Although renewal EAD applicants will already have been 
vetted during the adjudication of their initial EAD applications, DHS 
disagrees that review at subsequent stages, including upon the filing 
of a renewal EAD application, is duplicative. Aliens may engage in 
criminal activity after entry, for example, and new derogatory 
information, including that which is newly obtained despite having 
occurred previously, may appear at any stage. DHS will continue to 
prioritize vetting with the filing of every benefit request, and DHS

vetting in conjunction with the application and a determination that

10. Other Alternatives and Recommendations
    Comment: A commenter discussed Continuous Immigration Vetting (CIV) 
as a more effective timely identification of national security and 
public safety risks than point-in-time screening and vetting that 
occurs only upon application submissions. Multiple commenters asked why 
DHS cannot utilize ``concurrent vetting,'' an apparent reference to 
CIV, as an alternative to the procedures implemented by the IFR. 
Commenters noted that DHS currently employs CIV in some contexts. 
Specifically, commenters noted that, ``DHS already has a system that 
protects security while letting people keep working, and it has not 
explained why it cannot keep using it.''
    Response: DHS appreciates the commenters' focus on the role of CIV 
and other automated screening tools in enhancing national security and 
public safety. CIV is an event-based vetting tool that automates and 
streamlines the process of notifying USCIS of potential derogatory 
information in Government databases that may relate to individuals in 
USCIS systems, as new information is discovered.\135\ DHS agrees that 
continuous screening and vetting capabilities (including systems such 
as CIV and ATLAS, along with interagency information sharing) are 
important components of DHS's security efforts.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \135\ DHS, Privacy Impact Assessment for the Continuous 
Immigration Vetting, (Feb. 14, 2019), https://www.dhs.gov/publication/dhsuscispia-076-continuous-immigration-vetting.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    However, these tools are not a substitute for the full adjudicative 
process that occurs when USCIS considers a new application for an 
immigration benefit, including a renewal of employment authorization. 
Continuous vetting may identify new information or trigger further 
review, but it does not, by itself, resolve questions of eligibility 
(including whether the alien warrants a favorable exercise of 
discretion, if applicable), assess all relevant evidence, or provide 
the structured context in which USCIS officers make determinations 
about continued eligibility and the exercise of discretion, if 
applicable. Eligibility determinations are complex and require an 
officer to examine all the facts and evidence of a case prior to a 
finding. Vetting, like CIV, is one part of the overall process.
    A core concern addressed by the IFR and this final rule is that 
automatic extensions of EADs allow employment authorization to continue 
for up to 540 days based solely on the filing of a renewal application, 
without USCIS first completing adjudicative review and the related 
vetting, including the resolution of any derogatory information. That 
is, the benefit is granted without USCIS first performing the following 
actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening 
checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in 
connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment 
authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if 
applicable. Even with continuous vetting in place, an alien could 
remain work authorized under an automatic extension and use that 
authorization to obtain or maintain other documents, such as driver's 
licenses, including REAL ID compliant driver's licenses in some 
jurisdictions, during a period when USCIS has not yet reevaluated 
eligibility in light of any new information or changed circumstances.
    Accordingly, DHS has determined that automatic extensions are not 
compatible with its current security and benefit integrity priorities, 
even in an environment where CIV and other continuous vetting tools are 
used. Those tools complement but do not replace the requirement that 
renewed employment authorization be granted only after USCIS has 
completed the actions discussed above. Therefore, DHS declines to rely 
on CIV as a basis for retaining automatic extensions of EADs.
    Comment: Multiple commenters requested that USCIS withdraw or delay 
the implementation of the IFR until DHS could guarantee timely EAD 
processing for all categories.
    Several commenters requested a grace period or transitional period 
to mitigate the abrupt impacts of the IFR. Some commenters reasoned 
that the IFR provided no grace period for applicants who relied on the 
prior policy at the time of filing, imposing undue hardship on 
individuals and families who would face employment gaps threatening 
their livelihoods and financial security.
    Some commenters requested specific transitional measures, 
including:
     Granting the automatic extension to all applicants whose 
renewal applications were postmarked before the effective date of the 
rule, even if received later;
     Delaying the effective date of the IFR by at least 90 
days;
     Providing a transition period of at least 12 months for 
employers and employees to adjust workforce planning and compliance 
systems;
     A phased transition to prevent work authorization gaps 
during EAD adjudication; and
     Coordinating with the Department of Health and Human 
Services, the Health Resources and Services Administration, the 
Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid 
Services to assess workforce impacts prior to full implementation.
    A few commenters urged DHS to delay implementation and open a full 
notice and comment period.
    Response: DHS understands that the IFR and this final rule, and any 
resulting gaps in continued employment authorization, may have adverse 
impacts on employers and applicants to the extent that individuals 
experience disruptions in employment. However, as stated earlier in the 
preamble DHS expects that overall EAD filing rates will substantially 
decline and free up adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD 
processing times. Decreasing processing times would result in a reduced 
need for aliens filing renewal EAD applications to rely on an automatic 
extension of their EAD to avoid potential lapses. DHS notes that USCIS 
has, as expected, seen a steady decrease in overall EAD filings since



January 2025. See Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
    In addition, as discussed in Section IV.C.2.iv. of the preamble, 
proper planning by an alien may allow the alien to timely file a 
renewal EAD application thus mitigating the risk of experiencing 
prolonged lapses in their employment authorization and/or EAD validity. 
Ultimately, granting benefits without proper vetting and full 
adjudication is contrary to the DHS mission to enhance benefit 
integrity and better protect public safety and national security.\136\ 
DHS believes that these policy goals outweigh concerns about potential 
backlogs and operational challenges that may result in a temporary 
lapse of employment authorization and/or EAD validity. Therefore, DHS 
declines to adopt the commenters' suggested transitional measures or 
otherwise delay implementation of this rule.

concerns with the automatic extension framework. For example, employers 
are required to use an applicant's unsecure Form I-797, Notice of

how long, an alien employee remains in an automatically extended period 
of employment authorization. Further, additional outreach would not 
address the fact that employers do not receive direct notice if their 
alien employees' pending EAD renewal applications have been denied,

nefarious motives.

    After considering these concerns, DHS determined that continued 
reliance on the 540-day automatic extension, even with expanded 
outreach and educational materials, would not sufficiently address 
these compliance and program integrity risks. DHS will continue to 
provide clear, accessible information about employment authorization 
validity through its public-facing resources.
    DHS notes that the justification for the IFR and this final rule is 
to enhance benefit integrity and better protect public safety and 
national security. While employer confusion is relevant to the 
integrity of the EAD program, conducting more outreach to employers to 
eliminate potential confusion would not address the primary concerns 
addressed by the IFR and this final rule. Therefore, DHS declines to 
adopt this suggestion.
    Comment: Additional alternatives and recommendations included 
suggestions of specific remedies for applicants:
     Implementing 90-day Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with 
fee refunds for delays.
     Allowing automatic extensions for applicants who file 
their EAD applications at least nine months before their current EADs 
expire and committing to adjudicating those applications within nine 
months.
     Enabling interim I-9 verification during card production.
     Allowing automatic extensions for certain EAD categories 
for which vetting may take longer than others.
    Response: DHS has considered the alternatives noted above as well 
as a return to previous practices. USCIS generally does not refund fees 
to applicants for immigration benefits. See 8 CFR 103.2(a). While DHS 
continues to focus on ways to improve processes, DHS will not commit to 
allowing automatic extensions or interim verification for certain EAD 
application categories because the time it takes to vet an applicant is 
entirely dependent on the applicant and his or her case history and 
vetting is just one part of the overall adjudicative review to 
determine continued eligibility and that the applicant continues to 
merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. DHS is also 
not enabling interim I-9 verification during EAD production because 
approval notices are not secure documents establishing proof of current 
work authorization. USCIS notices can only be used in the very limited 
circumstances where DHS has expressly authorized a specific combination 
for I-9 purposes in the M-274 Handbook for Employers.\138\

11. Administrative Procedure Act
i. ``Good Cause'' for Bypassing the Notice and Comment Period
    Comment: Numerous commenters stated that DHS failed to demonstrate 
valid ``good cause'' to bypass the standard notice and comment process. 
Commenters said that immediate implementation without notice and 
comment rulemaking represents a ``significant procedural failure.'' Two 
commenters requested that USCIS reconsider the decision to immediately 
implement the IFR and that fair advance notice should be given in the 
future.
    Other commenters stated that the described ``security vulnerability 
that could allow bad actors to continue to work and generate income to 
potentially finance nefarious activities that pose an imminent threat 
to the American public'' had no causal connection to the automatic 
extension, was speculative, unsupported by any reliable evidence, and 
at any rate that a single example of potential adverse consequence is 
insufficient to establish the meticulous and demanding good cause 
standard. Commenters indicated that the analysis was devoid of specific 
factual allegations of harm or threat to public safety.
    Commenters also indicated that the IFR failed to explain how the 
incident in Boulder was related to the automatic work authorization 
extension provision or why this one incident, even if related, would 
justify the impact the termination of this rule would have on hundreds 
of thousands of workers and their U.S. employers.

    DHS believes that commenters may have misunderstood the risks 
associated with granting automatic extensions of an alien's expired

applicant's eligibility or background. As explained in the IFR, aliens 
could obtain an automatic extension even if they no longer qualified

information that would render them ineligible for employment 
authorization, or would not merit a favorable exercise of discretion, 
if applicable. These aliens could properly file a timely renewal 
application to obtain the benefit of continued employment authorization 
and/or an EAD for up to 540 days. This would allow aliens who could be 
public safety or national security threats to use associated 
documentation to potentially obtain other credentials, such as driver's

    Unfortunately, aliens committing harmful acts and those engaging in 
nefarious activities do not operate on a schedule that aligns neatly 
with them seeking benefits applications. They may or may not engage in 
harmful activity post-approval of an application granting immigration 
status. Attacks, such as the one in Boulder, Colorado, are tough to 
predict, but they may not be impossible to stop with proper and 
thorough vetting and intelligence sharing among government agencies 
each time an alien is seeking immigration benefits.\142\ Congress has 
long emphasized the importance of vetting each and every applicant 
before an immigration benefit is granted.\143\ Fully vetting each 
applicant during every USCIS encounter helps identify patterns, flags 
activities, alerts officials to potential threats, and protects U.S. 
residents from harm. The attack in Boulder, Colorado--committed by an 
alien in possession of an EAD that was automatically extended--provided 
clear evidence of the ongoing public emergency, exposed the security 
vulnerability of the automatic extension, and demonstrated that every 
time USCIS is granting a benefit without fully vetting an applicant, an 
opportunity is lost to detect bad actors and protect the public. The 
public's response to the Boulder event underscored the urgency to act 
to safeguard public safety,\144\ and DHS acted accordingly.

    Finally, DHS is not aware of any case law--and the commenters did 
not cite to any--requiring that good cause can only be demonstrated if

thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public 
interest.'' \147\ This standard is met when, inter alia, there is an 
emergency; when delay caused by the APA's notice and comment procedures 
would result in serious harm to life, property or an immediate threat

public interest.\148\ DHS has met the standard.

Secretary of Homeland Security, in fulfilling the Secretary's 
responsibilities under the APA and this rulemaking, to refer to 
Secretary Rubio's determination. This approach ensures also that the 
government presents a unified position on issues related to entry, 
status, immigration and the removal of aliens, in alignment with the 
President's foreign policy determination and objectives.\155\

goods, including money across the U.S. border, these actions fall

iii. Reasoned Decision-Making Requirement
    Comment: Many commenters, including organizations and a form letter 
campaign, said that, not even a year ago, DHS determined that a 540-day 
automatic extension of employment authorization was necessary to meet a 
Congressional mandate. However, the IFR eliminates automatic extensions

such a reversal. The commenters reasoned that the IFR fails to satisfy 
the ``reasoned decision-making'' requirement of the APA and cited FCC 
v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502 (2009).
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertion that the IFR 
did not provide a reasoned justification for the rulemaking. The IFR 
discussed the prior rulemakings pertaining to EAD automatic extensions 
and then explained that this administration's priority is the robust 
vetting of all aliens in our country to better protect the safety of 
American workers and the public at large. 90 FR 48799, 48808 (Oct. 30, 
2025). The IFR also explained that this rulemaking will enhance public 
safety by ensuring proper vetting before issuing renewal EADs, which 
are important benefits, and improve program integrity. See 90 FR 48799, 
48804 (Oct. 30, 2025). DHS is enhancing its vetting and screening 
efforts, increasing its ability to detect aliens with potentially 
harmful intent, deter fraud, and place removable aliens into 
proceedings. DHS uses all applicable provisions under the law to help 
protect the United States from those who pose a risk to public safety 
and national security.
    The IFR, and this final rule, ends the practice of automatically 
extending the validity of employment authorization documents, so that 
DHS can take appropriate action before an immigration benefit is again 
provided to an alien. The IFR discussed specific examples of the harm 
that could result from continuing to automatically extend an alien's 
expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a timely 
renewal EAD



application.\156\ The IFR also explained that such automatic extensions 
grant the benefit without USCIS first performing the following actions: 
an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, 
resolving potential hits of derogatory information, and a determination 
that the employment authorization should be granted in the exercise of 
discretion, if applicable.\157\ Without the IFR, and this final rule, 
aliens could still obtain an automatic extension despite derogatory 
information that could flag them as a national security or public 
safety risk. As described above, vetting and screening might not be 
completed and derogatory information reviewed and resolved before the 
alien's EAD expires. The automatic extension, therefore, poses a 
security vulnerability that could allow bad actors to continue to work 
and generate income to potentially finance nefarious activities that 
pose an imminent threat to the American public. Granting benefits 
without proper vetting and full adjudication is contrary to the DHS 
mission to enhance benefit integrity and better protect public safety 
and national security.\158\

v. Reliance Interests
    Comment: Many commenters stated that the IFR disregarded 
significant reliance interests that DHS itself reaffirmed when it 
issued a permanent 540-day automatic extension less than one year 
before the IFR. Commenters said the 2025 IFR eliminates extensions 
entirely, imposing consequences DHS recently deemed economically 
harmful and operationally unworkable. Several commenters added that 
this reversal in policy, without new evidence or a reasoned 
explanation, violates the APA.
    Several commenters stated that for nearly a decade, USCIS has 
automatically provided an extension of some length to some groups of 
workers with expiring EADs. The commenters said that employers and 
workers structured hiring, staffing, payroll planning, and employee 
retention around that assurance, and now, DHS cannot abruptly withdraw 
the permanent 540-day automatic extension without addressing these 
significant reliance interests. The commenters said that doing so 
violates core administrative law principles, because Dep't of Homeland 
Sec. v. Regents of the Univ. of Cal., 591 U.S. 1, 30 (2020), concluded 
that agencies must meaningfully consider reliance interests when 
abandoning prior policy.
    Several commenters stated that the IFR failed to consider the 
reliance interests of broader stakeholders, including state and local 
governments, service providers, regional economies, and federal 
agencies, all of whom depend on stable workforces. A commenter stated 
that in Maine, automatic extensions are especially critical for the 
thousands of immigrants who rely on regulatory stability and plan their 
lives around this expectation, and DHS's actions failed to properly 
consider these significant reliance interests and have ``pulled the rug 
out from under them without explanation.''
    Response: DHS disagrees with the assertion that the IFR did not 
sufficiently consider the reliance interests of the regulated public on 
the prior rules that provided for automatic extension of EADs and/or 
employment authorization based on a timely filed renewal application. 
The IFR specifically discussed and acknowledged reliance interests and 
explained why DHS has determined that any reliance interests are 
outweighed by the removal of automatic extensions for aliens in certain 
employment authorization categories. See 90 FR 48809-10. In preparing 
this final rule, DHS further considered all comments that articulated 
specific reliance interests.
    DHS believes that the benefits of this rule to the United States 
outweigh any reliance interests held by the alien, his or her family, 
the employer or the public at-large in the automatic extensions of EADs 
to avoid temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD 
validity. The Federal Government has a duty to protect U.S. national 
security, public safety, and the integrity of immigration benefits, and 
in the context of the IFR and this final rule, to better ensure that 
employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with 
prohibiting the unlawful employment of aliens. Any reliance interest in 
the prior regulatory framework and policy does not outweigh the need to 
protect public safety and the integrity of immigration benefits and 
employment authorization.
vi. Failure To Consider Alternatives
    Comment: A commenter argued that DHS's rejection of two 
alternatives ((1) returning to a 180-day automatic work permit 
extension period and (2) issuing interim EAD cards) without substantive 
analysis and based upon unsubstantiated risks to national security does 
not satisfy the APA's requirement of ``meaningful consideration of 
alternatives.''
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenter's assertion that it did 
not meaningfully consider reasonable alternatives. These were 
reasonable alternatives for DHS to consider since they are prior DHS 
policies. As DHS explained in the IFR, and reiterates in this final 
rule, these and the other sub regulatory alternatives mentioned above 
suffer the same flaws as the up-to-540-day automatic extension. The 
automatic extension of an EAD, whether for 180 days, 540 days, or 
through the issuance of an interim EAD, grants the benefit of extending 
an alien's expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing 
a timely renewal EAD application. That is, the benefit is granted 
without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility 
determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving 
potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the aliens, 
and a determination that the employment authorization should be granted 
in the exercise of discretion, if applicable. If DHS pursued these 
options, aliens with derogatory information flagged during the 
background check process would nevertheless still obtain an automatic 
extension of 180 days, or an interim EAD, even if derogatory 
information cannot be reviewed and resolved, and their application 
denied, before the alien's EAD expires. These automatic extensions 
therefore pose a security vulnerability that could allow bad actors to 
continue to work and generate income to potentially finance nefarious 
activities that pose an imminent threat to the American public.
    Comment: Multiple commenters stated that the IFR failed to consider 
reasonable alternatives to eliminating automatic extensions entirely, 
which violates the standards of ``rational decision-making'' required 
under the APA. A commenter said DHS did not articulate any 
consideration of alternative, sub-regulatory means to achieve increased 
security for the American public, such as providing direction to staff 
to prioritize the vetting of EAD renewal applications, which



would be appropriate and a better option to meet the agency's security 
goals than the rule's termination of the post-2024 practice of 
providing automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs 
for 540 days for eligible aliens who timely filed. A commenter stated 
that DHS ignores the straightforward solution of printing extension 
confirmations on secure paper or commonsense alternatives such as 
issuing multiple EADs with consecutive validity periods or improving 
USCIS data systems to identify and expedite renewal applications for 
applicants whose EAD will imminently expired, and that rejecting a 
simple administrative fix in favor of a rule that foreseeably creates 
widespread employment interruptions reflects precisely the sort of 
arbitrary and capricious decision-making the APA prohibits.
    Another commenter said that DHS's failure to address consecutive 
EAD validity periods underscores the inadequacy of its ``proper 
planning'' rationale and confirms that the agency did not meaningfully 
consider reasonable, less disruptive alternatives, which is in 
violation of the APA.
    Response: DHS considered the alternatives suggested by the 
commenters but declined to adopt them. This administration's priority 
is the robust vetting of all aliens in our country to better protect 
the safety of American workers and the public at large. The IFR, and 
this final rule, will enhance public safety by ensuring proper vetting 
before issuing renewal EADs, which are important benefits, and improve 
program integrity. DHS is enhancing its vetting and screening efforts, 
increasing its ability to detect aliens with potentially harmful 
intent, deter fraud, and place removable aliens into proceedings. DHS 
uses all applicable provisions under the law, to protect the United 
States from those who are a risk to public safety and national 
security. This includes more frequent vetting of aliens, including more 
frequent determinations that an alien granted an EAD continues to 
remain eligible for employment authorization, and continues to merit a 
favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable. DHS believes that it 
would be inconsistent with these policy goals for USCIS to issue, 
concurrently or in close proximity, multiple EADs to the same alien 
with consecutive validity periods. Essentially, this would allow an 
alien to submit multiple EAD applications at or around the same time, 
and consecutive EADs would be tantamount to one EAD with a longer 
validity period. The result of this alternative would be less frequent 
vetting and eligibility determinations, which would be directly 
contrary to DHS's stated policy goal of the IFR and this final rule.
    DHS does not agree that identifying and expediting renewal 
applications for applicants whose EAD will imminently expire is a 
reasonable alternative. Such an approach, even if operationally 
feasible, would simply encourage and incentivize applicants to wait 
until the last minute before filing the EAD renewal application. 
Expediting the applications of those who wait to file would have the 
unintended consequence of delaying the adjudication of those who filed 
six months in advance of their EAD expiration. DHS does not believe it 
is reasonable to reward applicants who wait until the last minute to 
file their renewal EAD application by moving those applications to the 
front of the processing queue to the disadvantage of other applicants 
who filed months in advance.
    Furthermore, DHS does not agree that a reasonable alternative is to 
issue evidence of an automatic extension of employment authorization on 
secure paper, as that would not further the policy goal of more 
frequently vetting, screening, and adjudicating continued eligibility 
and that the alien continues to merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, as applicable. Secure paper would also not resolve the 
issue DHS noted in the IFR \162\ pertaining to the risks associated 
with automatic extension of employment authorization and the potential 
for employer confusion as to when the automatic extension of employment 
authorization ends. The potential confusion stems from the fact that 
the alien, not their employer, is the party to the renewal application 
and is the one notified if the renewal application is denied. Their 
employer is not separately notified and is dependent on notification 
from the alien that their renewal application has been denied and they 
are no longer employment authorized. If the alien does not immediately 
notify their employer, the employer could unknowingly employ an alien 
who is no longer authorized to work in the United States. The use of 
secure paper to print evidence of the automatic extension would have no 
effect on this issue, or the need to ensure more frequent vetting and 
screening and that the alien continues to be eligible for employment 
authorization and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as 
applicable.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \162\ See 90 FR 48799, 48808-48809 (Oct. 30, 2025).
