vii. Comment Period
    Comment: Several commenters requested that DHS extend the comment 
period beyond the December 1, 2025 deadline. An individual commenter 
requested that DHS extend the comment period to 60 days beyond December 
1, 2025. Additional commenters requested that DHS rescind the IFR's 
implementation and provide a full 90-day comment period. One commenter 
requested that DHS reopen the comment period for at least 60 days.
    Response: DHS believes that the 33-day comment period from October 
30, 2025, to December 1, 2025, was sufficient and reasonable, given the 
straightforward purpose of the IFR, as evidenced by the quality of 
comments that DHS carefully considered in the promulgation of this 
final rule.
    The APA does not specify a minimum comment period. On January 20, 
2025, the President issued E.O. 14159, Protecting the American People 
Against Invasion (Jan. 20, 2025), 90 FR 8443, 8446 (Jan. 29, 2025), 
which put the public on notice that it was the President's priority to 
take all appropriate action to alien any departmental activities with 
the policies set out by the President and to ensure, among others, 
``that employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with 
section 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324a, and that employment 
authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien in the United 
States.''
    Additionally, on Jan. 20, 2025, the President also issued E.O. 
14161, Protecting the United States from Foreign Terrorists and other 
National Security and Public Safety Threats, which directs the 
coordination among the departments to identify all resources that may 
be used to ensure that all aliens seeking admission to the United 
States, or who are already in the United States, are vetted and 
screened to the maximum degree possible. On October 29, 2025, the IFR 
was published for public inspection, which allowed individuals to 
familiarize themselves with the rule. On October 30, 2025, the comment 
period opened with the publication of the rule in the Federal Register 
and commenters had 33 days, that is to December 1, 2025, to provide 
comments. DHS believes that the 33-day period is sufficient given the 
straightforward purpose of the IFR.
    Comment: Commenters stated that the post-promulgation comment 
period offered by DHS was insufficient to bypass the APA's notice and 
comment procedures. Courts have repeatedly held that such after-the-
fact opportunities



cannot substitute for prior notice and comment. Once a rule takes 
effect, the ability to influence the agency's decision-making is, as a 
practical matter, diminished. The commenters added that pre-
promulgation notice and comment are not optional--they are statutory 
prerequisites for a legislative rule to be valid, especially in this 
instance where the IFR will have far reaching effects. A commenter said 
they were not afforded the customary notice and comment period to 
conduct a full, data-driven economic or labor market impact analysis 
prior to implementation, which undermines their ability to provide DHS 
with the comprehensive, evidence-based assessment that this rule 
warrants. A different commenter similarly stated that with more time 
and a comment period that accounts for stakeholder input prior to 
implementation, they would have submitted more feedback directly 
relevant to the IFR. A few commenters requested that DHS conduct a full 
notice and comment process to consider stakeholder input.
    Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters that allowing for post-
promulgation comments when issuing the IFR may be insufficient for 
purposes of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and that the rule 
may be invalid or otherwise procedurally deficient. Unless a statutory 
exception to notice and comment rulemaking applies, the APA requires 
agencies to publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal 
Register before the rule has legal effect. See 5 U.S.C. 553(b). The APA 
requires that the notice of proposed rulemaking contain reference to 
the legal authority under which the rule is proposed and either the 
terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the 
subjects and issues involved. See 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(2)-(3). DHS has 
complied with the requirements under the APA. The IFR explained the 
relevant issues and the Department's rationale why it was ending the 
automatic extensions of employment authorizations and/or EADs under 8 
CFR 274a.13. DHS also demonstrated that it had good cause to bypass 
standard notice and comment procedures under the APA. With the issuance 
of the IFR, DHS invited the public to participate in the rulemaking, 
thus giving stakeholders an opportunity to provide comments on every 
aspect of this rule, including potential modifications. DHS is now 
considering all comments received on the IFR and responded to them in 
this preamble, thereby providing the notice and comment process sought 
by commenters. DHS thus has met every statutory requisite for the IFR 
and this final rule to be a properly issued legislative rule under the 
APA.\163\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \163\ Cf. Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul Home 
v. Pennsylvania, 591 U.S. 657, 683-84 (2020) (finding that an IFR 
satisfied the APA's notice requirements).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: Several commenters expressed that the issuance of the rule 
as an IFR with immediate effect that same day deprived stakeholders of 
any meaningful opportunity to review, comment, or prepare for 
compliance.
    Response: As stated in the IFR, DHS issued the IFR without prior 
notice or public procedures because DHS was invoking the ``good cause'' 
exception under the APA, 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). For the same reason, DHS 
found that a delayed effective date of 30-days was not required. See 5 
U.S.C. 553(d)(3). Both provisions allow an agency to publish a measure 
immediately if acting expeditiously is warranted. DHS further explained 
in the IFR why it was necessary for the agency to move so expeditiously 
in promulgating and implementing this rule. With the issuance of the 
IFR, however, DHS invited the public to participate in the rulemaking, 
thus giving stakeholders an opportunity to provide comments on every 
aspect of this rule, including potential modifications. DHS has now 
considered all comments received on the IFR and responded to them in 
this preamble, thereby providing the notice and comment process sought 
by commenters. Furthermore, DHS also explained in the IFR that the 
regulatory amendment involves a foreign affairs function under 5 U.S.C. 
553(a)(1) and that therefore, the agency may forego notice and comment 
rulemaking and a delayed effective date. Therefore, the IFR and this 
final rule complied with the process required under the APA for rules 
that are excepted from notice and comment.
viii. Comment Submission Requirements
    Comment: A couple of commenters stated that DHS's requirement that 
comments be submitted in English deprived many asylum seekers and other 
immigrants of their right to comment on the IFR and to provide input 
grounded in their own lived experiences. The commenter stated that many 
asylum seekers come from countries where English is not the primary 
language and may not have the ability and resources to prepare comments 
in English.
    Response: DHS does not agree that the requirement that comments be 
submitted in English, or accompanied by an English translation, 
deprived aliens of the opportunity to comment on the IFR.
    As stated in the IFR, comments ``must be submitted in English, or 
an English translation must be provided.'' \164\ That requirement is 
consistent with longstanding USCIS practice and with E.O. 14224, 
Designating English as the Official Language of the United States, 90 
FR 11363 (Mar. 1, 2025). This requirement does not limit who may submit 
comments. It only specifies the language in which comments must appear 
in the rulemaking record so that they can be reviewed and considered on 
a consistent basis as part of the administrative process.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \164\ 90 FR 48799-800.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Nothing in the IFR prevented non-English-speaking individuals, 
including asylum seekers and other immigrants, from participating in 
this rulemaking. Individuals and organizations were free to submit 
comments translated into English, whether prepared by the commenter or 
with the assistance of online translation tools or counsel, community 
organizations, or other representatives. Many of the comments DHS 
received came from advocacy and legal-services organizations that 
described, in detail, the lived experiences and concerns of asylum 
seekers and other non-English-speaking communities.
    The English-language requirement for comments in this rulemaking 
does not restrict who may have their views considered in the 
development of this final rule.
    Comment: A commenter said that the FRN states that the comments 
must include the agency and docket number, but that requirement is 
arbitrary and capricious with respect to online submissions. Online 
submissions are linked to the specific FRN so there is no ambiguity as 
to which FRN is at issue. The commenter said that any decision to 
exclude comments from consideration because of these administrative 
barriers violates the APA and the whole purpose of soliciting comments 
from the public. Another commenter asked why comments must have USCIS 
Docket No. USCIS-2025-0271 for DHS to consider them.
    One commenter stated that comments should be restricted to U.S. 
citizens.
    Response: DHS considered all comments received in the docket. 
Accordingly, commenters' concerns about DHS's requirements for labeling 
comments are moot.
    Finally, the APA requires that a rule be published in the Federal 
Register



and, unless an exception to the notice and comment procedures applies, 
to give interested people an opportunity to participate in the 
rulemaking. See 5 U.S.C. 553(b). The APA does not restrict public 
participation in rules to U.S. citizens, and DHS would not have a legal 
basis to do so.
12. Regulatory Impact Analysis
i. Methodology
    Comment: Many commenters stated that the IFR fails to provide any 
substantive economic impact analysis of eliminating automatic EAD 
extensions and did not reconcile its position with DHS's recent finding 
that automatic extensions yield substantial economic benefits.
    Multiple commenters stated that the IFR failed to meet the 
standards required by E.O. 12866 for economically significant rules. 
They stated that such rules must be supported by a clear statement of 
need, a thorough examination of alternative approaches, and a detailed 
benefit-cost analysis.
    Several commenters remarked that USCIS relies on ``conjectural 
concerns'' such as a remittance-based theory that are inconsistent with 
DHS's own statistics.
    One commenter stated that the rule declined to quantify 
productivity losses or turnover costs, elements that were addressed in 
the 2024 rule with detailed estimates of economic impact. The commenter 
noted that DHS speculated that renewal filings would decrease but did 
not account for the number of current EAD holders who would need to 
renew or the implications of shortened validity periods, which might 
require more frequent renewals.
    One commenter provided a conservative scenario analysis to 
demonstrate that the economic impact would exceed the $100 million 
threshold for economically significant rules under Executive Order 
12866.
    Multiple commenters expressed concern that eliminating automatic 
extensions would disrupt a significant portion of the U.S. labor force. 
They cited DHS's acknowledgment that foreign-born workers constitute 
roughly 20% of the U.S. civilian workforce and argued that eliminating 
automatic extensions would not simply affect individual households or 
hypothetical outflows abroad but would disrupt up to one-fifth of the 
U.S. labor force and the U.S. employers, tax revenues, and economic 
activity tied to that workforce.
    One commenter specifically noted that the impact would be 
significantly more severe in New York City, where the foreign-born 
workforce comprises approximately 1.8 million people, about 44.3 
percent of the city's total labor force.
    Another commenter stated that California alone is home to over 10.5 
million immigrants, comprising 27.3 percent of the state's population, 
and that in California, immigrants have contributed $168.1 billion in 
taxes and have $404.4 billion in spending power. The commenter stated 
that California relies on the contribution of working immigrants to 
stimulate the economy.
    Response: DHS believes it conducted an analysis in full compliance 
with E.O. 12866, and DHS described that this rule would affect those 
aliens who would no longer receive an automatic EAD extension. DHS did 
designate the IFR as a ``significant regulatory action'' and 
economically significant as defined under section 3(f)(1) of E.O. 
12866, because its annual effects on the economy may exceed $100 
million in any year of the analysis. Although there is likely to be 
variation and uncertainty in populations and filing behavior, DHS 
estimated in this final rule the number of EADs that are expected to 
lapse, and the estimated duration of the lapse, for a specific 18-month 
window based on some specific assumptions. See Section V.B.1 of this 
preamble for more information.
    In previous rules, DHS attempted to stabilize aliens' earnings and 
avoid labor turnover costs of employers. DHS also continues to work to 
improve processing times and reduce backlogs. However, the Department 
has shifted focus to prioritizing public safety, national security and 
benefit integrity. Due to this shift, DHS acknowledges that there will 
be impacts to EAD renewal applicants for the classes covered in the 
previous extension actions and their employers. DHS disagrees with the 
comment that this rule would destabilize up to one-fifth of the 
national labor force and the employers, tax revenues, and economic 
activity that depend on that workforce or that the discussion about 
remittances in the IFR is inconsistent with DHS statistics. The 
reference in the IFR to the total percentage of foreign-born workers in 
the United States was in the context of the foreign affairs exception 
and a broader discussion about the significance of remittances, 
including by aliens affected by this rule, on foreign affairs. This 
rule applies directly to certain categories of renewal applications 
that were previously provided automatic extensions and not, as the 
commenter suggests, to every foreign-born worker in the U.S. economy.
ii. Impact on Individuals
    Comment: One commenter remarked that the IFR would severely harm 
Colorado's economy and businesses and that the automatic extension that 
come from the temporary final rules of 2022 and 2024 resulted in wage 
stabilization worth $10 billion to employment authorized aliens and 
average cost savings of $3.5 billion to U.S. employers over that 
period.
    Another commenter stated that recent and proposed immigration 
policies will raise the cost of goods and services for U.S. families.
    Response: In previous rules providing for the automatic extension 
of employment authorization and/or EADs based on the timely filing of a 
renewal EAD application, DHS attempted to stabilize aliens' earnings 
and avoid labor turnover costs of employers; however, the Department 
has shifted focus to prioritizing public safety, national security and 
benefit integrity. Due to this shift, DHS acknowledges that there will 
be impacts on a portion of the U.S. labor force. DHS disagrees that 
this specific immigration policy alone is going to be the sole reason 
for the costs of goods and services to increase.
iii. Impact on the U.S. Economy, Employers, and Labor Force
    Comment: Multiple commenters provided input on the RIA's assessment 
of impacts on the economy. One submission expressed concern that USCIS 
recognized the negative impacts of removing the automatic extension 
period on aliens and employers but declined to conduct any economic 
analysis during the rulemaking. The commenter said that such an 
approach disregarded an estimated $4 billion in turnover costs and 
additional burdens on employers and Form I-9 vendors to update systems 
and policies. By omitting quantification of significant costs, the 
commenter reasoned that DHS cannot credibly claim it weighed the IFR's 
benefits against its costs, as the IFR provided no numeric estimates 
despite prior rules showing costs in the billions of dollars. 
Furthermore, the commenter said that the immediate effect of the IFR 
would place significant burdens on employers and vendors. The commenter 
concluded that DHS's justification for immediate implementation--to 
prevent a surge in renewal applications--would not outweigh the 
operational and economic strain imposed on employers and industry.
    Likewise, another commenter expressed concern that the IFR offered



no new economic analysis and did not reconcile its approach with DHS's 
recent determination that automatic extensions provide substantial 
economic benefits. The commenter said that although DHS conducted 
detailed modeling less than a year earlier, the IFR stated the agency 
could not quantify the impact of eliminating extensions while bypassing 
notice and comment procedures. The commenter remarked that DHS 
previously found extensions stabilize billions in earnings, reduce 
turnover costs, and increase tax revenue, yet the IFR relied on 
speculative concerns instead of updated data. Moreover, the commenter 
said DHS's own figures, removing extensions could destabilize up to 
one-fifth of the labor force, creating systemic risks to employers, tax 
revenues, and economic activity that the 2024 Final Rule had 
acknowledged but the IFR failed to address.
    Similarly, one commenter stated that DHS had not estimated or 
considered the economic value and workforce impact of EADs in the IFR. 
The commenter remarked that existing research had shown that work 
authorization allowed migrants with temporary protections to make 
significant economic contributions. For example, when the TPS 
population was about 354,000 in 2021, estimates indicated billions in 
tax contributions and spending power, and other studies suggested large 
contributions to GDP. Similar findings were reported for DACA 
recipients, including tax payments, household spending power, and wage 
increases after receiving EADs. Additional research has shown that EADs 
were associated with higher employment rates and wage gains for TPS 
holders and asylum seekers. The commenter said that such studies 
suggested that work authorization had positive effects on earnings, job 
quality, and economic stability. The commenter concluded that if DHS 
had conducted an economic analysis, it could have accounted for these 
impacts before finalizing the rule.
    One commenter said that DHS's own figures indicated that 
eliminating automatic EAD extensions could disrupt a significant 
portion of the U.S. workforce and impose substantial economic costs. 
The commenter reasoned that such figures underscore the need for DHS to 
complete a thorough economic analysis before finalizing the IFR. 
Therefore, the commenter requested that DHS provide a comprehensive 
economic analysis.
    A commenter stated that DHS's prior analysis projected 293,000-
449,000 timely EAD renewal applicants would face work authorization 
lapses, and USCIS data showed backlogs were already increasing before 
the IFR, making lapses inevitable. The commenter further stated even 
short lapses could cause thousands of dollars in lost wages per worker 
and major operational disruptions. Lastly, the commenter stated that 
DHS acknowledged the IFR would cause lost wages, productivity, payroll 
tax contributions, as well as turnover costs, but failed to quantify 
the aggregate impact.
    Response: DHS agrees that this rule reverses some of the impacts 
described in the prior automatic extension rules. As DHS acknowledged 
in the IFR, temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD 
validity could result in cost and transfer impacts such as lost 
compensation to workers, transfers between workers losing their 
employment authorizations to replacement workers, employers' lost 
productivity when they are not able to quickly replace employees with 
lapses, and turnover costs for employers to find replacement employees.
    DHS's 2024 final rule analysis projected that automatic extensions 
would prevent a significant number of future lapses, but anticipated 
that lapses would generally cease beginning in April 2026, even without 
the 540-day extension.\165\ DHS acknowledges that the December 2025 
reduction in EAD validity periods may lead to more frequent renewal 
applications, potentially affecting this projection.\166\ However, 
recent declines in the affected population and changes in filing 
behavior make it nearly impossible to reliably estimate the number and 
duration of lapses.

    DHS has concluded that the need to ensure proper vetting and 
screening, and continued eligibility, before granting renewed 
employment authorization and issuing secure evidence of that 
authorization outweighs the risk that some applicants might experience 
a temporary lapse in employment authorization and/or EAD validity. The 
prior automatic extension framework allowed aliens to continue working 
for up to 540 days based solely on a pending renewal application, 
during which time USCIS might identify, but not yet resolve, derogatory 
information bearing on eligibility or security concerns. DHS has 
determined that extending this benefit without updated adjudication and 
screening is inconsistent with its mission and with E.O.s directing DHS 
to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to unauthorized 
aliens and that aliens in the United States are vetted and screened to 
the maximum degree possible.\167\ DHS disagrees with the comment that 
this rule would destabilize up to one-fifth of the national labor force 
and the employers, tax revenues, and economic activity that depend on 
that workforce. This rule applies directly to certain categories of 
renewal applications that were previously eligible for automatic 
extensions.

iv. Other Comments on the RIA
    Comment: A commenter asked that USCIS suspend further action with 
the rule until it prepares and publishes a full RIA, an Initial 
Regulatory Flexibility Analysis, and reopen the comment period for 60 
days following the publishing of those materials.
    Response: DHS published an RIA in the IFR providing a qualitative 
assessment of benefits, transfers, and costs. In that analysis, DHS 
acknowledged the possibility that some renewal applicants could 
experience EAD lapses. However, due to factors such as population 
changes, reduced filings, shorter validity periods for certain EADs, 
DHS determined that the conditions are too uncertain to accurately 
estimate the number or duration of lapses. Additionally, lower filing 
volumes may allow DHS to address the backlog more rapidly.
    While many renewal applicants covered by the two TFRs who received 
automatic extensions may have eventually obtained five-year EADs, 
projecting how many new and renewal EADs will be subject to the 18-
month validity period is highly speculative. As a result, DHS cannot 
reliably estimate processing times, which are essential for calculating 
lapses and their duration.
    Within the IFR, DHS referenced prior analyses from the TFRs and 
2024 final rule to demonstrate that it is aware of the past situations 
of large lapses, but could not use prior historical data to



forecast the IFR's impact. Assuming prior spikes in EAD filings would 
continue is inconsistent with recent data. See Table 1 in Section 
IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble. Therefore, at the time of the IFR and the 
issuance of this final rule, DHS could not reliably estimate the number 
or duration of lapsed EADs.
    The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.) 
requires agencies to prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis 
when issuing a notice and comment rulemaking. DHS disagrees with the 
claims that a proper regulatory flexibility analysis was not conducted. 
The RFA's regulatory flexibility analysis requirements apply only to 
those rules for which an agency is required to publish a general notice

V. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements

A. Administrative Procedure Act: Delayed Effective Date

    This final rule is exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act 
(APA)'s delayed effective date requirement under 5 U.S.C. 553(d) 
because DHS has for good cause found that it is unnecessary to delay 
implementation of this final rule.
    Although the good cause exception for the 30-day effective date in 
5 U.S.C. 553(d) mirrors the ``good cause'' language of 5 U.S.C. 553(b), 
the good cause exception from the 30-day effective date requirement is 
easier to meet because these provisions have different purposes. See 
Riverbend Farms, Inc. v. Madigan, 958 F.2d 1479, 1485 (9th Cir. 1992); 
see also U.S. Steel Corp. v. EPA, 605 F.2d 283, 289-90 (7th Cir. 1979) 
(good cause more easily found as to 30-day waiting period). Unlike the 
notice-and-comment requirement, which is designed to ensure public 
participation in rulemaking, the 30-day waiting period is intended to 
give affected parties time to



adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect. See Riverbend 
Farms, 958 F.2d at 1485.
    It is unnecessary to delay this final rule's effective date because 
in this final rule, DHS is addressing public comments solicited as part 
of the IFR that has been in effect since October 30, 2025. In this 
final rule, DHS is not making any substantive or non-substantive 
changes to the IFR published in October 2025. There is no need to give 
affected parties additional time to adjust their behavior before this 
final rule takes effect. Therefore, a delayed effective date serves no 
purpose, and this final rule is effective immediately.

B. Executive Order 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), Executive 
Order 13563 (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and 14192 
(Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation)

    E.O.s 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess the costs and 
benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is 
necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. 
E.O. 13563 emphasizes the importance of quantifying costs and benefits, 
reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting flexibility. E.O. 
14192 directs agencies to significantly reduce the private expenditures 
required to comply with Federal regulations and provides that ``any new 
incremental costs associated with the new regulations shall, to the 
extent permitted by law be offset by the elimination of existing costs 
associated with at least 10 prior regulations.''
    This final rule has been designated a ``significant regulatory 
action'' and economically significant as defined under section 3(f)(1) 
of E.O. 12866, because its annual effects on the economy may exceed 
$100 million in any year of the analysis. Accordingly, this rule has 
been reviewed by the OMB.
    This final rule is not an E.O. 14192 regulatory action because it 
is being issued with respect to an immigration-related function of the 
United States. The rule's primary direct purpose is to implement or 
interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as described in 
INA sec. 101(a)(17), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17)) or any other function 
performed by the U.S. Federal Government with respect to aliens. See 
OMB Memorandum M-25-20, ``Guidance Implementing Section 3 of E.O. 
14192, titled `Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation' '' (Mar. 26, 
2025).
    This final rule reaffirms and finalizes changes made by the IFR to 
DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the 
validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I-766 or EADs) 
for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in 
certain employment authorization categories. The purpose of this change 
is to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure 
continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment 
authorization and/or a new EAD. This final rule does not affect the 
validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to the IFR. In 
previous rules providing for the automatic extension of EADs based on 
the timely filing of a renewal EAD application, DHS attempted to 
stabilize aliens' earnings and avoid labor turnover costs of employers. 
However, as explained in the IFR, the Department has shifted focus to 
prioritizing public safety and national security, and ensuring that 
aliens continue to be eligible and merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, as applicable, before being granted continued employment 
authorization. See 90 FR 48799, 48816 (Oct. 30, 2025).
    DHS has prepared two types of quantified estimates of the impacts 
that could be generated by this final rule. For a single 18-month 
window (starting in May 2027) from about 20,000 and 33,000 EADs are 
estimated to lapse, based on several assumptions. This rule may result 
in some EAD holders incurring a loss of earnings (``reduced earnings'') 
because of USCIS process delays for renewal EAD applications, as under 
this rule there could be disruption to their earnings due to a lapsed 
EAD. Such earnings loss to aliens could comprise beneficial transfers 
to other U.S. workers if the substitution of the latter for the former 
is relatively frictionless. Additionally, to the extent this rule 
affects EAD holders' jobs going unfilled, there will be impacts to tax 
transfers from businesses and employees to the Federal Government.\181\ 
This rule will also generate labor turnover costs to businesses that 
employ the affected-lapsed EAD holders, as under this rule there would 
be a disruption to the EAD holders' employment authorization and/or 
document validity. In conducting these estimates DHS emphasizes that 
variation in factors involved in the impact, including impact 
processing times, filing volumes, the timing of renewal filings, and 
underlying benefit requests, will cause variation in the impacts.

    \181\ This rule could also result in a reduction in State and 
local tax revenue, but this impact is not quantified in this 
analysis due to variations in state and local tax laws and 
individual's tax scenarios.

    \183\ DHS utilized the SAS JMP PRO 17 software. The ``State 
Space Smoothing'' suite utilizes machine learning algorithms to 
offer the best model information criterion to assess fit and 
forecasting technique for queued time series data, given dozens of 
potential model specifications. Based on the Akaike Information 
Criterion (AIC) DHS forecasted the data via a multiplicative error-
multiplicative (undamped) trend, non-seasonal component (MMN) setup. 
The MMN model fits five parameters, but these are not reported here 
since the goal is limited to forecasting and not hypothesis testing. 
The fit results are very good according to the diagnostics: R-
squared = .932, AIC = 405.6, and the residuals display no 
discernable pattern and are purged of serial correlation (at any 
lag, as all p-values of the Ljung-Box statistic are far greater than 
.05). In principal DHS could rely on each prediction interval around 
a monthly forecast to develop an aggregate range. In practice, the 
intervals applicable to the data are not plausible, for the 
following reasons. The standard error is large to begin with due to 
some sharp movements in the underlying data; and with a downward 
trending time series, the standard error takes on increasing 
relative weigh as the forecast values decline. The result is a 
``division by zero'' issue in which the lower bound is pulled 
towards zero. But the increased relative weight of standard error 
does not discriminate between the upper and lower bounds, and it 
therefore enacts a proportional effect to the upper level, causing 
it to diverge on an unstable path. For this reason, the forecast 
prediction interval at a 95% confidence level is not reliable.

Module B
    The purpose of this rulemaking is to prioritize benefits integrity 
and the proper vetting and screening of aliens before granting a new 
period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD by ending the 
practice of automatically extending the validity of employment 
authorization and/or EADs for aliens who have timely filed an 
application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization 
categories. While prior automatic extensions reduced the risk of 
employers employing aliens with lapsed employment authorization and/or 
EAD validity, this final rule will also reduce the risk that affected 
employers will continue to employ an alien who is no longer authorized 
to work. For example, within their automatic extension period, an 
alien's application could have been adjudicated and denied. The 
obligation is on the alien employee to notify his or her employer that 
he or she is no longer work authorized, which puts employers at risk of 
unknowingly employing an unauthorized alien. Absent the IFR and this 
final rule, employers assess the applicability of the automatic 
extension based in part on a non-secure document (such as Form I-797C, 
Notice of Action, which is printed on plain paper). With this final 
rule ending the practice of providing automatic extensions based on the 
timely filing of a renewal EAD application, DHS is reducing the 
potential for fraud and instances where employers unknowingly employ 
aliens beyond their employment authorization and/or EAD validity.
    This rule reverses some of the impacts described in the prior 
automatic extension rules. Employment lapses could result in cost and 
transfer impacts such as lost compensation to workers, transfers 
between workers losing their employment authorizations to replacement 
workers, employers' lost productivity when they are not able to quickly 
replace employees with lapses, and turnover costs for employers to find 
replacement employees. In the following section, DHS discusses impacts 
but cannot reliably quantify these impacts due to uncertainty.
    As was described earlier in the Affected Population section, DHS 
determined that an expected impact of this final rule is that some EADs 
will lapse while the alien's renewal EAD application is pending with 
USCIS. In this section, the estimated lapse is developed into a 
quantified impact, which will constitute an earnings change to aliens. 
The employment lapse impacts, a loss of income to aliens, could result 
in either transfers of compensation to other workers or costs to 
employers, depending on employers' ability to replace workers with 
lapsed employment authorization and/or EAD validity. In cases where, in 
the absence of an automatic extension period, businesses would have 
been able to easily find reasonable labor substitutes for aliens with a 
lapsed employment authorization and/or EAD validity, this rule results 
in transfers of the earnings of affected aliens to others, who might 
fill in for or replace the renewal EAD applicants during their earnings 
lapse. In cases where, absent the automatic extension period, 
businesses may not easily find reasonable labor substitutes, employers 
may incur lost productivity and turnover costs or other disruptions. 
This could result in losses to native-owned businesses and their native 
employees. DHS assumes the value of lost productivity is at least as 
high as the compensation the employer would have paid the affected 
alien.
    The employer turnover cost is generally reported as a share of 
annual wages.\194\ DHS would calculate the turnover costs by 
multiplying the number of impacted lapsed employees by the hourly wage 
rate, hours worked per year, and the share of annual wages.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \194\ In the 2024 Automatic Extension Temporary Final Rule, DHS 
estimated the turnover costs as a percentage of annual wages, using 
a mean of 23 percent (Table 11). Temporary Increase of the Automatic 
Extension Period of Employment Authorization and Documentation for 
Certain Employment Authorization Document Renewal Applicants, 89 FR 
24669 (April 8, 2024).

    This final rule is expected to generate labor turnover costs to 
some employers of affected EAD holders. DHS bases the assessment of 
these impacts on the assumption that the estimated population of aliens 
with lapsed EADs because of this final rule would involuntarily 
separate from an employer, or otherwise cease employment, and that the 
separation or cessation would not be due to other factors.
    Employment separations or cessation can generate labor turnover 
costs to employers. First are the direct or ``hard'' costs that involve 
separation and replacement costs. These include exit interviews, 
severance pay, and costs of temporarily covering the employee's duties 
and functions with other employees, which may require overtime or 
temporary staffing. The replacement costs typically include expenses of 
advertising positions, search and agency fees, screening applicants, 
interviews, background verification, employment testing, hiring 
bonuses, and travel and relocation costs. Once hired, employers face 
additional training, orientation, and assessment costs.
    Second, direct costs involve loss of productivity and possibly 
profitability due to operational disruptions, which can include errors 
from employees that may temporally fill the position. A third cost 
segment is a type of indirect cost that encompasses loss of 
institutional knowledge, networking, and impacts to work-culture, 
morale, and interpersonal relationships. This last type of cost is 
almost impossible to measure quantitatively.\207\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \207\ For additional descriptions of the components of labor 
turnover costs, see Ghase Charba, ``Employee retention: The Real 
Cost of Losing an Employee,'' PeopleKeep, (updated February 2, 
2023), https://www.peoplekeep.com/blog/employee-retention-the-real-cost-of-losing-an-employee.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    There are studies and reports concerning labor turnover costs 
available from Human Resource entities that are cited across 
correspondent literature, and turnover cost can be measured in slightly 
different ways. The turnover cost is generally reported as a share of 
annual earnings or an actual cost per employee. Usually, these reports 
measure the more direct, or hard costs associated with turnover and not 
intangible effects such as worker morale or lost productivity. Many 
reports cite a 2012 Center for American Progress (CAP) report that 
surveyed more than 30 studies that considered both direct (e.g., 
separation and replacement) and indirect (e.g., loss of institutional 
knowledge) costs.
    The CAP and other reports confirm three central aspects of turnover 
cost: (1) that they vary substantially across industries and jobs; (2) 
that they tend to grow (in absolute and percentage terms) according to 
skill level and earnings; and (3) that they are higher for salaried 
workers compared to hourly wage earners.\208\ The report notes that 
specialized technical jobs and highly paid jobs in line with senior or 
executive levels, which involve high levels of education, credentials, 
and stringent hiring criteria, can generate disproportionately high 
replacement costs that can reach more than 100 percent of the salary--
compared to jobs with low educational and technical requirements.\209\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \208\ See Heather Boushey and Sarah Jane Glynn, ``There Are 
Significant Business Costs to Replacing Employees,'' Center for 
American Progress, (Nov. 16, 2012), https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/economy/reports/2012/11/16/44464/there-are-significant-business-costs-to-replacing-employees/.

Employee Turnover,'' Built In, https://builtin.com/recruiting/cost-of-turnover (last updated June 23, 2023).

reasonable labor substitutes for the positions the renewal EAD 
applicants lost, businesses lose little or no productivity. 
Accordingly, this rule could result in $276.2 million (primary 
estimate, undiscounted) being transferred from affected renewal EAD 
applicants to workers currently in the labor force (whom are not 
presently employed full time) or induced back into the labor force and 
this rule would result in $0 costs to businesses for prevented 
productivity losses.
    Scenario 2: Conversely, if all businesses would be unable to, 
within the period of analysis, find reasonable labor substitutes for 
the position the EAD holder filled, then businesses would lose 
productivity. Accordingly, $276.2 million is the estimated monetized 
costs from this rule for productivity losses and this rule will result 
in $0 being transferred from affected renewal EAD applicants to 
replacement labor. Because under this scenario businesses would not 
have been able to find replacement labor, the rule may also result in 
additional costs to employers for profit losses; and may result in a 
reduction in tax transfer payments from businesses and employees to the 
government. DHS has not estimated all potential tax effects but notes 
that earnings of $276.2 million would result in employment tax losses 
to the Federal Government (i.e., Medicare and Social Security) of $29.0 
million.
    In both scenarios, whether without this rule employers would have 
been able to find replacement labor or not, DHS assumes that businesses 
would have incurred labor turnover costs for having to search for a 
replacement for affected renewal EAD applicants. Accordingly, DHS 
estimates the rule will also result in additional labor turnover costs 
to businesses of $312.1 million.
    Table 7 below summarizes these two scenarios and the primary 
estimate of this rule. Because DHS does not know the overall proportion 
of businesses that would have been able to easily find replacement 
labor in the absence of this rule, for DHS's primary estimate we assume 
that replacement labor would have been immediately found for half of 
all renewal EAD applicants and not found for the other half (i.e., an 
average of the two extreme scenarios described above). The June 2026 
unemployment and job openings data indicate there are as many jobs 
available as there are people looking for jobs.\213\ Accordingly, we 
believe the impacts of this rule will likely skew towards Scenario 1, 
with the rule resulting in mostly transfers of compensation from 
renewal EAD applicants to other workers and turnover costs for 
employers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \213\ Bureau of Labor Statistics data show that, as of June 
2026, there were 1.0 unemployed persons per job opening. See U.S. 
Department of Labor, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, ``Number of 
unemployed persons per job opening, seasonally adjusted,'' https://www.bls.gov/charts/job-openings-and-labor-turnover/unemp-per-job-opening.htm (last visited Aug. 19, 2026).

C. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)

    The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.), as 
amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 
1996, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of 
regulations on small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, and 
small organizations during the development of their rules. The term 
``small entities'' comprises small businesses, nonprofit organizations 
that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their 
fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 
50,000. The RFA's regulatory flexibility analysis requirements apply 
only to those rules for which an agency is required to publish a 
general notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553 or any 
other law.\214\ DHS did not issue a notice of proposed rulemaking for 
this action. Accordingly, DHS is not required to certify either that 
this final rule would not have a significant economic impact on a 
substantial number of small entities nor conduct a regulatory 
flexibility analysis.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \214\ See 5 U.S.C. 604(a).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Further, this final rule directly regulates individuals, and 
individuals are not defined as ``small entities'' by the Regulatory 
Flexibility Act. The rule indirectly impacts certain employers if, in 
the future, processing times exceed the expiration dates of EADs.
    DHS is unsure what backlogs may continue in the future; however, 
DHS anticipates that, due to other DHS actions described in Section 
IV.C. of this final rule, it is possible that the backlog may end. If 
the backlogs are eliminated outside of this rule, employers will no 
longer be indirectly impacted by this final rule.
    In the alternate scenario of a backlog in renewal EAD processing, 
some employers could experience indirect costs or transfer effects. The 
transfers would be in the form of lost compensation (wages and 
benefits). A portion of this lost compensation might be transferred 
from renewal EAD applicants to others who are currently in the U.S. 
labor force. A portion of the effects of this rule would also be borne 
by companies that would have continued to employ renewal EAD applicants 
had they been in the labor market longer; however, they were unable to 
find available replacement labor. These companies may incur an indirect 
cost, as they will be losing the productivity and potential profits the 
EAD applicant would have provided. Companies may also incur opportunity 
costs by having to choose the next best alternative to the immediate 
labor the applicant would have provided and by having to pay workers to 
work overtime hours. DHS does not know what this next best alternative 
may be for those companies. If companies can find reasonable labor 
substitutes for the positions the alien occupied, they will bear little 
or no costs. Conversely, if companies are unable to find reasonable 
labor substitutes for the position the applicant would have maintained 
then there would be no transfers and companies may experience turnover 
costs or other disruptions.



D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA)

    The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) is intended, among 
other things, to curb the practice of imposing unfunded Federal 
mandates on State, local, and Tribal governments.\215\ Title I of UMRA 
provides certain exceptions to its requirements and definitions. UMRA 
does not apply to rules from independent regulatory agencies or rules 
issued with no notice of proposed rulemaking. UMRA exempts legislative 
provisions and rules relating to individual constitutional rights, 
discrimination, emergency assistance, grant accounting and auditing 
procedures, national security, treaty obligations, and elements of 
Social Security legislation.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \215\ The term ``Federal mandate'' means a Federal 
intergovernmental mandate or a Federal private sector mandate. See 2 
U.S.C. 1502(1) and 658(5) and (6).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Title II of UMRA requires each Federal agency to prepare a written 
statement assessing the effects of any Federal mandate in a proposed 
rule, or final rule for which USCIS published a proposed rule, which 
includes any Federal mandate that may result in a $100 million or more 
expenditure (adjusted annually for inflation) in any one year by State, 
local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private 
sector. See 2 U.S.C. 1532(a). This rule is exempt from the written 
statement requirement because DHS did not publish a notice of proposed 
rulemaking for this rule. This final rule does not contain a federal 
mandate as the term is defined under UMRA.\216\ Therefore, the 
requirements of Title II of UMRA do not apply, thus DHS has not 
prepared a statement under UMRA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \216\ See 2 U.S.C. 1502(1), 658(6).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

E. Congressional Review Act (CRA)

    The Congressional Review Act (CRA) was included as part of the 
Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (SBREFA) by 
subtitle E of SBREFA, Public Law 104-121, tit. II, 110 Stat. 847, 868, 
et seq. This final rule meets the criteria set forth in 5 U.S.C. 804(2) 
because it is likely to result in an annual effect on the economy of 
$100 million or more. See 5 U.S.C. 804(2)(A). DHS has complied with the 
CRA's reporting requirements and has sent this rule to Congress and to 
the Comptroller General as required by 5 U.S.C. 801(a)(1). The CRA 
generally provides a 60-day delayed effective date for rules that meet 
the 5 U.S.C. 804(2) criteria. See 5 U.S.C.801(a)(3). Because this rule 
makes permanent the October 2025 IFR that would otherwise continue to 
apply for months before this final rule has practical effect, DHS has 
for good cause found that the 60-day delay typically required under 5 
U.S.C. 801(a)(3)(A) is unnecessary. Therefore, this rule is effective 
immediately upon publication consistent with 5 U.S.C. 808(2).

F. Executive Order 13132 (Federalism)

    This final rule will not have substantial direct effects on the 
States, on the relationship between the National Government and the 
States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the 
various levels of government. Therefore, in accordance with section 6 
of E.O. 13132, Federalism, 64 FR 43255 (Aug. 4, 1999), it is determined 
that this final rule does not have sufficient federalism implications

G. Executive Order 12988 (Civil Justice Reform)

    This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with E.O. 
12988, Civil Justice Reform. This final rule was written to provide 
clear legal standards for affected conduct and was reviewed carefully 
to eliminate drafting errors and ambiguities, as to minimize litigation 
and undue burden on the Federal court system. DHS has determined that

H. Family Assessment

    DHS has reviewed this rule in line with the requirements of section 
654 of the Treasury and General Appropriations Act, 1999,\217\ enacted 
as part of the Omnibus Consolidated and Emergency Supplemental 
Appropriations Act, 1999.\218\ DHS has systematically reviewed the 
criteria specified in section 654(c) of the Treasury and General 
Appropriations Act by evaluating whether this regulatory action: (1) 
impacts the stability or safety of the family, particularly in terms of 
marital commitment; (2) impacts the authority of parents in the 
education, nurture, and supervision of their children; (3) helps the 
family perform its functions or substitutes governmental activity for 
the function; (4) affects disposable income or poverty of families and 
children; (5) only financially impacts families, if at all, to the 
extent such impacts are justified; (6) may be carried out by State or 
local government or by the family; or (7) establishes a policy 
concerning the relationship between the behavior and personal 
responsibility of youth and the norms of society. If the agency 
determines a regulation may negatively affect family wellbeing, then 
the agency must provide an adequate rationale for its implementation.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \217\ See 5 U.S.C. 601 note.
    \218\ See Public Law 105-277, 112 Stat. 2681 (1998).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As articulated in the IFR and this final rule, DHS is discontinuing 
the practice of providing an automatic extension of the EAD or 
employment authorization upon the filing of a renewal EAD application 
because it grants a benefit without an eligibility determination, 
without completing vetting and screening checks and without resolving 
the potential hits and derogatory information. DHS has determined that 
the implementation of this regulation may potentially negatively affect 
family wellbeing as outlined in section 654 of the Treasury General 
Appropriations Act, 1999. Specifically, the IFR and this final rule has 
the potential to affect disposable income of families and children, and 
therefore, also impacts the family financially. However, DHS believes 
that it has an adequate rationale for its implementation. DHS believes 
that the consequences of the IFR and this final rule, the possibility 
that an alien is not authorized to work during the pendency of the 
alien's renewal EAD application and thus, that families have less 
disposable income, are justified in light of the national security and 
public safety risk that automatically issuing immigration benefits, 
such as an automatic extension of an EAD, poses to the public. 
Additionally, DHS is not removing the alien's ability to obtain a 
renewal of their employment authorization and/or EAD. DHS is also not 
preventing eligible aliens from obtaining an EAD for purposes such as 
proof of identity. The issuance of a renewal EAD depends in large part 
on the applicant's timely application for a renewal EAD. The proper 
planning by the alien, and monitoring of EAD processing times, allows 
the alien to timely file a renewal EAD application far enough in 
advance of their EAD expiration date, which may mitigate the risk that 
the alien could experience a lapse in their employment authorization 
and/or EAD validity and have to temporarily stop working. For these 
reasons, DHS believes that the benefit this rule provides by improving 
the security posture as it relates to the issuance of automatic 
extensions outweighs the impact, if any, on families and their 
children. Better



protecting public safety and national security before providing 
immigration benefits, such as automatic extensions of employment 
authorizations based on the filing of a renewal EAD application, is 
paramount.

I. Executive Order 13175 (Indian Tribal Governments)

    This final rule would not have Tribal implications under E.O. 
13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, 
because it would not have a substantial direct effect on one or more 
Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and 
Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities 
between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.

J. National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)

    DHS and its components analyze proposed regulatory actions to 
determine whether the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 
U.S.C. 4321, et seq., applies and, if so, what degree of analysis is 
required. DHS Directive 023-01 Rev. 01 ``Implementing the National 
Environmental Policy Act'' (Dir. 023-01 Rev. 01) and Instruction Manual 
023-01-001-01 Rev. 01 (Instruction Manual) \219\ establish the policies 
and procedures that DHS and its components use to comply with NEPA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \219\ The Instruction Manual contains DHS's procedures for 
implementing NEPA and was issued on November 6, 2014, https://www.dhs.gov/ocrso/eed/epb/nepa (last updated July 29, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish, in their NEPA 
implementing procedures, categories of actions (``categorical 
exclusions'') that experience has shown do not, individually or 
cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human environment and, 
therefore, do not require an environmental assessment or environmental 
impact statement.\220\ The Instruction Manual, Appendix A lists the DHS 
Categorical Exclusions.\221\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \220\ See 42 U.S.C. 4336(a)(2), 4336e(1).
    \221\ See Instruction Manual, Appendix A, Table 1.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under DHS NEPA implementing procedures, for an action to be 
categorically excluded, it must satisfy each of the following three 
conditions: (1) The entire action clearly fits within one or more of 
the categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger 
action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the 
potential for a significant environmental effect.\222\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \222\ See Instruction Manual at V.B(2)(a) through (c).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This final rule responds to public comments provided in response to 
the IFR and adopts the IFR as final without change. This final rule 
therefore retains the changes made to the DHS regulations by the IFR, 
discontinuing the practice of providing an automatic extension of 
employment authorization and/or EAD validity upon the filing of a 
renewal EAD application. Through the IFR, and now this final rule, DHS 
is ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of EADs to 
prioritize the completion of vetting and eligibility screening of 
aliens before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or 
a new EAD.
    This final rule is strictly administrative and procedural. DHS has 
reviewed this final rule and finds that no significant impact on the 
environment, or any change in environmental effect will result from the 
amendments being promulgated in this final rule.
    Accordingly, DHS finds that the promulgation of this final rule's 
amendments to current regulations clearly fits within categorical 
exclusion A3 established in DHS's NEPA implementing procedures as an 
administrative change with no change in environmental effect, is not 
part of a larger Federal action, and does not present extraordinary 
circumstances that create the potential for a significant environmental 
effect. Therefore, regulatory amendments are categorically excluded 
from further NEPA review.

K. Paperwork Reduction Act

    Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, Public Law 104-13, all 
agencies are required to submit to OMB, for review and approval, any 
reporting requirements inherent in a rule. This rule does not impose 
any new reporting or recordkeeping requirements under the Paperwork 
Reduction Act.
    However, this rule requires the use of USCIS Form I-765. This form 
has previously been approved by OMB under the Paperwork Reduction Act. 
The OMB control number(s) for this information collection is 1615-0040.

that amended DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically 
extending the validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I-
766 or EADs) for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew

screening of aliens before granting a new period of employment 
authorization and/or a new EAD.

II. Notice of Consideration of Issuance of Amendments to Facility 
Operating Licenses and Combined Licenses and Proposed No Significant 
Hazards Consideration Determination

    For the facility-specific amendment requests shown in this notice, 
the Commission finds that the licensees' analyses provided, consistent 
with section 50.91 of title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 
CFR) ``Notice for public comment; State consultation,'' are sufficient 
to support the proposed determinations that these amendment requests 
involve NSHC. Under the Commission's regulations in 10 CFR 50.92, 
operation of the facilities in accordance with the proposed amendments 
would not (1) involve a significant increase in the probability or 
consequences of an accident previously evaluated; or (2) create the 
possibility of a new or different kind of accident from any accident 
previously evaluated; or (3) involve a significant reduction in a 
margin of safety.
    The Commission is seeking public comments on these proposed 
determinations. Any comments received within 30 days after the date of 
publication of this notice will be considered in making any final 
determinations.
    Normally, the Commission will not issue the amendments until the 
expiration of 60 days after the date of publication of this notice. The 
Commission may issue any of these license amendments before expiration 
of the 60-day period provided that its final determination is that the 
amendment involves NSHC. In addition, the Commission may issue any of 
these amendments prior to the expiration of the 30-day comment period 
if circumstances change during the 30-day comment period such that 
failure to act in a timely way would result, for example in derating or 
shutdown of the facility. If the Commission takes action on any of 
these amendments prior to the expiration of either the comment period 
or the notice period, it will publish in the Federal Register a notice 
of issuance. If the Commission makes a final NSHC determination for any 
of these amendments, any hearing will take place after issuance. The 
Commission expects that the need to take action on any amendment before 
60 days have elapsed will occur very infrequently.

A. Opportunity To Request a Hearing and Petition for Leave To Intervene

person (petitioner) whose interest may be affected by any of these 
actions may file a request for a hearing and petition for leave to 
intervene (petition) with respect to that action. Petitions shall be 
filed in accordance with the Commission's ``Agency Rules of Practice 
and Procedure'' in 10 CFR part 2. Interested persons should consult 10 
CFR 2.309. If a petition is filed, the Commission or a presiding 
officer will rule on the petition and, if appropriate, a notice of a 
hearing will be issued.

publication of this notice in accordance with the filing instructions 
in the ``Electronic Submissions (E-Filing)'' section of this document.

are filed after the deadline will not be entertained absent a 
determination by the presiding officer that the filing demonstrates

B. Electronic Submissions (E-Filing)

AGENCY: Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.

ACTION: Proposed amendment; notice of intent.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DATES: October 14, 2026.

ADDRESSES: 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, Virginia 22152.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Drug and Chemical Evaluation Section, 
Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration; Telephone:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The notice of intent contained in this 
document is issued pursuant to the temporary scheduling provisions of 
21 U.S.C. 811(h). The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) intends to 
issue a temporary scheduling order \1\ (in the form of a temporary 
amendment) to add 7-hydroxymitragynine \2\ and mitragynine pseudindoxyl 
\3\ above a specified threshold described herein, including their 
isomers, esters, ethers, salts, and salts of isomers, esters, and 
ethers, whenever the existence of such isomers, esters, ethers, and 
salts is possible, to schedule I under the Controlled Substances Act 
(CSA).\4\ The specified threshold for reflects the recommendation made 
by the Assistant Secretary for Health (Assistant Secretary) of the 
Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) in a letter to the 
Administrator of DEA dated October 8, 2026, which described the 
threshold as follows:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ Though DEA has used the term ``final order'' with respect to 
temporary scheduling orders in the past, this notice of intent 
adheres to the statutory language of 21 U.S.C. 811(h), which refers 
to a ``temporary scheduling order.'' No substantive change is 
intended.
    \2\ Chemical name: Methyl (E)-2-((2S,3S,7aS)-3-ethyl-7a-hydroxy-
8-methoxy-1,2,3,4,6,7,7a,12b-octahydroindolo[2,3-a]quinolizin-2-yl)-
3-methoxyacrylate (also known as: ([alpha]E,2S,3S,7aS,12bS)-3-ethyl-
l,2,3,4,6,7,7a,12b-octahydro-7a-hydroxy-8-methoxy-a-
(methoxymethylene)-indolo[2,3-a]quinolizine-2-acetic acid, methyl 
ester).
    \3\ Chemical name: Methyl (E)-2-((1'S,6'S,7'S)-6'-ethyl-4-
methoxy-3-oxo-3',5',6',7',8',8a'-hexahydro-2'H-spiro[indoline-2,1'-
indolizine]-7'-yl)-3-methoxyacrylate (commonly known as mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl).
    \4\ On July 6, 2026, DEA published a notice of intent to place 
7-hydroxymitragynine above a specified threshold in schedule I of 
the CSA. See Schedules of Controlled Substance: Temporary Placement 
of 7-Hydroxymitragynine Above a Specified Threshold in Schedule I, 
91 FR 40917 (July 6, 2026). DEA is withdrawing that notice of intent 
elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register. On August 26, 2026, 
DEA published a temporary order that placed mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl, along with two other 7-hydroxymitragynine-related 
substances, in schedule I of the CSA. See Schedules of Controlled 
Substances: Temporary Placement of Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl, MGM-
15, and MGM-16 in Schedule I, 91 FR 54948 (Aug. 26, 2026). That 
temporary order is effective until August 26, 2028, or until a new 
temporary order placing mitragynine pseudindoxyl above a specified 
threshold is published and the previous order withdrawn, whichever 
occurs first.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The substances [7-hydroxymitragynine] and [mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl] be controlled in schedule I [pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 
811(h)] when either substance alone, or their combined amount if both 
present, is:
    (A) Above a specified threshold concentration, that is, greater 
than 1 mg per gram (for solid powders, encapsulated material, or other 
solid forms) or greater than 1 mg per milliliter (for liquid 
preparations), OR
    (B) The mass of mitragynine present divided by the mass of [7-
hydroxymitragynine], or [mitragynine pseudoindoxyl], or the combined 
amount of [7-hydroxymitragynine] and [mitragynine pseudoindoxyl] if 
both present, is less than 100.\5\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ Letter from Assistant Secretary for Health of HHS Admiral 
Brian Christine, M.D., to DEA, at page 8 (Oct. 8, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The temporary scheduling order will be published in the Federal 
Register on or after November 13, 2026.

Legal Authority

    The CSA provides the Attorney General with the authority to 
temporarily place a substance in schedule I of the CSA for two years 
without regard to the requirements of 21 U.S.C. 811(b), if he finds 
that such action is necessary to avoid an imminent hazard to public 
safety.\6\ In addition, if proceedings to control a substance are 
initiated under 21 U.S.C. 811(a)(1) while the substance is temporarily 
controlled under section 811(h), the Attorney General may extend the 
temporary scheduling for up to one year.\7\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \6\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1).
    \7\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Where the necessary findings are made, a substance may be 
temporarily scheduled if it is not listed in any other schedule under 
21 U.S.C. 812, or if there is no exemption or approval in effect for 
the substance under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic 
Act, 21 U.S.C. 355.\8\ The Attorney General has delegated scheduling 
authority



under 21 U.S.C. 811 to the Administrator of DEA (Administrator).\9\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \8\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1); 21 CFR part 1308.
    \9\ 28 CFR 0.100.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Background

    The CSA requires the Administrator to notify the Secretary of the 
Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) of this intent to issue a 
temporary scheduling order.\10\ By letter dated October 8, 2026, 
Assistant Secretary for Health sent a letter to DEA that, among other 
things, recommended controlling 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl when either substance alone, or their combined amount if 
both are present, is above a specified threshold in schedule I. By 
letter dated October 8, 2026, the Administrator transmitted the 
required notice to place 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl above the specified threshold recommended by HHS in 
schedule I on a temporary basis to the Assistant Secretary.\11\ By 
letter dated March 6, 2026, the Assistant Secretary advised that based 
on a review by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), there were 
currently no investigational new drug applications (IND) or approved 
new drug applications (NDA) for 7-hydroxymitragynine above a specified 
threshold. In a separate letter dated January 20, 2026, the Assistant 
Secretary advised that based on a review by the Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA), there were currently no investigational new drug 
applications (IND) or approved new drug applications (NDA) for 
mitragynine pseudoindoxyl as of that date. The Assistant Secretary 
provided no contrary information in its October 8, 2026, letter. 
Neither 7-hydroxymitragynine nor mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is currently 
listed in any other schedule than schedule I under the CSA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \10\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(4).
    \11\ The Secretary of HHS has delegated to the Assistant 
Secretary for Health of HHS the authority to make domestic drug 
scheduling recommendations. Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and 
Control Act of 1970, Public Law 91-513, As Amended; Delegation of 
Authority, 58 FR 35460 (July 1, 1993).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    To find that placing a substance temporarily in schedule I of the 
CSA is necessary to avoid an imminent hazard to public safety, the 
Administrator must consider three of the eight factors set forth in 21 
U.S.C. 811(c): the substance's history and current pattern of abuse; 
the scope, duration and significance of abuse; and what, if any, risk 
there is to public health.\12\ This consideration includes any 
information indicating actual abuse, diversion from legitimate 
channels, and clandestine importation, manufacture, or distribution of 
either 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl.\13\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \12\ 21 U.S.C. 811(c)(4)-(6), (h)(3).
    \13\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(3).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Substances meeting the statutory requirements for temporary 
scheduling may only be placed in schedule I.\14\ Substances in schedule 
I have high potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use in 
treatment in the United States,\15\ and a lack of accepted safety for 
use under medical supervision.\16\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \14\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1).
    \15\ When finding schedule I placement on a temporary basis is 
necessary to avoid imminent hazard to the public, 21 U.S.C 811(h) 
does not require DEA to consider whether the substance has a 
currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States. 
Nonetheless, there is no evidence suggesting that 7-
hydroxymitragynine or mitragynine pseudoindoxyl has a currently 
accepted medical use in treatment in the United States. First, DEA 
looks to whether the drug or substance has FDA approval. When no FDA 
approval exists, DEA has traditionally applied a five-part test to 
determine whether a drug or substances has a currently accepted 
medical use: (1) the drug's chemistry must be known and 
reproducible; (2) there must be adequate safety studies; (3) there 
must be adequate and well-controlled studies proving efficacy; (4) 
the drug must be accepted by qualified experts; and (5) the 
scientific evidence must be widely available. Marijuana Scheduling 
Petition; Denial of Petition; Remand, 57 FR 10499 (Mar. 26, 1992), 
pet. for rev. denied, Alliance for Cannabis Therapeutics v. Drug 
Enforcement Admin., 15 F.3d 1131, 1135 (D.C. Cir. 1994). DEA applied 
the traditional five-part test and concluded the test was not 
satisfied. In a recent published letter in a different context, HHS 
applied an additional two-part test to determine currently accepted 
medical use for substances that do not satisfy the five-part test: 
(1) whether there exists widespread, current experience with medical 
use of the substance by licensed health care providers operating in 
accordance with implemented jurisdiction-authorized programs, where 
medical use is recognized by entities that regulate the practice of 
medicine, and, if so, (2) whether there exists some credible 
scientific support for at least one of the medical conditions for 
which part (1) is satisfied. On April 11, 2024, the Department of 
Justice's Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) issued an opinion, which, 
among other things, concluded that HHS's two-part test would be 
sufficient to establish that a drug has a currently accepted medical 
use. Office of Legal Counsel, Memorandum for Merrick B. Garland 
Attorney General Re: Questions Related to the Potential Rescheduling 
of Marijuana at 3 (April 11, 2024). For purposes of this notice of 
intent, there is no evidence that health care providers have 
widespread experience with medical use of 7-hydroxymitragynine or 
mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is recognized by entities that regulate 
the practice of medicine, so the two-part test also is not 
satisfied. In HHS's letter dated January 20, 2026, HHS advised DEA 
that there were currently no approved new drug applications or 
investigational new drug applications for mitragynine pseudoindoxyl. 
By letter dated March 6, 2026, the Assistant Secretary responded to 
this notice and advised that based on a review by the Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA), there were currently no investigational new 
drug applications (IND) or approved new drug applications (NDA) for 
7-hydroxymitragynine. The Assistant Secretary provided no contrary 
information in its October 8, 2026 letter.
    \16\ 21 U.S.C. 812(b)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

7-Hydroxymitragynine Above a Specified Threshold

    7-Hydroxymitragynine is a psychoactive alkaloid found in Mitragyna 
speciosa (M. speciosa) plant, a tropical evergreen tree indigenous to 
Southeast Asia. While the use of the plant was once geographically 
limited, the use of M. speciosa has since extended to the United States 
and other global markets. Among the numerous alkaloids identified in M. 
speciosa, the indole alkaloids mitragynine (major) and 7-
hydroxymitragynine (minor) are primarily responsible for the plant's 
psychoactive effects. In its natural botanical form, 7-
hydoxymitragynine makes up less than two percent of the total alkaloid 
content or occurs in trace amount in M. speciosa. However, 7-
hydroxymitragynine can be synthesized from mitragynine through a one-
step chemical reaction, and it also exists as an active oxidized 
metabolite of mitragynine in vivo. Despite the different origins of 7-
hydroxymitragynine, the chemical structures of synthetic and naturally 
occurring 7-hydroxymitragynine are identical.
    Recently, the United States has seen a proliferation of 7-
hydroxymitragynine products. Evidence suggests that commercially 
available products, including extracts and synthetic formulations, 
contain a significantly higher concentration of 7-hydroxymitragynine 
than what is found in botanical M. speciosa. These products are 
commonly sold on the internet and in retail outlets, such as gas 
stations and smoke shops, in various forms, including powders, tablets, 
gummies, and sublingual films designed for rapid absorption. To date, 
the safety profile of these concentrated products in humans remains 
unknown because no controlled clinical trials have been conducted to 
establish safe consumption limits or standardized dosing.
    7-Hydroxymitragynine has opioidergic activity, sharing a similar 
pharmacological profile to schedule II opioids like morphine. 
Preclinical data indicates that 7-hydroxymitragynine carries a high 
abuse potential with safety risks, including tolerance, dependence, and 
respiratory depression, which are comparable to those of classic opioid 
analgesics. The United States has recently seen an emergence of 
products containing 7-hydroxymitragynine, which are often characterized 
by



ambiguous dosages and misleading marketing, frequently being labeled as 
``natural M. speciosa extracts.'' While sellers promote these products 
for their euphoric and opioidergic effects, evidence demonstrates they 
may also contain other opioid alkaloids, such as mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl. These combinations, coupled with a lack of regulatory 
oversight, pose significant safety risk to unsuspecting consumers by 
exposing them to high doses of opioids. The absence of clinical 
evidence to support vendor health claims is deeply concerning. 
Consequently, 7-hydroxymitragynine products sold as unregulated dietary 
supplements pose significant health risks, as essential information 
regarding their purity, identity, quantity and long-term safety remain 
unknown.
    7-Hydroxymitragynine does not meet the United States Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) definitions for drugs, dietary supplements, or 
dietary ingredients. FDA has issued warning letters to companies 
clarifying that 7-hydroxymitragyine is not an FDA-approved drug product 
and no food additive regulation has authorized the use of 7-
hydroxymitragynine in food supply. Furthermore, FDA has warned 
consumers against using products labeled as 7-hydroxymitragynine, as 
they have not been proven safe or effective for any use.\17\ Fatal 
overdoses involving 7-hydroxymitragynine have been reported, making its 
wide availability and unknown safety profile a significant threat to 
public health, which is particularly concerning in the midst of an 
opioid crisis. The availability of 7 hydroxymitragynine-containing 
substances in the United States' M. speciosa consumer market poses an 
imminent hazard to the public safety.
