Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl

    The prevalence and misuse of Mitragyna speciosa (commonly known as 
kratom) and its psychoactive alkaloids, including mitragynine and 7-
hydroxymitragynine, have led to the proliferation of commercial 
products containing opioids chemically synthesized from mitragynine or 
7-hydroxymitragynine. In recent years, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, which 
is a chemical rearrangement product of 7-hydroxymitragynine has 
recently emerged on the Mitragyna speciosa consumer markets. The 
chemical scaffolds of mitragynine or 7-hydroxymitragynine were used in 
scientific research to develop mitragynine pseudoindoxyl via chemical 
modifications of purified isolates. Evidence from the Mitragyna 
speciosa retail markets demonstrates that mitragynine pseudoindoxyl 
transitioned from experimental substances studied in research to widely 
available commercial products. These products are commonly sold in 
different forms such as powders, tablets, and liquid shots. This is a 
significant evolution from the traditional administration of Mitragyna 
speciosa, which was once restricted to either chewing raw leaves or 
steeping the leaves into water decoctions and teas.
    These products are sold under numerous brand names like Kama, 
Hydroxie, Fruity Perks, and Happie Tabs,\18\ and they are easily 
purchased on the internet, as well as in gas stations, corner shops, 
and vape shops. These products are available in consumer-friendly forms 
to include flavored chewable tablets, which increases their appeal to a 
broader demographic. Also, the aggressive marketing of mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl, which is a semi-synthetic opioid, as ``precision-
formulated products,'' ``botanical extracts,'' or as ``mood boosters'' 
for the treatment of health conditions is deeply concerning. The 
branding creates a false sense of safety for unknowing consumers who 
may equate the term ``botanical'' with lower risk. Furthermore, there 
is paucity of data on quality control or standardized dosage available 
for these products, making their use especially dangerous.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is a potent opioid that shares a similar 
pharmacological profile with 7-hydroxymitragynine. Available 
pharmacology data demonstrate that mitragynine pseudoindoxyl exhibit 
strong affinity for the mu-opioid receptor (MOR) and function as MOR 
agonists.19 20 Data from preclinical studies show that this 
substance produce analgesic effect that is more potent than 
morphine.\21\ Because mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is a potent MOR 
agonist, it poses similar health risks as other mu-opioid agonists 
(i.e., morphine and fentanyl), including physical and psychological 
dependence, and respiratory depression.

    A scan of retail data on the internet shows that vendors explicitly 
market mitragynine pseudoindoxyl products for their ``clean and 
powerful'' opioid-receptor activation, utilizing deceptive terminology 
to target individuals seeking alternatives to pharmaceutical opioids. 
These combinations and marketing strategies pose significant safety 
risks to unsuspecting consumers who use these products by exposing them 
to high doses of opioids. Recently, reports have confirmed the positive 
identification of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in toxicology cases in the 
United States, and evidence demonstrates that these substances are 
being misused. The lack of clinical data regarding its safety and 
efficacy, coupled with the risk of life-threatening respiratory 
depression and addiction, underscores the danger of marketing this 
unapproved, highly potent opioid under the guise of therapeutic or 
wellness products.
    Available data and information for 7-hydroxymitragynine and 
mitragynine pseudoindoxyl summarized below, indicate that these 
substances have a high potential for abuse, no currently accepted 
medical use in treatment in the United States, and a lack of accepted 
safety for use under medical supervision. DEA's three-factor analysis 
and HHS's October 8, 2026 letter are available in their entirety under 
``Supporting and Related Material'' of the public docket for this 
action at www.regulations.gov under Docket Number DEA-1570.

Factor 4. History and Current Pattern of Abuse

7-Hydroxymitragynine

    7-Hydroxymitragynine is most commonly used in isolated form or as



component of M. speciosa. Historically, M. speciosa has been used for a 
variety of purposes, including as an opium substitute and a treatment 
of various opioid withdrawal symptoms, such as pain, cough, anxiety, 
diarrhea, and intestinal difficulty.\22\ While its use was once 
geographically limited, the marketing in the United States of 7-
hydroxymitragynine products has been aggressive and often 
indistinguishable from the sale of M. speciosa.\23\ In recent years, 7-
hydroxymitragynine has been falsely marketed as a dietary supplement 
\24\ or natural extract despite failing to meet FDA's definitions for 
drugs, dietary supplements, or dietary ingredients. Anecdotal 
information from users who post on social media indicates that many 
users are self-treating chronic pain with unregulated 7-
hydroxymitragynine products.\25\

Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl

    Mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is a synthetic derivatives of the indole 
alkaloids, mitragynine or 7-hydroxymitragynine, of the Mitragyna 
speciosa plant. Unlike the indole alkaloids mitragynine and 7-
hydroxymitragynine, which are naturally occurring in the plant, 
mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is produced through synthetic modifications 
of purified mitragynine isolates or 7-hydroxymitragynine.\29\ The 
chemical scaffolds of mitragynine or 7-hydroxymitragynine were used in 
scientific research to develop novel mitragynine pseudoindoxyl. The 
first mention of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in scientific literature 
dates to 1974 when mitragynine pseudoindoxyl was isolated as a 
metabolite from bio transformed mitragynine.

Current Patterns of Use Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl

    Users seek mitragynine pseudoindoxyl for its psychoactive effects 
and products are often advertised as mood enhancers or alternative to 
prescription opioid analgesics (see Factor 5). These products are 
commonly sold in different product forms, such as powders, tablets, or

Factor 5. Scope, Duration, and Significance of Abuse

7-Hydroxymitragynine

    The abuse of 7-hydroxymitragynine is increasing and widespread. 
Given its pharmacological profile as an opioid agonist and high abuse 
potential,\34\ the marketing of 7-hydroxymitragynine products to 
consumers as botanical supplements constitute a significant public 
health risk. 7-Hydroxymitragynine, a potent opioid, presents overdose 
risk and toxicity to users because its chemical manufacturing process 
is inconsistent and does not adhere to good manufacturing practices. 
This lack of oversight may lead to variation in doses and composition 
in final products. Further, 7-hydroxymitragynine is sold as sublingual 
pouch/tablet, a formulation known to deliver drugs rapidly into the 
systemic circulation. This rapid delivery, coupled with 7-
hydroxymitragynine's known pharmacokinetic profile, presents a 
significance of abuse.\35\

Law Enforcement Encounters

    The number of seizures for 7-hydroxymitragynine as reported in law 
enforcement systems is currently limited, primarily because forensic 
chemists often prioritize the identification of mitragynine, the major 
alkaloid in M. speciosa, rather than extending analysis to the 
identification minor alkaloids, such as 7-hydroxymitragynine. 
Furthermore, because 7-hydroxymitragynine is not federally controlled 
under the CSA, specific forensic identification may be limited. 
Consequently, some forensic laboratories may not place emphasis on 
analyzing or tracking the encounters of non-controlled substances, 
making it unlikely to be fully reported to forensic laboratories 
databases. Nonetheless, available data from the National Forensic 
Laboratory Information System (NFLIS) database \37\ shows that, in 
2025, there were 42 reports of 7-hydroxymitagynine from 12 states. This 
law enforcement data illustrates the widespread and increasing 
availability of products containing 7-



hydroxymitragynine within the domestic kratom drug market.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

FDA Warning Letters

    Between June and July 2025, FDA issued seven warning letters \38\ 
to marketers and distributors in response to the unauthorized claim of 
7-hydroxymitragynine as a drug, dietary supplement, or dietary 
ingredient. The warning letters explicitly stated that 7-
hydroxymitragyine is not an FDA-approved drug product and that no food 
additive regulation has authorized the use of 7-hydroxymitragynine in 
food. FDA further classified 7-hydroxymitragynine as a ``new dietary 
ingredient'' under section 413(d) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 350b(d), 
because there is no evidence demonstrating it was marketed as a dietary 
ingredient in the United States before October 15, 1994. Additionally, 
some letters noted that, as a dietary supplement, 7-hydroxymitraghynine 
is considered adulterated under section 402(f)(l)(B) of the FD&C Act, 
21 U.S.C. 342(f)(l)(B). This is because there is inadequate information 
providing reasonable assurance that the ingredient does not present a 
significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury. Of note was 
FDA's warning letter issued on June 25, 2025, to a company selling 
``7OHMZ 7-Hydroxymitragynine Gummies,'' \39\ in which FDA cautioned 
that such products may be appealing to children due to their packaging. 
Other warning letters targeted the illegal sale of unapproved 7-
hydroxymitragynine products marketed for the treatment of pain, 
relaxation, mood enhancement, and other medical conditions.\40\ Vendors 
utilized websites and social media pages to make unproven medical 
claims for 7-hydroxymitragynine, such as describing tablets as 
``expertly formulated to provide a potent dose'' or promising ``intense 
relaxation and a feeling of pure bliss.''

such as Arizona, Colorado, South Carolina, and Texas, have set

    The significance of 7-hydroxymitragynine abuse is demonstrated by

7-hydroxymitragynine was historically limited within the national 
poison data system (NPDS); however, specific data codes for this 
substance were recently implemented between February and May 2025. 
During the initial tracking period from February 2025 to April 2025, 
NPDS recorded a total of 53 case reports involving 7-
hydroxymitragynine. Of these exposure calls, 37 cases involved single-
substance exposure of 7-hydroxymitragynine alone, and 24 cases were 
classified as abuse involving other substances in combination with 7-
hydroxymitragynine. Among the single-substance exposure calls, 16 cases 
were categorized as intentional abuse, while 13 calls involved moderate 
medical outcomes where the patients exhibited pronounced and prolonged 
systemic symptoms.
    Expanded data from U.S. poison centers indicates a rapid escalation 
in reported incidents.\43\ From January 1 through July 31, 2025, there 
were 165 exposure cases involving 7-hydroxymitragynine. Of those 
reporting exposures to 7-hydroxymitragynine alone, 35 percent of these 
cases resulted in serious health problems, and 67 percent of 
individuals were treated at a healthcare facility. Patients exposed to 
7-hydroxymitragynine frequently exhibit a range of severe physiological 
and neurological symptoms, including: gastrointestinal (nausea and 
vomiting), neurological (agitation, confusion, loss of consciousness, 
and seizure), cardiovascular (sweating, tachycardia, and hypertension), 
and respiratory (difficulty breathing). According to HHS' review, users 
report several reasons regarding the use of 7-hydroxymitragynine, 
including the following:

    In summary, the abuse of 7-hydroxymitragynine in the United States

lack of regulatory controls, and the relative ease of obtaining 7-
hydroxymitragynine products via smoke shops and the internet.\44\ 
Furthermore, the consumption of 7-hydroxymitragynine alongside other 
mind-altering substances may exacerbate the potential acute and long-
term hazards and risks to the user, especially drug dependence. FDA 
responded to the increase in sales of 7-hydroxymitragynine products and 
unsubstantiated medical claims by issuing warning letters to companies 
to protect public safety. Available information from published 
literatures and poison control centers suggests that 7-
hydroxymitragynine is used by a diverse population for the self-
treatment of various health conditions. The ingestion of 7-
hydroxymitragynine, a potent opioid, alone or co-ingestion with other 
substances, commonly a CNS depressant, is of serious concern. The 
poison control center data and popularity of 7-hydroxymitragynine-
products collectively underscores the severity and significance of 
abuse of 7-hydroxymitragynine in the United States.

Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl

    The abuse of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is concerning due to its 
high opioid potency and commercial availability. Mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl products are sold in formulations that facilitate ease of 
use, bypass the traditional, lower-alkaloid preparation (chewing leaves 
or drinking tea) and provide a highly potent effect that mimics 
classical opioids such as morphine.

Deceptive Branding and Market Infiltration of Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl

    Analysis of marketed mitragynine pseudoindoxyl products revealed 
misleading marketing strategies with claims that the products are 
``kratom.'' Available information on vendor website indicates that the 
concentrated alkaloid products often contain more than one alkaloid 
with opioid activity (e.g., 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl). These substances combinations and marketing practices 
pose significant safety risk to unsuspecting consumers by exposing them 
to high doses of opioids (see Table 1). It is known that repeated use 
of opioids can lead to psychological and physical dependence. In fact, 
data show that chronic use of 7-hydroxymitragynine has sent users to 
opioid detox clinic and the need for opioid use disorder 
medication.\45\ Furthermore, these products are labeled for ``strong 
mood enhancement'' and ``analgesic properties.'' Finally, the presence 
of these products containing mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is deeply 
concerning because the identity, purity, and quality of these products' 
formulation are uncertain, thus presenting additional safety concerns 
for unsuspecting users.

Factor 6. What, If Any, Risk There Is to Public Health

7-Hyrdoxymitragynine

    7-Hydroxymitragynine has opioidergic and addictive properties. 
Available preclinical data demonstrates that 7-hydroxymitragynine has 
an abuse potential similar to that of schedule I and II opioids, such 
as heroin, morphine, and fentanyl.\53\ The abuse of 7-
hydroxymitragynine presents a severe of risks to public health, 
including tolerance, dependence and addiction, respiratory depression, 
and death. Public health assessment is further complicated because 7-
hydroxymitragynine is a known metabolite of mitragynine, making it 
difficult to distinguish between the ingestion of M. speciosa and other 
isolated 7-hydroxymitragynine products.

Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl

    Mitragynine pseudoindoxyl functions as potent MOR agonist. This 
mechanism of action is inherently associated with high potential of 
abuse, physical dependence, and psychological dependence, consistent 
with the effects of controlled schedule I and II opioid substances. As 
of early 2026, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl products are sold in smoke 
shops, gas stations, and through numerous online marketplaces, often 
marketed alongside traditional supplements, which mask their potent 
opioid nature. Data from preclinical studies demonstrate that 
mitragynine pseudoindoxyl is about 100 times more potent than 
mitragynine at the MOR.\62\ Because of the potency of this compound, it 
can be abused in smaller, concentrated doses. It has been demonstrated 
that mitragynine pseudoindoxyl may cause development of signs of opioid 
physical dependence after chronic use in rodents. Pre-clinical studies 
demonstrated that chronic twice-daily administration of mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl in rodents induces signs of opioid physical dependence 
and withdrawal symptoms in morphine addiction rodent models as 
evidenced by increased diarrhea, jumping, and rearing frequency 
occurring when naloxone was administered or when treatment with this 
alkaloid was tapered.\63\

Finding of Necessity of Schedule I Placement To Avoid Imminent Hazard 
to Public Safety

    In accordance with 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(3), based on the available data 
and information summarized above, the uncontrolled manufacture, 
distribution, reverse distribution, importation, exportation, conduct 
of research and chemical analysis, possession, and abuse of 7-
hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl poses an imminent 
hazard to public safety. DEA is not aware of any currently accepted 
medical uses for either 7-hydroxymitragynine or mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl in the United States. A substance meeting the statutory 
requirements for temporary scheduling, found in 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1), 
may only be placed in schedule I. Substances in schedule I are those 
that have a high potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use 
in treatment in the United States, and a lack of accepted safety for 
use under medical supervision. Available data and information for 7-
hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl indicate that these 
substances have a high potential for abuse, no currently accepted 
medical use in treatment in the United States, and a lack of accepted 
safety for use under medical supervision. However, because both 7-
hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl have supposedly been 
found in trace amounts in some botanical kratom products, this 
temporary scheduling order is only temporarily placing 7-
hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl when either substance 
alone, or their combined amount if both are present, is above a 
specified threshold in schedule I. Individuals should not infer from 
this notice of intent that DEA views 7-hydroxymitragynine or 
mitragynine pseudoindoxyl below this threshold as safe for consumption. 
DEA still views kratom and its two major psychoactive ingredients, 
mitragynine and 7-hydroxymtragynine, as drugs of concern.\68\

with a possible extension of an additional year, pending completion of 
the regular (permanent) scheduling process.\70\ The Administrator 
intends to issue a temporary scheduling order as soon as possible after 
the expiration of 30 days from the date of publication of this 
document. Upon publication of the temporary order, 7-hydroxymitragynine 
and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl when either substance alone, or their 
combined amount if both are present, is above a specified threshold 
will then be subject to the CSA's schedule I regulatory controls and 
administrative, civil, and criminal sanctions applicable to the 
manufacture, distribution, reverse distribution, importation, 
exportation, research, conduct of instructional activities and chemical 
analysis, and possession.

substances. Regular scheduling actions in accordance with 21 U.S.C. 
811(a) are subject to formal rulemaking procedures ``on the record 
after opportunity for a hearing'' conducted pursuant to the provisions 
of 5 U.S.C. 556 and 557.\71\ The regular scheduling process of formal 
rulemaking affords interested parties appropriate process and the 
government any additional relevant information needed to make a 
determination. It is DEA's intention to pursue formal rulemaking 
proceedings under 21 U.S.C. 811(a) in this instance by gathering the

Regulatory Analyses

    The CSA provides for expedited temporary scheduling actions where 
necessary to avoid an imminent hazard to public safety. Under 21 U.S.C.



811(h)(1), the Administrator (as delegated by the Attorney General) 
may, by order, temporarily schedule substances in schedule I. Such 
orders may not be issued before the expiration of 30 days from: (1) the 
publication of a notice in the Federal Register of the intent to issue 
such order and the grounds upon which such order is to be issued, and 
(2) the date that notice of the proposed temporary scheduling order is 
transmitted to the Assistant Secretary of HHS, as delegated by the 
Secretary of HHS.\74\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \74\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Inasmuch as section 811(h) directs that temporary scheduling 
actions be issued by order and sets forth the procedures by which such 
orders are to be issued, including the requirement of a publication in 
the Federal Register of a notice of intent, the notice-and-comment 
requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 553, 
do not apply to this notice of intent. The APA expressly differentiates 
between an order and a rule, as it defines an ``order'' to mean a 
``final disposition, whether affirmative, negative, injunctive, or 
declaratory in form, of an agency in a matter other than rule making.'' 
\75\ This contrasts with permanent scheduling actions, which are 
subject to formal rulemaking procedures done ``on the record after 
opportunity for a hearing,'' and final decisions that conclude the 
scheduling process and are subject to judicial review.\76\ The specific 
language chosen by Congress indicates its intent that DEA issue orders 
instead of proceeding by rulemaking when temporarily scheduling 
substances. Given that Congress specifically requires the Administrator 
(as delegated by the Attorney General) to follow rulemaking procedures 
for other kinds of scheduling actions,\77\ it is noteworthy that, in 
section 811(h)(1), Congress authorized the issuance of temporary 
scheduling actions by order rather than by rule.

    \75\ 5 U.S.C. 551(6) (emphasis added).

any further delays in the process for issuing temporary scheduling 
orders would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest given 
the manifest urgency to avoid an imminent hazard to public safety.

scheduling order is not subject to the notice-and-comment requirements

Administrator took into consideration comments submitted by the 
Assistant Secretary in response to the notice that DEA transmitted to 
the Assistant Secretary pursuant to such subsection.

subject to the requirements of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA).

flexibility analysis in 5 U.S.C. 603(a) are not applicable where, as

issuing this notice of intent pursuant to DEA's authority to issue a 
temporary scheduling order.\78\ Therefore, in this instance, since DEA

summary:
The Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) 
is issuing this notice of intent to publish a temporary order to 
schedule 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (including 
their isomers, esters, ethers, salts, and salts of isomers, esters, and 
ethers, whenever the existence of such isomers, esters, ethers, and 
salts is possible) when either substance alone, or their combined 
amount if both are present, is above a specified threshold, in schedule 
I of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). Based on a different 
threshold provided by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) 
in July of 2025, DEA published a notice of intent to temporarily 
schedule 7-hydroxymitragynine above that lower threshold on July 7, 
2026. Additionally, DEA published a temporary order placing mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl without a threshold in schedule I of the CSA on August 
26, 2026. On October 8, 2026, HHS sent a letter recommending that DEA 
place of the CSA 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in 
schedule I when either substance alone, or their combined amount if 
both are present, is above a new specified threshold. Based on the 
October 8, 2026 letter, DEA is issuing this notice of intent. While the 
new threshold recommended by HHS would permit certain products to 
remain in the marketplace without being subject to schedule I controls, 
neither HHS nor DEA has made a finding that these substances are safe 
to use at below-threshold levels. When a temporary order is issued, it 
will impose the regulatory controls and administrative, civil, and 
criminal sanctions applicable to schedule I controlled substances on 
persons who handle (manufacture, distribute, reverse distribute, 
import, export, engage in research, conduct instructional activities or 
chemical analysis with, or possess) or propose to handle 7-
hydroxymitragynine and/or mitragynine pseudoindoxyl above the specified 
threshold. In a separate document contained in this issue of the 
Federal Register, DEA is withdrawing the July 7, 2026 notice of intent 
related to 7-hydroxymitragynine. The August 26, 2026 temporary order 
placing mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in schedule I of the CSA without a 
threshold remains in effect until either it expires or the new 
temporary order is published and the previous order is withdrawn, 
whichever occurs first.

safety.\3\ In addition, if proceedings to control a substance are 
initiated under 21 U.S.C. 811(a)(1) while the substance is temporarily 
controlled under section 811(h), the Attorney General may extend the 
temporary scheduling for up to one year.\4\

Background

    The CSA requires the Administrator to notify the Secretary of the 
Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) of this intent to issue a 
temporary scheduling order.\7\ By letter dated October 6, 2026, 
Assistant Secretary for Health of HHS (Assistant Secretary) sent a 
letter to DEA that, among other things, recommended controlling 
mitragynine pseudoindoxyl above a certain threshold in schedule I. 
Importantly, HHS did not recommend controlling MGM-15 or MGM-16 above 
any threshold, and, therefore, the October 6, 2026 letter has no impact 
on any of DEA's prior findings and conclusions regarding MGM-15 and 
MGM-16. By letter dated October 8, 2026, the Administrator transmitted 
the required notice to place MGM-15 and MGM-16 in schedule I on a 
temporary basis to the Assistant Secretary.\8\ By letter dated January 
20, 2026, the Assistant Secretary advised that based on a review by the 
Food and Drug Administration (FDA), there were currently no 
investigational new drug applications (IND) or approved new drug 
applications (NDA) for MGM-15 and MGM-16. The Assistant Secretary also 
stated that HHS had no objection to the temporary placement of these 
substances in schedule I of the CSA. The Assistant Secretary provided 
no contrary information in its October 6, 2026 letter. MGM-15 and MGM-
16 are not currently listed in any other schedule than schedule I under 
the CSA.

the scope, duration and significance of abuse; and what, if any, risk 
there is to public health.\9\ This consideration includes any 
information indicating actual abuse, diversion from legitimate 
channels, and clandestine importation, manufacture, or distribution of 
MGM-15, and MGM-16.\10\

    Substances meeting the statutory requirements for temporary 
scheduling may only be placed in schedule I.\11\ Substances in schedule 
I have high potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use in 
treatment in the United States,\12\ and a lack of accepted safety for

    \11\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1).
    \12\ When finding schedule I placement on a temporary basis is 
necessary to avoid imminent hazard to the public, 21 U.S.C 811(h) 
does not require DEA to consider whether the substance has a 
currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States. 
Nonetheless, there is no evidence suggesting that MGM-15 and MGM-16 
have a currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United 
States. First, DEA looks to whether the drug or substance has FDA 
approval. When no FDA approval exists, DEA has traditionally applied 
a five-part test to determine whether a drug or substances has a 
currently accepted medical use: (1) the drug's chemistry must be 
known and reproducible; (2) there must be adequate safety studies; 
(3) there must be adequate and well-controlled studies proving 
efficacy; (4) the drug must be accepted by qualified experts; and 
(5) the scientific evidence must be widely available. Marijuana 
Scheduling Petition; Denial of Petition; Remand, 57 FR 10499 (Mar. 
26, 1992), pet. for rev. denied, Alliance for Cannabis Therapeutics 
v. Drug Enforcement Admin., 15 F.3d 1131, 1135 (D.C. Cir. 1994). DEA 
applied the traditional five-part test and concluded the test was 
not satisfied. In a recent published letter in a different context, 
HHS applied an additional two-part test to determine currently 
accepted medical use for substances that do not satisfy the five-
part test: (1) whether there exists widespread, current experience 
with medical use of the substance by licensed health care providers 
operating in accordance with implemented jurisdiction-authorized 
programs, where medical use is recognized by entities that regulate 
the practice of medicine, and, if so, (2) whether there exists some 
credible scientific support for at least one of the medical 
conditions for which part (1) is satisfied. On April 11, 2024, the 
Department of Justice's Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) issued an 
opinion, which, among other things, concluded that HHS's two-part 
test would be sufficient to establish that a drug has a currently 
accepted medical use. Office of Legal Counsel, Memorandum for 
Merrick B. Garland Attorney General Re: Questions Related to the 
Potential Rescheduling of Marijuana at 3 (April 11, 2024). For 
purposes of this notice of intent, there is no evidence that health 
care providers have widespread experience with medical use of MGM-15 
and MGM-16, or that the use of these substances is recognized by 
entities that regulate the practice of medicine, so the two-part 
test also is not satisfied. In HHS's letter dated January 20, 2026, 
HHS advised DEA that there were currently no approved new drug 
applications or investigational new drug applications for MGM-15 and 
MGM-16. Additionally, HHS noted it had no objections to the 
temporary placement of these substances in schedule I of the CSA. 
The Assistant Secretary provided no contrary information in its 
October 6, 2026 letter.

Two 7-Hydroxymitragynine-Related Substances: MGM-15 and MGM-16

    The prevalence and misuse of Mitragyna speciosa (commonly known as 
kratom) and its psychoactive alkaloids, including mitragynine and 7-
hydroxymitragynine, have led to the proliferation of commercial 
products containing opioids chemically synthesized from mitragynine or 
7-hydroxymitragynine. In recent years, MGM-15, which is a derivative of 
7-hydroxymitragynine, has recently emerged on the Mitragyna speciosa 
consumer markets. MGM-16 is a highly potent opioid and shares a similar 
pharmacological profile with mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15. The 
chemical scaffolds of mitragynine or 7-hydroxymitragynine were used in 
scientific research to develop MGM-15 and MGM-16 via chemical 
modifications of purified isolates. Evidence from the Mitragyna 
speciosa retail markets demonstrates that MGM-15 has transitioned from 
experimental substances studied in research to widely available 
commercial products. These products are commonly sold in different 
forms such as powders, tablets, and liquid shots. This is a significant 
evolution from the traditional administration of Mitragyna speciosa, 
which was once restricted to either chewing raw leaves or steeping the 
leaves into water decoctions and teas.
    These products are sold under numerous brand names and they are 
easily purchased on the internet, as well as in gas stations, corner 
shops, and vape shops. These products are available in consumer-
friendly forms to include flavored chewable tablets, which increases 
their appeal to a broader demographic. Also, the aggressive marketing 
of these semi-synthetic opioids as ``precision-formulated products,'' 
``botanical extracts,'' or as ``mood boosters'' for the treatment of 
health conditions is deeply concerning. The branding creates a false 
sense of safety for unknowing



consumers who may equate the term ``botanical'' with lower risk. 
Furthermore, there is paucity of data on quality control or 
standardized dosage available for these products, making their use 
especially dangerous.
    MGM-15 and MGM-16 are potent opioids that share a similar 
pharmacological profile with 7-hydroxymitragynine. Available 
pharmacology data demonstrate that MGM-15 and MGM-16 exhibit strong 
affinity for the mu-opioid receptor (MOR) and function as MOR 
agonists.14 15 Data from preclinical studies show that these 
substances produce analgesic effects that is more potent than 
morphine.\16\ Because MGM-15, and MGM-16 are potent MOR agonists, they 
pose similar health risks as other mu-opioid agonists (i.e., morphine 
and fentanyl), including physical and psychological dependence, and 
respiratory depression.

    A scan of retail data on the internet shows that vendors explicitly 
market MGM-15 for their ``clean and powerful'' opioid-receptor 
activation, utilizing deceptive terminology to target individuals 
seeking alternatives to pharmaceutical opioids. These combinations and 
marketing strategies pose significant safety risks to unsuspecting 
consumers who use these products by exposing them to high doses of 
opioids. Recently, reports have confirmed the positive identification 
of MGM-15 in toxicology cases in the United States and evidence 
demonstrates that these substances are being misused. The lack of 
clinical data regarding their safety and efficacy, coupled with the 
risk of life-threatening respiratory depression and addiction, 
underscores the danger of marketing these unapproved, highly potent 
opioids under the guise of therapeutic or wellness products.
    While no evidence supports the presence of MGM-16 on the Mitragyna 
speciosa consumer market, its profile as a highly potent opioid that is 
structurally related to 7-hydroxymitragynine lends itself as an 
attractive substitute that could emerge on the illicit drug market. 
MGM-16 is synthetically manufactured for research purposes and is not 
approved for any clinical indication in the United States. DEA's 
investigation of publicly available information, including popular 
online platform, revealed that at least some individuals intend to 
abuse MGM-16. Recent online surveillance of a vendor site \17\ lists 
MGM-16 for upcoming sale. The sale of products containing mitragynine 
pseudoindoxyl, and MGM-15, and the potential sale of MGM-16 poses an 
imminent hazard to public safety.

15, and MGM-16, summarized below, indicate that these substances have a 
high potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use in 
treatment in the United States, and a lack of accepted safety for use

October 6, 2026 letter are available in their entirety under

Factor 4. History and Current Pattern of Abuse

    MGM-15 and MGM-16 are synthetic derivatives of the indole 
alkaloids, mitragynine or 7-hydroxymitragynine, of the Mitragyna 
speciosa plant. Unlike the indole alkaloids mitragynine and 7-
hydroxymitragynine, which are naturally occurring in the plant MGM-15 
and MGM-16 are produced through synthetic modifications of purified 
mitragynine isolates or 7-hydroxymitragynine.\18\ The chemical 
scaffolds of mitragynine or 7-hydroxymitragynine were used in 
scientific research to develop. In 2014, as part of a drug discovery 
research, MGM-15 and MGM-16 were developed as potent opioid agonists, 
with potential therapeutic utility for pain.\19\

September 2025.\20\ The introduction of MGM-15 into the Mitragyna

laboratory, botanical, and research purposes only'' and ``not intended

Current Patterns of Use

    Users seek 7-hydroxymitragynine-related products for their 
psychoactive effects and products are often advertised as mood 
enhancers or alternative to prescription opioid analgesics (see Factor 
5). These products are commonly sold in different product forms, such 
as powders, tablets, or liquid shots, which is a sharp contrast from 
the traditional mode of administration of Mitragyna speciosa, which was 
confined to either water decoctions or brewed into tea or chewing of 
fresh leaves. A review of vendor websites \22\ show that these products 
are explicitly marketed as ``potent'' and ``fast-acting'' substances 
and sold at low prices. For example, MGM-15 tablets are sold in varying 
fruit flavors and in bright colors and prices vary from about $2-4 per 
tablet or $34.99 per pack (single pack and 10-pack bulk). Of great 
concern to DEA is that the price of these products may facilitate high-
frequency and rapid escalation of use (see Table 1). Further, open-
source signal detection demonstrates that users are seeking MGM-16 with 
the intent to abuse.\23\

Factor 5. Scope, Duration, and Significance of Abuse

    The abuse of MGM-15 is concerning due to its high opioid potency 
and commercial availability. MGM-15 products are sold in formulations 
that facilitate ease of use, bypass the traditional, lower-alkaloid 
preparation (chewing leaves or drinking tea) and provide a highly 
potent effect that mimics classical opioids such as morphine.

Deceptive Branding and Market Infiltration

    Available information on vendor website indicates that the 
concentrated alkaloid products often contain more than one alkaloid 
with opioid activity (e.g., mitragynine and MGM-15). These substance 
combinations and marketing practices pose significant safety risk to 
unsuspecting consumers by exposing them to high doses of opioids (see 
Table 1). It is known that repeated use of opioids can lead to 
psychological and physical dependence. In fact, data show that chronic 
use of 7-hydroxymitragynine has sent users to opioid detox clinic and 
the need for opioid use disorder medication.\24\ Furthermore, these 
products are labeled for ``strong mood enhancement'' and ``analgesic 
properties.'' Finally, the presence of these products containing MGM-15 
is deeply concerning because the identity, purity, and quality of these 
products' formulation are uncertain, thus presenting additional safety 
concerns for unsuspecting users. The potential presence of MGM-16 in 
designer drug products would have similar concerns.

National E-commerce

    Data from online sources show that the availability of MGM-15 
products is not isolated to a single region but have rapidly spread 
across the United States. Products containing MGM-15 are sold on the 
internet and are delivered to most states where there are currently no 
kratom use restrictions, suggesting national distribution network 
facilitated by online sales and mass-market retail channels. The 
significance of the abuse of MGM-15 is underscored by the potent opioid 
pharmacological profile of these substances and the specific health 
warnings acknowledged even by those who are marketing the substances.

pattern of use that characterizes the abuse of these compounds:

Forensic Surveillance and Identification

    Recent monographs \27\ by Center for Forensic Science Research and 
Education (CFSRE), report that MGM-15 has been detected in at least 2 
drug materials. MGM-15 was detected as a



tan solid drug that originated from New England. The paucity or lack of 
seizure data for some of these 7-hydroxymitragynine-related substances 
as reported in forensic laboratories casework may be due to lack of 
readily available analytical reference standards and other analytic 
challenges. Because these are new substances, it often takes time for 
forensic laboratories to develop and validate the necessary testing 
methods required for substance identification. Specifically, since 
these 7-hydroxymitragynine-related substances are not federally 
controlled under the CSA, some forensic laboratories may not analyze 
and track encounters of non-controlled substances and thus reporting 
could be limited.

    The population likely to abuse MGM-15 and MGM-16 appear to be the 
same as those abusing Mitragyna speciosa and prescription opioid 
analgesics. According to data from the National Survey on Drug Use and 
Health (NSDUH),\28\ as of 2021, an estimated 1.7 million people aged 12

2019 NSDUH survey data showed that kratom users base predominately non-
Hispanic White and male. The survey finding also revealed a link

Factor 6. What, If Any, Risk There Is to Public Health

    MGM-15 and MGM-16 function as potent MOR agonist. This mechanism of 
action is inherently associated with high potential of abuse, physical 
dependence, and psychological dependence, consistent with the effects 
of controlled schedule I and II opioid substances. As of early 2026, 
MGM-15 products are sold in smoke shops, gas stations, and through 
numerous online marketplaces, often marketed alongside traditional 
supplements, which mask their potent opioid nature. Data from 
preclinical studies demonstrate that MGM-15 and MGM-16 are about 50 and 
240 times more potent than morphine in animal models, respectively.\30\ 
Because of the potency of these compounds, they can be abused in 
smaller, concentrated doses. These products are easily accessible in 
unregulated retail environments often with no age restrictions, 
amplifying public health concerns, particularly to vulnerable 
populations. Vendor descriptions provide insight into the public health 
threat posed by the abuse of these compounds:

    As with any MOR agonist, the potential health and safety risks for 
users of 7-hydroxymitragynine-related substances are high. MGM-15 and 
MGM-16 abuse carry a high risk of cardiotoxicity, hepatic and renal 
toxicity, respiratory depression, neurological effects, and physical 
dependence and withdrawal. According to data from poison control 
centers, from January to July 2025, there have been 1,690 exposure 
calls involving kratom, a significant increase from 2024 exposure 
calls. Recent monographs by CFSRE report that MGM-15 (n =1) has been 
detected in at least 12 toxicology cases. MGM-15 was co-identified with 
mitragynine, 7-hydroxymitragynine, and trace ketamine.
    The sale of products with combination of high-potency opioids, 
explicit marketing for medical ailments, and the acknowledged potential 
for life-threatening respiratory depression and addiction highlights 
the danger posed by MGM-15. While MGM-15 has already been identified in 
fatal toxicological screening, the pharmacological profile of MGM-16 
presents a significant health risk. As previously mentioned, MGM-16 is 
an opioid agonist with approximately 240-times the antinociceptive 
potency of morphine in animal studies. Recent online surveillance of a 
vendor site \34\ lists MGM-16 for upcoming sale. This transition from a 
research grade chemical to an accessible consumer product, combined 
with its opioid mechanism of action, underscores its potential as a 
highly attractive but lethal substitute. Thus, to schedule MGM-15 
without MGM-16 would create a regulatory loophole that manufacturers 
are already poised to exploit. Its inclusion is necessary to prevent a 
market shift toward an even more potent derivative that poses a 
significant risk of respiratory depression.

Finding of Necessity of Schedule I Placement To Avoid Imminent Hazard 
to Public Safety

    In accordance with 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(3), based on the available data 
and information summarized above, the uncontrolled manufacture, 
distribution, reverse distribution, importation, exportation, conduct 
of research and chemical analysis, possession, and abuse of MGM-15 and 
MGM-16 pose an imminent hazard to public safety. DEA is not aware of 
any currently accepted medical uses for MGM-15 and MGM-16 in the United 
States. A substance meeting the statutory requirements for temporary 
scheduling, found in 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1), may only be placed in 
schedule I. Substances in schedule I are those that have a high 
potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use in treatment in 
the United States, and a lack of accepted safety for use under medical 
supervision. Available data and information for MGM-15 and MGM-16 
indicate that these substances have a high potential for abuse, no 
currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States, and a 
lack of accepted safety for use under medical supervision.
    As required by 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(4), the Administrator notified the 
Assistant Secretary, via letter dated October 8, 2026, of DEA's 
intention to temporarily place MGM-15 and MGM-16 in schedule I.

Conclusion

    Although DEA has already published a temporary order in the Federal 
Register that placed MGM-15 and MGM-16 in schedule I of the CSA on 
August 26, 2026, HHS has since sent a letter dated October 6, 2026, to 
DEA, in which HHS now recommends controlling mitragynine pseudoindoxyl 
above a specified threshold in schedule I of the CSA. However, as noted 
above, HHS did not recommend imposing any threshold for either MGM-15 
or MGM-16. This notice of intent provides the 30-day notice pursuant to 
21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1) of DEA's intent to issue a new temporary scheduling 
order that will continue to impose the regulatory controls and 
administrative, civil, and criminal sanctions applicable to schedule I 
controlled substances on persons who handle (manufacture, distribute, 
reverse distribute, import, export, engage in research, conduct 
instructional activities or chemical analysis with, or possess) or 
propose to handle these two 7-hydroxymitragynine-related substances. In 
accordance with 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1) and (3), the Administrator 
considered available data and information, herein set forth the grounds 
for his determination that it is necessary to temporarily schedule MGM-
15 and MGM-16 in schedule I of the CSA, and finds that placement of 
these substances in schedule I of the CSA is necessary in order to 
avoid an imminent hazard to the public's safety.
    The temporary placement of MGM-15 and MGM-16 in schedule I of the 
CSA will take effect pursuant to a temporary scheduling order, which 
will not be issued before November 13, 2026. Additionally, to avoid an 
enforcement gap, the current temporary order that placed MGM-15 and 
MGM-16 in schedule I remains in effect until either that order expires 
or the new temporary order is published and the previous order is 
withdrawn, whichever occurs first. Because the Administrator hereby 
finds that this temporary scheduling order is necessary to avoid an 
imminent hazard to public safety, it will take effect on the date the 
order is published in the Federal Register and remain in effect for two 
years, with a possible extension of an additional year, pending 
completion of the regular (permanent) scheduling process.\35\ The 
Administrator intends to issue a temporary scheduling order as soon as 
possible after the expiration of 30 days from the date of publication 
of this document. Upon publication of the new temporary order, MGM-15 
and MGM-16 will continue to be subject to the CSA's schedule I 
regulatory controls and administrative, civil, and criminal sanctions 
applicable to the manufacture, distribution, reverse distribution, 
importation, exportation, research, conduct of instructional activities 
and chemical analysis, and possession.

Regulatory Analyses

    The CSA provides for expedited temporary scheduling actions where 
necessary to avoid an imminent hazard to public safety. Under 21 U.S.C. 
811(h)(1), the Administrator (as delegated by the Attorney General) 
may, by order, temporarily schedule substances in schedule I. Such 
orders may not be issued before the expiration of 30 days from: (1) the 
publication of a notice in the Federal Register of the intent to issue 
such order and the grounds upon which such order is to be issued, and 
(2) the date that notice of the proposed temporary scheduling order is 
transmitted to the Assistant Secretary of HHS, as delegated by the 
Secretary of HHS.\39\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \39\ 21 U.S.C. 811(h)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Inasmuch as section 811(h) directs that temporary scheduling 
actions be issued by order and sets forth the procedures by which such 
orders are to be issued, including the requirement of a publication in 
the Federal Register of a notice of intent, the notice-and-comment 
requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 553, 
do not apply to this notice of intent. The APA expressly differentiates 
between an order and a rule, as it defines an ``order'' to mean a 
``final disposition, whether affirmative, negative, injunctive, or 
declaratory in form, of an agency in a matter other than rule making.'' 
\40\ This contrasts with permanent scheduling actions, which are 
subject to formal rulemaking procedures done ``on the record after 
opportunity for a hearing,'' and final decisions that conclude the 
scheduling process and are subject to judicial review.\41\ The specific 
language chosen by Congress indicates its intent that DEA issue orders 
instead of proceeding by rulemaking when temporarily scheduling 
substances. Given that Congress specifically requires the Administrator 
(as delegated by the Attorney General) to follow rulemaking procedures 
for other kinds of scheduling actions,\42\ it is noteworthy that, in 
section 811(h)(1), Congress authorized the issuance of temporary 
scheduling actions by order rather than by rule.

II. Background

A. Purpose and Summary of the Proposed Regulatory Action

    The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5). 
That regulation instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior 
determination of a petitioner's, applicant's, or beneficiary's 
eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129, Petition 
for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same 
underlying facts.\1\ This requirement most often applies when a 
petitioning employer seeks to extend a petition for an alien's 
employment or authorized stay in the United States under the same 
previously approved nonimmigrant worker classification. Under the 
current regulation, USCIS must generally defer to the prior 
determination of eligibility for the nonimmigrant worker classification 
unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material 
information. 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ For most nonimmigrant classifications that use Form I-129, 
the filer is referred to as the ``petitioner.'' However, for some 
classifications (for example, the E and TN classifications), the 
filer is referred to as the ``applicant.'' For simplicity, 
references in this preamble to a ``petitioner'' also include an 
``applicant,'' and references to a ``petition'' also include an 
``application.''
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    When DHS promulgated 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), the agency stated that 
petitioners would ``continue to have the burden to present all required 
and relevant evidence'' to establish eligibility for the requested 
nonimmigrant worker classification notwithstanding the prior approval. 
See Modernizing H-1B Requirements, Providing Flexibility in the F-1 
Program, and Program Improvements Affecting Other Nonimmigrant Workers, 
89 FR 103054, 103093 (Dec. 18, 2024). The agency also stated that 
``deference does not equate to a lack of USCIS review of the 
petition.'' Id.
    DHS now believes, however, that the practical effect of the 
deference regulation is inconsistent with those statements. In 
particular, the deference regulation and policy effectively shift the 
burden from the petitioner to the USCIS officer to justify departing 
from a prior approval. DHS is also concerned that the deference policy 
has had the practical effect of encouraging USCIS officers to 
prioritize consistency with prior approvals and efficiency in 
adjudication of extension requests rather than fully exploring all 
facts and evidence to ensure continued eligibility for the nonimmigrant 
worker benefit. As a result, DHS believes that some petitioners have 
interpreted the deference policy as reducing their obligation to 
demonstrate continued eligibility for the requested nonimmigrant worker 
classification when seeking an extension of a prior approval. Overall, 
the deference regulation and policy risk undermining program integrity 
by potentially reducing scrutiny of extension requests of nonimmigrant 
worker classifications, thereby potentially perpetuating erroneous 
prior approvals and creating an environment in which fraudulent and 
meritless petitions are less likely to be detected before approval. See 
Section III of this preamble.
    Therefore, DHS proposes to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5). DHS believes 
that this change would better align DHS regulations and USCIS 
adjudicatory practice with the agency's longstanding interpretation of 
the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA or Act), which places the 
burden of proof in establishing eligibility for all immigration 
benefits on the petitioner. See INA sec. 291, 8 U.S.C. 1361; Matter of 
Chawathe, 25 I. & N. Dec. 369, 375 n.7 (USCIS AAO, 2010) (``The burden 
of proving eligibility for the benefit sought remains entirely with the 
applicant''). Removing the deference requirement would also help to 
ensure that USCIS officers fully review the facts and evidence in every 
case to ensure continued eligibility. Overall, DHS believes that this 
change would promote more complete adjudications, strengthen program 
integrity in the adjudication of nonimmigrant worker benefits, reduce 
the risk of perpetuating erroneous approvals, and support the 
Administration's broader efforts to better protect U.S. workers and 
more faithfully enforce the immigration laws enacted by Congress.\2\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

C. Extensions of Stay and Petition Validity

    Many aliens come to the United States under a nonimmigrant visa 
classification. Some of these classifications permit aliens to be 
employed or otherwise provide services in the United States for 
temporary periods. See INA secs. 101(a)(15) and 214, 8 U.S.C. 
1101(a)(15) and 1184. Each classification for purposes of employment or 
otherwise performing services in the United States has its own 
eligibility requirements and requirements related to the period of 
admission or status, maintenance of status, the ability to change jobs 
or employers, and the ability to extend nonimmigrant status. Id.
    For certain nonimmigrant visa classifications, a petitioner seeking 
the services of an alien beyond the previously granted period of 
admission may file an extension of stay request on Form I-129, Petition 
for Nonimmigrant Worker.\5\ 8 CFR 214.1(c)(1). An extension of stay is 
ordinarily only granted if the alien is still in, and has maintained, 
his or her nonimmigrant status at the time the request is filed. 8 CFR 
214.1(c)(6). When requesting an extension of stay on Form I-129, the 
petitioner must submit evidence that the alien maintained his or her 
status along with all other initial evidence specified in the 
regulations and in accordance with form instructions. See 8 CFR 
214.1(c)(1), (6); Form I-129 Instructions, Instructions for Petition 
for Nonimmigrant Worker, https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/forms/i-129instr.pdf (Sept. 9, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ The petitioner must file Form I-129 to request an extension 
of stay for E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B, H-1B1, H-2A, H-2B, H-3, L-1, O-1, 
O-2, P-1, P-2, P-3, P-1S, P-2S, P-3S, Q-1, R-1, or TN nonimmigrant 
workers. For dependents of such workers, extension of stay requests 
may be filed on Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change 
Nonimmigrant Status.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    An extension of stay request is often submitted together with a 
request for an extension of petition validity, which is a request to 
allow the alien to continue to work for his or her current employer in 
the same nonimmigrant classification.\6\ The petition extension and 
extension of stay request are filed on Form I-129 along with evidence 
of continued eligibility for the nonimmigrant classification, and all 
other initial evidence specified in the regulations and in accordance 
with form instructions.\7\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \6\ USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 ``Extension 
of Stay, Change of Status, and Extension of Petition Validity, 
https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-a-chapter-4 (last 
visited July 13, 2026) (``The burden of proof to establish 
eligibility for an immigration benefit always falls solely on the 
benefit requestor. The burden of proof never shifts to USCIS.'').
    \7\ Typically, determinations on extensions of petition validity 
are made by USCIS when adjudicating the Form I-129; however, in 
certain circumstances, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and U.S. 
Department of State may also make a determination on eligibility for 
an extension of petition validity.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    A request for an extension of petition validity follows a previous 
finding of eligibility for the nonimmigrant classification. Although 
there is a previous finding of eligibility, the burden of proof in any 
immigration request--including a request for an extension of petition 
validity--remains on the petitioner. See INA sec. 291, 8 U.S.C. 
1361.\8\ Officers are not bound to approve subsequent petitions seeking 
immigration benefits where eligibility has not been demonstrated, 
merely because of a prior approval.\9\ The prior approval may have been 
erroneous, in which case giving deference to that prior determination 
of eligibility because the adjudicating officer was not aware of the 
error may perpetuate unmeritorious approvals. Even if the prior 
approval was not erroneous, the burden of proof remains on the 
petitioner to establish eligibility in each benefit request. USCIS 
decides each matter according to the evidence of record on a case-by-
case basis.\10\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \8\ See also Matter of Chawathe, 25 I&N Dec. 369 (AAO 2010); 
Matter of Skirball Cultural Center, 25 I&N Dec. 799 (AAO 2012);

195 (D.D.C. 2024); Krasniqi v. Dibbins, 558 F.Supp.3d 168 (D. N.J. 
2021); 8 CFR 103.2(b)(1) (``An applicant or petitioner must 
establish that he or she is eligible for the requested benefit at 
the time of filing the benefit request and must continue to be 
eligible through adjudication.'').
    \9\ USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 ``Extension 
of Stay, Change of Status, and Extension of Petition Validity, 
https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-a-chapter-4 (last 
visited July 13, 2026); Matter of Church Scientology Intl, 19 I&N 
Dec. 593, 597 (Commissioner 1988).
    \10\ 8 CFR 103.2(b)(1) (``An applicant or petitioner must 
establish that he or she is eligible for the requested benefit at 
the time of filing the benefit request and must continue to be 
eligible through adjudication.''); USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2,
