---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Despite these well-established principles, the regulation at 8 CFR 
214.1(c)(5) instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior 
determination of eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form 
I-129 involving the same parties and the same underlying facts unless 
the officer determines that there was a material error involved with a 
prior approval, a material change in circumstances or eligibility 
requirements, or new, material information that adversely impacts 
eligibility. As discussed in Section III. of this preamble, DHS 
believes that the deference regulation is in tension with the statutory 
requirement that the petitioner must bear the burden to demonstrate 
eligibility for an immigration benefit, and it may unduly limit 
adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority in certain 
cases.

D. History of Deference in USCIS Adjudications

    While the codification of deference was relatively recent, USCIS 
has had a history of implementing and rescinding deference through a 
series of policy actions beginning in 2004. First, in April 2004, USCIS 
issued a memorandum discussing the significance of prior USCIS 
adjudications. See USCIS, ``The Significance of a Prior CIS Approval of 
a Nonimmigrant Petition in the Context



of a Subsequent Determination Regarding Eligibility for Extension of 
Petition Validity,'' HQPRD 72/11.3 (Apr. 23, 2004). This memorandum, 
while recognizing USCIS' authority to question prior determinations and 
that each matter must be decided according to the evidence of record on 
a case-by-case basis, first set out the policy instructing 
adjudications officers to give deference to a prior determination of 
eligibility in matters relating to an extension of nonimmigrant 
petition validity involving the same parties (petitioner and 
beneficiary) and the same underlying facts, unless there was material 
error, a substantial change in circumstances, or new material 
information.
    In October 2017, USCIS issued a memorandum which rescinded the 2004 
guidance, expressing concerns that the 2004 memorandum improperly 
shifted the burden from the petitioner to USCIS. See USCIS, 
``Rescission of Guidance Regarding Deference to Prior Determinations of 
Eligibility in the Adjudication of Petitions for Extension of 
Nonimmigrant Status,'' PM-602-0151 (Oct. 23, 2017). In the 2017 
memorandum, USCIS also expressed concerns that the deference policy 
unduly limited adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority 
in certain cases.
    In April 2021, USCIS reinstituted its deference policy and 
incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual. See USCIS Policy Manual, 
Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 ``Extension of Stay, Change of Status, and 
Extension of Petition Validity.'' The policy manual acknowledges that 
officers are not required to approve subsequent petitions where 
eligibility has not been demonstrated strictly because of a prior 
approval but stressed that they should defer to prior determinations 
involving the same parties and underlying facts. According to the 
policy manual, if an officer determines that deference to a prior 
approval is not appropriate, the officer must acknowledge the previous 
approval(s) in the denial, Request for Evidence (RFE), or Notice of 
Intent to Deny (NOID) and articulate the reason for not deferring to 
the previous determination (for example, due to a material error, 
change in circumstances, or new adverse material information). See id. 
Officers must provide the petitioner with an opportunity to respond to 
the new information consistent with 8 CFR 103.2(b)(16)(i). See id.
    In December 2024, DHS codified its deference policy at 8 CFR 
214.1(c)(5) through the final rule Modernizing H-1B Requirements, 
Providing Flexibility in the F-1 Program, and Program Improvements 
Affecting Other Nonimmigrant Workers, 89 FR 103054 (Dec. 18, 2024) 
(Modernization Final Rule). Current 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) states that when 
adjudicating a Form I-129, Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker, involving 
the same parties and the same underlying facts, USCIS gives deference 
to its prior determination of eligibility unless there is a material 
error, a material change, or new material information that adversely 
impacts eligibility.

III. Discussion of Proposed Rule

    DHS proposes to remove its regulation at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), and the 
deference policy, which instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a 
prior determination of the petitioner's or beneficiary's eligibility 
when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129 involving the same 
parties and the same underlying facts, unless there was a material 
error, a material change, or new material information that adversely 
impacts eligibility.\11\ This proposed change would apply to all 
benefit requests filed using Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant 
Worker. This proposal would not prohibit USCIS officers from 
considering a prior approval where relevant. Rather, it would remove 
the requirement that officers begin from a position of deference to the 
prior approval. DHS believes that this change would better ensure that 
officers fully consider all relevant facts and evidence to ensure 
continued eligibility, and adjudicate each petition or request on a 
case-by-case basis to determine whether the petitioner has met its 
burden of proof to demonstrate continued eligibility for the benefit. 
Overall, DHS believes that removing deference would enhance program 
integrity and thereby better protect the interests of U.S. workers, 
consistent with this Administration's priorities.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \11\ If this proposed rule becomes final, USCIS would make 
corresponding changes to the current policy guidance on deference. 
See USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 ``Extension of 
Stay, Change of Status, and Extension of Petition Validity,'' 
https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-a-chapter-4 (last 
visited July 13, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Restoring the Proper Allocation of the Burden of Proof

    Removing deference would better align DHS regulations with the 
agency's longstanding interpretation of section 291 of the INA, 8 
U.S.C. 1361, which places the burden of proof on the petitioner or 
applicant to establish eligibility for each immigration benefit sought. 
See also Matter of Chawathe, 25 I. & N. Dec. 369, 375 n.7 (USCIS AAO, 
2010) (``The burden of proving eligibility for the benefit sought 
remains entirely with the applicant.''). Although an agency may 
establish reasonable evidentiary presumptions, see e.g., Reno v. 
Flores, 507 U.S. 292, 313 (1993), any such presumption must be 
consistent with the statutory text and scheme, see Lin v. U.S. Dep't of 
Justice, 494 F.3d 296, 308 (2d Cir. 2007) (en banc). Whether or not the 
deference regulation is consonant with the statute, DHS now believes 
that it has the practical effect of shifting the burden of proof from 
the petitioner to the agency, in tension with section 291 of the INA, 8 
U.S.C. 1361, with respect to the eligibility criteria that Congress 
intended the agency to determine for each immigration benefit sought.
    When DHS promulgated 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), the agency stated that 
petitioners would continue to have the burden to demonstrate continued 
eligibility for the requested nonimmigrant worker classification. See 
89 FR 103094. In practice, however, the deference policy effectively 
shifts the burden from the petitioner to the adjudicating officer who 
must identify a material error or change in circumstances to justify 
deviating from the prior approval.\12\ In effect, this creates a 
default position that the prior approval was correct, and the 
petitioner and beneficiary remain eligible for the benefit unless the 
officer finds that an enumerated exception to the deference policy 
applies (i.e., that there was a material error, material change in 
circumstances or eligibility requirements, or new, material information 
that adversely impacts eligibility). This structure effectively shifts 
the burden from the petitioner to



the adjudicating officer. Instead of requiring the petitioner to 
establish that the alien is eligible to continue to work in the United 
States under a nonimmigration classification, the deference regulation 
and policy effectively require the officer to justify why the prior 
approval should not control.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \12\ Indeed, DHS also explained in the preamble of the 
Modernization Final Rule that under the deference regulation, USCIS 
officers must give ``close scrutiny before deviating from a prior 
approval involving the same parties and same underlying facts.'' 89 
FR 103094. USCIS implementing guidance also imposes several 
requirements on adjudicating officers who determine that deference 
is not appropriate, including acknowledging the previous approval, 
articulating the reasons for not deferring to that prior 
determination, obtaining supervisory approval before deviating from 
the prior approval, and giving the petitioner an opportunity to 
respond. See USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4, 
``Extension of Stay, Change of Status, and Extension of Petition 
Validity,'' https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-a-chapter-4 (last visited July 13, 2026). This further illustrates 
that the deference policy has the practical effect (if not the 
intent) of relaxing the petitioner's burden of proof by shifting the 
burden to the adjudicating officer to justify deviating from a prior 
approval. It also signals to officers that a less than thorough 
review is appropriate when adjudicating extension requests following 
a prior approval.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Enhancing USCIS Officer Fact-Finding Authority

    Removing deference would also better ensure that USCIS officers 
review the facts and evidence in every case to ensure continued 
eligibility before approving a petition extension and granting an 
extension of stay request. The deference policy suggests that a less 
than thorough review of each case may be acceptable and gives the 
impression of unduly limiting adjudicating officers' inherent fact-
finding authority. Some officers may view deference as a restriction on 
their ability to consider all the facts of the case. Rather than taking 
appropriate action if eligibility was not demonstrated in the petition 
(such as issuing an RFE), some officers may simply grant the benefit 
absent glaring errors or changes as a result of the deference policy.
    Indeed, as shown in Table 3 infra, the RFE rate increased by 2.9 
percent more than the RFE rate for the comparison group after the 
deference policy was rescinded in 2017. DHS acknowledges that other 
changes unrelated to deference may have, in part, contributed to this 
increased RFE rate. However, DHS believes that it is reasonable to 
conclude that the rescission of the deference policy was one of the 
contributing factors for this increased RFE rate. This increase is 
consistent with DHS's concern that the deference policy has had the 
effect of discouraging some officers from requesting additional 
evidence even in cases where the petitioner has not established 
eligibility for the nonimmigrant worker classification in connection 
with the current request.
    An adjudicating officer's fact-finding authority should not be 
constrained by any prior petition approval. Instead, officers should 
thoroughly review a petition for eligibility and request additional 
documentation as appropriate based on the merits of each case, 
consistent with USCIS policy regarding requests for evidence, notices 
of intent to deny, and the adjudication of petitions for nonimmigrant 
benefits. Because deference may be viewed as a default position upon 
beginning review of certain filings, the deference policy may, in some 
cases, have had the unintended effect of limiting the ability of 
officers to conduct a thorough review of the facts and limiting 
assessment of eligibility in each case. While officers may, of course, 
reach the same conclusion as in a prior decision, they should not be 
compelled to do so as a default starting point.\13\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \13\ DHS data also show that historical denial rates did not 
statistically differ during periods when the deference policy was in 
effect compared to when it was not in effect. One possible reason 
for this is that even when deference did not apply, petitioners may 
have been able to overcome issues raised in an RFE or NOID by 
submitting additional evidence or information. DHS believes, 
however, that the impact of the deference policy on officers' fact-
finding authority is best reflected in RFE rates rather than 
approval or denial rates. The ultimate adjudicative decision reached 
by the officer is not reflective of the extent to which an officer's 
fact-finding authority may have been restricted during the 
adjudicative review process. Rather, the variations in RFE rates 
during periods when deference applied versus the RFE rate when 
deference did not apply strongly suggests that deference has had the 
effect of discouraging some officers from requesting additional 
evidence. Policies that discourage officers from issuing RFEs, even 
when the officer determines that the petitioner has not yet 
established eligibility, undermine the integrity of the lawful 
immigration system and are inconsistent with enhancing an officer's 
fact-finding authority, regardless of the ultimate adjudicative 
decision.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition, deference increases the risk of officers not 
discovering material errors in prior adjudications. Although the 
deference policy allows officers to deviate from the prior decision if 
there was a material error, if officers limited their review of the 
cases before them because of an assumption that the prior decision was 
correct, it would necessarily limit the discovery of material error. 
Deferring to a determination of eligibility for nonimmigrant worker 
classification that was made potentially up to several years before the 
adjudication of the petition extension, and that may be based on 
inaccurate or outdated facts or adjudicated under regulations which 
have changed since the original approval was issued, is inconsistent 
with this Administration's efforts to strengthen the integrity of the 
nonimmigrant worker system.
    USCIS does not believe additional officer training or clarification 
on how to apply deference would sufficiently address these concerns. As 
discussed earlier in this preamble, USCIS has a history of applying 
deference over several years. Prior to its codification in the 
regulations in 2024, the deference policy was in place at USCIS from 
2004 until its rescission in 2017 and was reinstituted in 2021. 
Therefore, USCIS officers generally have had training and operational 
guidance on how to adjudicate petitions with the deference policy in 
place. Training, however, is not the issue or solution. Rather, any 
deference requirement itself conveys a fundamental tension with an 
officer's obligation to conduct a fulsome review to ensure that the 
petitioner met its burden before granting a nonimmigrant worker 
benefit. Indeed, the deference policy was based in part on a desire to 
increase efficiency by reducing the officer's need to revisit prior 
determinations of eligibility. That efficiency, however, has had the 
unintended effect of discouraging officers from thoroughly reviewing a 
case when adjudicating extension requests for nonimmigrant worker 
classifications. DHS now believes that the deference policy is 
inconsistent with ensuring that officers fully evaluate eligibility in 
every case, which is necessary to protect the integrity of the 
immigration benefits system and the interests of U.S. workers by 
ensuring that petitioners and beneficiaries are eligible for the 
requested nonimmigrant worker benefit.

C. Strengthening Program Integrity

    DHS also believes that deference may undermine program integrity, 
including by creating opportunities for unscrupulous petitioners to 
submit fraudulent or misleading petitions for nonimmigrant worker 
benefits. For example, an unscrupulous filer might submit a petition of 
questionable merit, hoping that if it is approved, the approval can be 
used as an anchor for later filings involving similar facts, related 
beneficiaries, or the same employer. They may even file multiple of 
these types of petitions and use the fact pattern that is the most 
advantageous or that is the most quickly approved. Similarly, a 
petitioner might overstate the beneficiary's role, compensation, or 
qualifications in the first filing, expecting that once approved, 
future filings will receive less scrutiny. Further, petitioners may be 
less forthcoming about changes affecting their business operations or 
the proffered position (such as reduced operations, loss of contracts, 
altered job duties, or other compliance issues) if they believe a prior 
approval is binding. If deference is expected, the petitioner may be 
incentivized to file extensions without fully disclosing those changes.
    Indeed, USCIS data provides some support for the concern that 
deference may undermine program integrity by reducing scrutiny in some 
cases and contributing to an environment in which misleading, non-
compliant, or fraudulent extensions of nonimmigrant worker petitions 
are more likely to be approved. For example, the data demonstrate 
higher percentages of fraud and non-compliance identified in the



H-1B and L-1A programs since the time when USCIS reinstituted its 
deference policy and incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual.\14\ 
Specifically, for H-1B extension cases from FY 2022 through FY 2025, 
the overall combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among H-
1B sites visited during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits 
was 22.39 percent. In comparison, when USCIS had a policy of no 
deference, the overall combined percentage of H-1B non-compliance and/
or fraud among H-1B sites visited during FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 
16.77 percent.\15\ For L-1A extension cases, the overall combined 
percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited 
during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits from FY 2022 
through FY 2025 was 24.46 percent. In comparison, the overall combined 
percentage of L-1A non-compliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited 
from FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 18.37 percent.\16\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \14\ USCIS, Releasable Data Regarding Fraud and Noncompliance in 
the H-1B and L-1A Programs (Jun. 6, 2026). This data represents 
administrative and targeted site visits conducted exclusively on H-
1B and L-1A extension petitions.
    \15\ USCIS excluded FY 2021 data from this subset because the 
deference policy was reinstated partway through FY 2021 (in April 
2021) and was not in effect for more than half of that fiscal year.
    \16\ USCIS excluded FY 2021 data from this subset because the 
deference policy was reinstated partway through FY 2021 (in April 
2021) and was not in effect for more than half of that fiscal year.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In other words, during the years that USCIS had a policy of 
deference, the combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among 
sites visited in the H-1B and L-1A programs was higher than in the 
years that USCIS did not have a policy of deference. This trend 
reflected in a subset of H-1B and L-1A extension filings supports the 
concern that deference undermines program integrity in potentially 
limiting USCIS' ability to thoroughly review an extension petition on a 
case-by-case basis, which in turn may incentivize frivolous or 
fraudulent filings that falsely assert no material change. While DHS 
acknowledges that other factors besides or in addition to deference may 
have led to this higher percentage of identifying fraud or non-
compliance, it is reasonable to conclude that deference was one of the 
contributing factors.
    Removing deference would potentially disincentivize fraudulent 
filings and help restore the integrity of the lawful immigration 
system. This, in turn, would also better protect U.S. workers by 
ensuring that petitions for nonimmigrant workers are only approved if 
eligibility is established by the petitioner based on evidence 
submitted in support of each petition.

D. Reconsideration of the Deference Policy

    DHS acknowledges the history of the deference policy and its recent 
codification at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) in the Modernization Final Rule. DHS 
also acknowledges that some of the statements in this proposed rule 
represent a shift from statements made in the Modernization Final Rule. 
In the Modernization Final Rule, some commenters voiced concern that 
codifying deference would constrain USCIS officers' fact-finding 
authority. See 89 FR 103093. Commenters stated that USCIS officers 
should not be constrained in requesting additional evidence in the 
adjudication process. They also stated that requiring USCIS officers to 
confirm all material facts before granting a benefit request would 
serve as a fraud detection mechanism and deterrent.
    At the time, DHS disagreed with the commenters' concerns. Id. 
However, DHS has reconsidered the issue since publication of the 
Modernization Final Rule and now believes that codification of the 
deference policy may have had the unintended effect of appearing to 
constrain USCIS officers' fact-finding authority, leading some USCIS 
officers to conduct a less than fulsome review, and thus undermining 
the agency's efforts to detect and deter fraud.\17\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \17\ See FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 
(2009) (``[I]t suffices that the new policy is permissible under the 
statute, that there are good reasons for it, and that the agency 
believes it to be better, which the conscious change of course 
adequately indicates.'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In the NPRM proposing to codify deference, DHS stated that the 
benefits of deference included promoting consistency and efficiency for 
both USCIS and its stakeholders, and creating predictability for 
petitioners and beneficiaries. DHS now believes that these benefits 
were overstated and were not adequately weighed against the negative 
impacts of deference. It is not clear that the codification of 
deference actually promoted consistency and efficiency in adjudication, 
and to any extent that it did, it did so at the expense of program 
integrity. As discussed in this preamble, deference may incentivize 
non-meritorious filings, give the appearance of unduly limiting 
adjudicators' inherent fact-finding authority, and increase the risk 
that erroneous prior approvals continue to serve as the basis for 
granting extension petitions for nonimmigrant workers. Quite simply, 
the deference policy is inconsistent with this Administration's focus 
on restoring the integrity of the legal immigration system to better 
protect U.S. workers by ensuring that only petitioners and 
beneficiaries who meet eligibility criteria and demonstrate eligibility 
are granted nonimmigrant worker benefits.

E. Reliance Interests and Alternatives Considered

    DHS recognizes that some U.S. employers and nonimmigrant workers 
may assert reliance interests in the continuation of the deference 
policy. For example, U.S. employers that expect the continued approval 
of their Form I-129 petitions may have made business arrangements based 
on an assumption that these nonimmigrant workers would be able to 
continue working for them. Similarly, nonimmigrant workers may have 
made career and/or personal plans in the United States based on the 
assumption that they would be able to continue their employment and 
legal presence in the United States.
    DHS has considered these reliance interests but believes that any 
such interests are limited. The deference regulation does not itself 
guarantee approval of an extension. Conversely, removing deference does 
not substantively change eligibility for the requested immigration 
benefit. This proposed change would not deprive U.S. employers of their 
ability to continue employing nonimmigrant workers, nor would it 
deprive nonimmigrant workers of their ability to continue working and 
living in the United States, so long as they are able to establish 
continued eligibility and obtain necessary approvals to continue such 
employment. Petitioners and beneficiaries do not have a legitimate 
expectation that an erroneous or unsupported prior approval would 
continue to result in future approvals.
    To the extent there are legitimate reliance interests in the 
continuation of deference, DHS believes the negative impacts of the 
deference policy, as discussed in this preamble, outweigh the potential 
benefits to employers and aliens who may seek to rely on deference as 
codified at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5). DHS believes that its interest in 
restoring integrity to the immigration system, including by ensuring 
that USCIS adjudicators conduct fulsome reviews of all benefits 
requests before granting a benefit, far outweighs any interest a 
petitioner or beneficiary may have in expecting continued approvals. 
This is especially true when deference increases the risk of USCIS 
failing to identify petitioners and beneficiaries who were not eligible 
for approval in the first place. DHS



therefore believes that removing 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) and ending the 
deference policy is necessary to ensure the integrity of the legal 
immigration system, which in turn better protects U.S. workers.
    DHS considered an alternative to removing the deference regulation 
whereby DHS would revise the regulation to more clearly state that 
USCIS has discretion whether to apply deference. This could be 
accomplished by revising the regulatory text to state that USCIS ``may 
give deference in its discretion'' instead of ``USCIS gives deference'' 
as currently stated at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5). However, DHS is not proposing 
this alternative because it would likely create unnecessary confusion 
and uncertainty for both petitioners and USCIS officers as to whether 
deference should be applied. Further, this alternative would not 
adequately address the concerns with deference discussed above in 
Section III.A through III.C of this preamble. Overall, DHS believes 
that removing deference entirely is the most practical alternative to 
enhance program integrity, including by ensuring that the burden 
remains on the petitioner to establish eligibility for the requested 
immigration benefit, and that USCIS adjudicators thoroughly review each 
nonimmigrant worker extension request on its own merits before 
extending the benefit.

IV. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements

A. Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), 13563 
(Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and 14192 (Unleashing 
Prosperity Through Deregulation)

    Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review) and 13563 
(Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review) direct agencies to assess 
the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if 
regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize 
net benefits. Executive Order 13563 emphasizes the importance of 
quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, of harmonizing 
rules, and of promoting flexibility. Executive Order 14192 (Unleashing 
Prosperity Through Deregulation) directs agencies to significantly 
reduce the private expenditures required to comply with Federal 
regulations and provides that ``any new incremental costs associated 
with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset 
by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior 
regulations.''
    The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not designated this 
rule as a ``significant regulatory action,'' under section 3(f) of 
Executive Order 12866. Accordingly, OMB has not reviewed it.
    This proposed rule is not an Executive Order 14192 regulatory 
action because it is being issued with respect to an immigration-
related function of the United States. The proposed rule's primary 
direct purpose is to implement or interpret the immigration laws of the 
United States (as described in INA sec. 101(a)(17), 8 U.S.C. 
1101(a)(17)) or any other function performed by the U.S. Federal 
Government with respect to aliens. See OMB Memorandum M-25-20, 
``Guidance Implementing Section 3 of Executive Order 14192, titled 
`Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation' '' (Mar. 26, 2025).
Summary of Changes
    The proposed rule would remove the deference provision at 8 CFR 
214.1(c)(5), which currently instructs USCIS officers to give deference 
to a prior determination for Form I-129 requests when the parties and 
underlying facts remain the same, unless there was a material error, a 
material change, or new material information that adversely impacts 
eligibility. As a result of a more thorough review of each petition, 
the number of requests for evidence (RFE) is expected to increase, 
resulting in additional time burden for petitioners to submit 
additional supporting documentation and evidence. The rule would also 
impose costs on petitioners by lengthening adjudication times and 
increasing uncertainty regarding continued employment. DHS estimates 
that the rule would produce new annual costs to petitioners of 
approximately $133,987 due to an increase in RFEs. In addition, the 
rule would impose costs on USCIS by increasing the adjudicative 
workload and operational costs, as officers would spend more time 
reassessing eligibility issues previously reviewed and may issue an 
increased number of RFEs, thereby increasing overall resource demands.
    There are primary benefits associated with removing the deference 
policy. Removal would clarify and reinforce that the statutory burden 
of proof remains on the petitioner, not the agency. Removal would also 
encourage a more thorough review of each petition and its supporting 
evidence. Implementing a more thorough review process is expected to 
improve the ability to detect prior errors, inconsistencies, or 
indicators of fraud, and to eliminate the need to determine when 
deference applies. For the broader public and the immigration system, 
the change is expected to enhance confidence in the integrity and 
reliability of the adjudication process and align with agency 
priorities related to system integrity and protection of U.S. workers' 
interests. Table 1 provides a detailed summary of estimated 
quantifiable and unquantifiable impacts of the proposed rule.

Background and Population
    The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), 
which instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior 
determination of the petitioner's, applicant's, or beneficiary's 
eligibility when adjudicating a request filed using Form I-129, 
Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the 
same underlying facts, unless there was a material error, a material 
change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility.
    The USCIS deference policy was first implemented and applied from 
April 2004 to October 2017. In April 2004, USCIS issued a memorandum 
directing officers to generally give deference to prior approvals when 
adjudicating petitions for extensions involving the same petitioner, 
the same beneficiary, and the same underlying facts. See USCIS, ``The 
Significance of a Prior CIS Approval of a Nonimmigrant Petition in the 
Context of a Subsequent Determination Regarding Eligibility for 
Extension of Petition Validity,'' HQPRD 72/11.3 (Apr. 23, 2004). While 
recognizing that each case must be decided on its own merits and that 
prior decisions could be revisited, the policy established that 
officers should defer to that prior determination of eligibility absent 
material error, substantial changed circumstances, or new material 
information. Id.
    In October 2017, USCIS issued a memorandum rescinding the April 
2004 guidance. See USCIS, ``Rescission of Guidance Regarding Deference 
to Prior Determinations of Eligibility in the Adjudication of Petitions 
for Extension of Nonimmigrant Status,'' PM-602-0151 (Oct. 23, 2017). 
The agency expressed concern that the deference policy improperly 
shifted the burden of proof away from the petitioner and unduly 
restricted officers' fact-finding authority. Id. From October 2017 to 
April 2021, officers were not instructed to defer to prior approvals 
and instead were instructed to make new determinations of eligibility 
without relying on earlier decisions.
    USCIS reinstated the deference policy in April 2021 and 
incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual. See USCIS Policy Manual, 
Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 ``Extension of Stay, Change of Status, and 
Extension of Petition Validity.'' The manual instructs officers to 
generally defer to prior approvals involving the same parties and the 
same underlying facts, unless there was a material error in the prior 
decision, a material change in circumstances, or new material 
information that adversely impacts the petitioner's or beneficiary's 
eligibility. Id. Then, in December 2024, DHS codified the reinstated 
policy at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) in the H-1B Modernization Final Rule, 
requiring deference to prior determinations in such cases unless one of 
the exceptions applies. See 89 FR 103054 (Dec. 18, 2024).
    Table 2 presents the total number of Form I-129 petitions for 
nonimmigrant workers and the subset of those petitions that are 
potentially eligible for deference for each fiscal year (FY) from FY 
2014-FY 2025. Percentages show the petitions eligible for deference as 
a share of total Form I-129 petitions. In the table, ``Deference Policy 
Status'' informs the baseline for the proposed rule and indicates the 
fiscal years in which the deference policy was in effect for USCIS 
officers. Across FY2014 through FY2025, total Form I-129 petitions 
generally increased over time, reaching 7,206,852 overall. Of these, 
2,168,394 petitions, or 30 percent, were eligible for deference. 
Eligibility generally ranged from 25 percent to 36 percent annually, 
with the highest share in FY2020. In the most recent period when the 
policy was in effect, FY2022



through FY2025, eligible petitions increased from 195,547 to 235,583, 
while the eligible share remained around 27 percent to 33 percent, with 
an average of 30 percent.
    To estimate the population that would be subject to this proposed 
rule over the next 10 years, we use the historical average from the 
four most recent fiscal years, FY 2022-FY 2025, because this period 
reflects consistent application of the deference policy. Since this 
rule is intended to remove the deference policy, the baseline 
population should represent a period in which the policy was fully in 
effect. Therefore, FY 2021 is excluded from the population estimation 
calculation because the deference policy was reinstated partway through 
the year (in April 2021) and was not in effect for more than half of 
that fiscal year.

Costs and Benefits of the Proposed Rule
    DHS expects that the proposed rule would generate both quantified 
and unquantified costs and benefits, assessed relative to a baseline in 
which the existing deference policy remains in effect.
Quantified Costs
    Quantified costs are captured as the additional time burden on 
petitioners resulting from more frequent RFEs. Removing the deference 
policy requires officers to more thoroughly assess eligibility, which 
may result in officers requesting additional documentation more often 
to independently verify eligibility for each extension request. Each 
RFE increases the time burden on petitioners, who must review the 
notice, collect and organize documents, and prepare and submit a 
response. To estimate the increase in RFEs attributable to removal of 
the deference policy, DHS uses historical data from October 1, 2013, to 
April 27, 2021, covering periods when the deference policy was in 
effect (October 1, 2013, to October 11, 2017) and when it was not in 
effect (October 12, 2017, to April 27, 2021).\18\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \18\ Although both periods (October 1, 2013 to October 11, 2017) 
and (April 28, 2021 to the present) operated under a deference 
policy, this analysis did not include period, April 28, 2021 to the 
present, because the objective is to estimate the impact of the 2017 
policy that removed deference, not the impact of the subsequent 
policy that reinstated deference.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In order to isolate the effect of removal of the deference policy 
on the number of RFEs, DHS uses a simple difference-in-difference (DID) 
approach.\19\ For this analysis, the DID approach compares changes in 
the RFE rate for the affected group (petitions affected by deference 
policy) during the periods when deference policy was in effect and when 
it was not in effect with changes in the RFE rate for the comparison 
group (petitions not affected by deference policy) over the same 
periods.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \19\ See Columbia University, Mailman School of Public Health, 
Difference-in-Difference Estimation, https://www.publichealth.columbia.edu/research/population-health-methods/difference-difference-estimation. Difference-in-difference (DID) is 
a quasi-experimental research design that makes use of longitudinal 
data from treatment and control groups to obtain an appropriate 
counterfactual to estimate a causal effect. DID is typically used to 
estimate the effect of a specific intervention or treatment (such as 
a passage of law, enactment of policy, or large-scale program 
implementation) by comparing the changes in outcomes over time 
between a population that is enrolled in a program (the intervention 
group) and a population that is not (the control group).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

and petitions not affected by the deference policy (comparison group).

4.5 percent from when the deference policy was in effect to when it was

uses the comparison group to account for those broader trends. Because 
the comparison group's RFE rate increased by 1.6 percent over the same 
period, the affected group's relative increase was



2.9 percent.\20\ This method provides a better estimate of the policy-
associated change than just the affected group change alone. DHS 
applied the same DID approach to denial rates and found no 
corresponding change.\21\ As a result, this analysis does not indicate 
an expected impact on denial rates.

Unquantified Costs
    Petitioners may experience longer adjudication times and increased 
uncertainty regarding continued employment when seeking extensions of 
stay and petition validity. Based on the average of the last four 
fiscal years (FY 2022-FY 2025), the difference in processing time 
between petitions with and without an RFE is 64 days; therefore, we use 
the additional processing time associated with petitions that receive 
an RFE, which is 64 calendar days.\27\ These longer timelines can delay 
the final decision, making it difficult for workers and employers to 
plan project timelines, staffing levels, and work assignments. During 
this extended period, petitioners may face added uncertainty as to the 
beneficiary's longer-term employment authorization and status, which 
could create operational challenges for employers, such as workforce 
planning and project scheduling and increase stress for workers who may 
have to wait significantly longer for clarity on their ability to 
continue employment beyond that already authorized. In cases where a 
petition to extend the beneficiary's stay has been timely filed, if the 
petition remained pending when the beneficiary's status expired, the 
beneficiary may remain in the United States in an authorized period of 
stay while awaiting the adjudication of the petition filed on their 
behalf and may be eligible to continue to work. See, e.g., 8 CFR 
274a.12(b)(20). The costs to beneficiaries then would be more related 
to unpredictability regarding when their petition is adjudicated.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \27\ Source: USCIS CDAO, CLAIMS3 & ELIS, PAER #21508, queried 
May 2026. Processing time is measured as the number of days between 
the petition receipt date and the date the initial decision is made. 
From FY 2022 to FY 2025, the average of the median processing times 
was 76 days for petitions with an RFE and 12 days for petitions 
without an RFE, a difference of 64 days.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS recognizes that removing deference may lead petitioners to 
devote additional time and resources to preparing extension petitions. 
USCIS did not find evidence that the Form G-28 filing rate increased as 
a result of removing deference.\28\ However, petitioners may take 
additional steps to ensure that submissions are complete and well-
organized at the outset, instead of merely relying on a prior approval. 
These efforts may help petitioners satisfy their burden of proof and 
may reduce the likelihood of deficiencies, but they may also impose 
unquantified costs in the form of additional staff time, attorney time, 
or other preparation costs. DHS is unable to quantify this cost with 
the available data.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \28\ To assess this potential impact, DHS examined the share of 
petitions that were filed with a Form G-28, which indicates attorney 
or accredited representative involvement. The share increased for 
both deference-eligible petitions, the treated group, and deference 
non-eligible petitions, the control group, from the pre-policy 
period, when deference was in effect, to the policy period, when 
deference was not in effect. However, the increase was smaller for 
treated petitions than for control petitions, resulting in a 
difference-in-differences estimate of close to zero percentage 
points. This suggests that, although G-28 usage among petitions 
increased overall, the increase was not greater for the group 
affected by the no-deference policy. Therefore, DHS does not have 
evidence that removing deference would cause a meaningful increase 
in petitioners' reliance on attorneys beyond the costs already 
considered in the analysis.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Unquantified Benefits
    Removing 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) and the deference policy would clarify 
and reinforce that the statutory burden of proof remains on the 
petitioner rather than on the agency, consistent with the statute. See 
INA sec. 291, 8 U.S.C. 1361; Matter of Chawathe, 25 I. & N. Dec. 369, 
375 n.7 (USCIS AAO, 2010) (``The burden of proving eligibility for the 
benefit sought remains entirely with the applicant''). This benefits 
the agency by underscoring that officers are not obligated to approve 
subsequent petitions seeking immigration benefits where eligibility has 
not been demonstrated, merely because of prior approval. Removing the 
deference policy would also compel adjudication officers not to rely on 
incomplete or outdated facts, and supports more accurate, record-based 
decisions. Clear allocation of the burden of proof can also promote 
more complete, better-organized filings, and may reduce the risk of 
erroneous approvals of extension petitions.
    Moreover, removing deference would reinforce DHS's authority to 
conduct a full, current review of the evidence in each petition, 
improving the ability to identify ineligibility or indicators of fraud. 
When officers need not defer to prior approvals, they can better 
evaluate documentation and eligibility criteria based on updated 
information, policies, or patterns that may not have been apparent at 
the time of the earlier decision. This full-scope review could help 
reveal discrepancies between past and current filings, highlight 
evolving risk indicators, and identify potential mistakes in prior 
decisions. This approach would strengthen program integrity by helping 
the agency to correct mistakes, detect emerging fraud schemes, and 
refine guidance and training based on issues identified through ongoing 
examination of repeat filers.
    Removing deference would also benefit the public and the broader 
immigration system by reinforcing that each petition is evaluated on 
the current record, which could increase confidence in the integrity of 
adjudications. Members of the public would have more assurance that 
approvals are not simply carried forward from prior decisions but are 
based on current facts and applicable standards. At the same time, 
removing deference would maintain the integrity of the immigration 
system and advance policies that better protect the interests of U.S. 
workers by supporting more accurate, evidence-driven decisions and 
reducing the risk that outdated or erroneous prior approvals continue 
to serve as the basis for granting immigration benefits.



Alternatives Considered
    This proposed rule seeks to clarify and reinforce that the 
statutory burden of proof remains on the petitioner, encourage a more 
thorough review of each petition and its supporting evidence, and 
better protect the integrity of the legal immigration system. DHS 
believes that removing deference would impose relatively small 
additional compliance costs and that the resulting benefits it provides 
justify these costs. Therefore, DHS believes that removing the 
deference provision for extension of stay petitions would be the most 
effective way to achieve the goals of this rulemaking.
    DHS considered an alternative to revise the deference regulation to 
more clearly state that USCIS has discretion whether to apply 
deference. DHS is not proposing this alternative because it would 
likely create unnecessary confusion and uncertainty for both 
petitioners and USCIS. Instead, DHS believes that removing deference 
entirely is the most practical alternative to enhance program 
integrity, including by ensuring that the burden remains on the 
petitioner to establish the nonimmigrant alien worker's eligibility to 
continue working in the United States, and that USCIS adjudicators 
thoroughly review each nonimmigrant worker extension request on its own 
merits before granting the benefit. DHS did not consider other 
alternatives. DHS welcomes public comments on this issue.

Costs to the Federal Government
    DHS is proposing to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) and the deference 
policy which may increase USCIS operational costs by requiring officers 
to assess eligibility for petitions that previously would have 
benefitted from deference, even when the underlying facts and 
circumstances remain unchanged. This additional effort would lead to 
greater use of adjudicative actions, particularly in the form of RFEs, 
which further increase agency resource demands and contribute to 
backlogs. Preparing and issuing RFEs, and reviewing responses to RFEs, 
require additional officer time, supervisory review, and administrative 
support, collectively raising the overall cost and time of processing.
    The INA provides for the collection of fees at a level that will 
ensure recovery of the full costs of providing adjudication and 
naturalization services, including administrative costs and services 
provided without charge to certain applicants and petitioners.\29\ Fees 
are established at an amount that is necessary to recover these 
assigned costs, such as clerical, officer, and managerial salaries and 
benefits, plus an amount to recover unassigned overhead (e.g., facility 
rent, IT equipment and systems) and immigration benefits provided 
without a fee charge. These costs would be captured in the fees 
collected for the benefit request from petitioners. DHS established the 
current fees in its FY 2024 fee rule based on empirical cost estimates. 
DHS notes that if this rule, if finalized as proposed, would increase 
USCIS' costs, then the fee schedule adjustment would be determined at 
USCIS' next comprehensive biennial fee review.

B. Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980

Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis
    The RFA, Public Law 96-354, as amended by the Small Business 
Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, Public Law 104-121, 5 
U.S.C. 601 through 612, requires Federal agencies to consider the 
potential impact of regulations on small businesses, small governmental 
jurisdictions, and small organizations during the development of their 
rules. The term ``small entities'' comprises small businesses, not-for-
profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are 
not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with 
populations of less than 50,000.\30\ An ``individual'' is not 
considered a small entity and costs to an individual are not considered 
a small entity impact for RFA purposes. In addition, the courts have 
held that the RFA requires an agency to perform a regulatory 
flexibility analysis of small entity impacts only when a rule directly



regulates small entities.\31\ Consequently, indirect impacts from a 
rule on a small entity are not considered as costs for RFA purposes. 
This proposed rule would affect small entities that submit Form I-129, 
Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker. Consequently, DHS has prepared an 
initial regulatory flexibility analysis below for public comment.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \30\ A small business is defined as any independently owned and 
operated business not dominant in its field that qualifies as a 
small business per the Small Business Act, 15 U.S.C. 632.
    \31\ See U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA), ``A Guide for 
Government Agencies: How to Comply with the Regulatory Flexibility 
Act.'' at 22 (Aug. 2017), https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/How-to-Comply-with-the-RFA.pdf. In Aeronautical 
Repair Station Association, Inc. v. FAA, the D.C. Circuit made clear 
that an entity is not ``subject to'' a regulation unless the 
regulation ``imposes responsibilities directly on'' the entity. 494 
F.3d 161, 177 (D.C. Cir. 2007); see also Mid-Tex Elec. Coop., Inc. 
v. FERC, 773 F.2d 327, 342 (D.C. Cir. 1985) (holding that the RFA's 
requirements apply only to ``small entities that would be directly 
regulated'' by a challenged rule).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. A Description of the Reason Why the Action by the Agency Is Being 
Considered
    The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) 
and the deference policy which instructs USCIS officers to give 
deference to a prior determination of the petitioner's, applicant's or 
beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-
129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and 
the same underlying facts, unless there was a material error, a 
material change, or new material information that adversely impacts 
eligibility. This proposed change would better align the regulation 
with the statute, which places the burden of proof in establishing 
eligibility on the petitioner.
2. A Statement of the Objectives of, and Legal Basis for, the Proposed 
Rule
    DHS's objectives and legal authority for this proposed rule are 
discussed earlier in the preamble.

    The unquantifiable cost of this rule is the increased uncertainty 
and potential operational disruption associated with longer 
adjudication times for extension petitions that receive an RFE. Based

of 64 additional calendar days to process, which may affect employer 
planning for staffing, project timelines, and work assignments, as well 
as workers' uncertainty regarding their longer-term employment 
authorization and status.

spent preparing and submitting additional RFEs resulting from the 
expected increase in RFEs. As discussed in the ``Quantified Costs''

petitioners would be $133,987 across all affected employers for 
preparing additional supporting documentation and evidence to re-
establish eligibility for an estimated 6,044 additional RFEs. DHS 
identified 22,748 unique employers affected by this rule. DHS estimates 
the cost per RFE by dividing the total estimated annual cost of 
$133,987 by the estimated increase in RFEs attributable to this rule, 
6044, resulting in an estimated cost of approximately $22 per RFE. 
Because the median number of petitions filed by small entities is 
one,\34\ a small entity that receives an RFE due to the removal of 
deference would need to spend time submitting additional supporting 
documentation and evidence and would incur an estimated cost of 
approximately $22. As shown in Table 3, the RFE rate during the period 
when the deference policy was not in effect was 23.4 percent. DHS 
therefore estimates that approximately 23.4 percent, or 3,637, of the 
small entities potentially affected by the rule would incur costs as a 
result of this rule. The estimated cost would be approximately $22 per 
affected small entity. Therefore, although the rule may affect a 
substantial number of small entities, DHS does not expect the economic 
impact on affected small entities to be significant. DHS welcomes 
public comments on this analysis, particularly those comments that

proposed rule.

4. A Description of the Projected Reporting, Recordkeeping, and Other

    The proposed rule would increase compliance requirements primarily

petitions, because officers would no longer apply deference to prior 
approvals and would instead more thoroughly examine eligibility for 
each request. As a result, certain petitioners would need to review RFE 
notices more frequently, collect and organize additional supporting 
documentation, and maintain more robust records of prior approvals and 
ongoing eligibility. DHS anticipates that these activities would 
generally be carried out by an HR specialist, an in-house attorney, or 
an outsourced attorney, who would be responsible for analyzing the 
RFEs, assembling the required documentation, and preparing timely, 
complete responses on behalf of the petitioner.
5. An Identification of All Relevant Federal Rules, to the Extent 
Practical, That May Duplicate, Overlap, or Conflict With the Proposed 
Rule
    DHS is unaware of any duplicative, overlapping, or conflicting 
Federal rules, but invites the public to provide comments and 
information regarding any such rules.
6. A Description of Any Significant Alternatives to the Proposed Rule 
That Accomplish the Stated Objectives of Applicable Statutes and That 
Minimize Any Significant Economic Impact of the Proposed Rule on Small 
Entities
    DHS did not consider any alternatives to the proposed rule other 
than revising the regulatory text to more clearly state that USCIS has 
discretion whether to apply deference. However, this alternative would 
not accomplish the stated objectives of this proposed rule. DHS 
believes that removing deference would impose relatively small 
additional compliance costs and that the resulting benefits justify 
these costs.

C. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995

    The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) is intended, among 
other things, to curb the practice of imposing unfunded Federal 
mandates on State, local, and Tribal governments. Title II of UMRA 
requires each Federal agency to prepare a written statement assessing 
the effects of any Federal mandate in a proposed rule, or final rule 
for which the agency published a proposed rule, that includes any 
Federal mandate that may result in a $100 million or more expenditure 
(adjusted annually for inflation) in any one year by State, local, and 
tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.\35\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35\ See 2 U.S.C. 1532(a).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The inflation adjusted value of $100 million in 1995 is 
approximately $211 million in 2025 based on the Consumer Price Index 
for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).\36\ This proposed rule does not 
contain a Federal mandate as the term is defined under UMRA.\37\ The 
requirements of title II of UMRA, therefore, do not apply, and DHS has 
not prepared a statement under UMRA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \36\ See DOL, BLS, ``Historical Consumer Price Index for All 
Urban Consumers (CPI-U): U.S. city average, all items, by month,'' 
(last visited July 29, 2026). Calculation of inflation: (1) 
Calculate the average monthly CPI-U for the reference year (1995) 
and the current year (2025); (2) Subtract reference year CPI-U from 
current year CPI-U; (3) Divide the difference of the reference year 
CPI-U and current year CPI-U by the reference year CPI-U; (4) 
Multiply by 100 = [(Average monthly CPI-U for 2025 - Average monthly 
CPI-U for 1995) / (Average monthly CPI-U for 1995)] x 100 = 
[(321.943 - 152.383) / 152.383] = (169.560 / 152.383) = 1.113 x 100 
= 111.3 percent = 111 percent (rounded). Calculation of inflation-
adjusted value: $100 million in 1995 dollars x 2.11= $211 million in 
2025 dollars.
    \37\ The term ``Federal mandate'' means a Federal 
intergovernmental mandate or a Federal private sector mandate. See 2 
U.S.C. 1502(1), 658(6).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

D. Executive Order 13132 (Federalism)

    This proposed rule would not have substantial direct effects on the 
States,



on the relationship between the National Government and the States, or 
on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various 
levels of government. Therefore, in accordance with section 6 of 
Executive Order 13132, Federalism, it is determined that this proposed 
rule does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the 
preparation of a federalism summary impact statement.

E. Executive Order 12988 (Civil Justice Reform)

    This proposed rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with E.O. 
12988, Civil Justice Reform. This proposed rule was written to provide 
a clear legal standard for affected conduct and was carefully reviewed 
to eliminate drafting errors and ambiguities, so as to minimize

    This proposed rule does not have ``tribal implications'' because it

G. National Environmental Policy Act

    DHS and its components analyze proposed regulatory actions to 
determine whether the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 
U.S.C. 4321 et seq., applies to them and, if so, what degree of 
analysis is required. DHS Directive 023-01 Rev. 01 ``Implementing the 
National Environmental Policy Act'' (Dir. 023-01 Rev. 01) and 
Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01 Rev. 01 (Instruction Manual) \38\ 
establish the policies and procedures that DHS and its components use 
to comply with NEPA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \38\ The Instruction Manual, which contains DHS's procedures for 
implementing NEPA, was issued on November 6, 2014, and is available 
at https://www.dhs.gov/ocrso/eed/epb/nepa (last updated Apr. 14, 
2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish, in their NEPA 
implementing procedures, categories of actions (``categorical 
exclusions'') that experience has shown do not, individually or 
cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human environment and, 
therefore, do not require an environmental assessment or environmental 
impact statement. See 42 U.S.C. 4336(a)(2), 4336e(1). The Instruction 
Manual, Appendix A lists the DHS Categorical Exclusions.\39\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \39\ See Appendix A, Table 1.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under DHS NEPA implementing procedures, for an action to be 
categorically excluded, it must satisfy each of the following three 
conditions: (1) the entire action clearly fits within one or more of 
the categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger 
action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the 
potential for a significant environmental effect.\40\ DHS is proposing 
to remove a regulatory provision at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) codifying 
deference to certain eligibility determinations to better align the 
regulation with the statute and better ensure the integrity of the 
immigration system, including the interests of U.S. workers. This 
proposed change to existing DHS regulations is strictly administrative 
in nature and the rule clearly fits within categorical exclusion A3(a).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \40\ Instruction Manual 023-01 at V.B(2)(a)-(c).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Accordingly, DHS finds that the proposed amendments to current 
regulations clearly fits within categorical exclusion A3 established in 
DHS's NEPA implementing procedures as an administrative change with no 
change in environmental effect, is not part of a larger Federal action, 
and does not present extraordinary circumstances that create the 
potential for a significant environmental effect. See Instruction 
Manual 023-01 at V.B(2)(a)-(c).

Background

Recission of Administrative Review, in Part

    Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), Commerce will rescind an 
administrative review, in whole or part, if the party that requested a 
review withdraws its request within 90 days of the date of publication 
of the notice of initiation. As noted above, the following companies 
timely withdrew their review requests and no other party requested an 
administrative review of these companies: Blue Sea Pack Import Export 
Company Limited, Goldsun Packaging and Printing Joint Stock Company, 
Vietnam Red Star Industry Company Limited, and Vietnam Red Star 
Industry Company Limited of Vietnam. Therefore, we are rescinding this 
administrative review with respect to these companies, pursuant to 19 
CFR 351.213(d)(1).

Methodology

    Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with section 
751(a)(1)(B) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). We have 
calculated constructed export price in accordance with section 772 of 
the Act. Because Vietnam is a non-market economy country within the 
meaning of section 771(18) of the Act, we have calculated NV in 
accordance with section 773(c) of the Act. For a full description of 
the methodology underlying our conclusions, see the Preliminary 
Decision Memorandum.

Vietnam-Wide Entity

    Commerce's policy regarding conditional review of the Vietnam-wide 
entity applies to this administrative review.\10\ Under this policy, 
the Vietnam-wide entity will not be under review unless a party 
specifically requests, or Commerce self-initiates, a review of the 
entity. Because no party requested review of the Vietnam-wide entity, 
the entity is not under review and the entity's rate (i.e., 92.34 
percent) \11\ will not be subject to change.

Assessment Rates

    Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(A) of the Act and 19 CFR 
351.212(b)(1), Commerce will determine, and U.S. Customs and Border 
Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate 
entries of subject merchandise in accordance with the final results of 
this review.\18\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \18\ See 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    If IPSC's weighted-average dumping margin is not zero or de minimis 
(i.e., less than 0.50 percent) in the final results of this review, 
Commerce intends to calculate importer-specific assessment rates on the 
basis of the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for each 
importer's examined sales to the total entered value of those sales. 
Where we do not have entered values for all U.S. sales to a particular 
importer, we will calculate an importer-specific, per-unit assessment 
rate on the basis of the ratio of the total amount of dumping 
calculated for the importer's examined sales to the total quantity of 
those sales.\19\ To determine whether an importer-specific, per-unit 
assessment rate is de minimis, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.106(c)(2), 
we also will calculate an importer-specific ad valorem ratio based on 
estimated entered values. If IPSC's weighted-average dumping margin is 
zero or de minimis or where an importer-specific ad valorem assessment 
rate is zero or de minimis, we will instruct CBP to liquidate 
appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.\20\

Comments Invited

    The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or 
arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed 
under ADDRESSES. Include ``Docket No. FAA-2026-11807; Project

11.35, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to

agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal 
contact received about this NPRM.

Confidential Business Information

    CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily 
and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of 
Information Act (FOIA) (5 U.S.C. 552), CBI is exempt from public 
disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial 
or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that 
you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to 
this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted 
comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing 
CBI as ``PROPIN.'' The FAA will treat such marked submissions as 
confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public 
docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to 
Farhan Alamgir, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, 
Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590. Any commentary that the FAA receives 
which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the 
public docket for this rulemaking.

Background

    The FAA issued AD 2024-18-01, Amendment 39-22835 (89 FR 80993, 
October 7, 2024), (AD 2024-18-01), for all Leonardo S.p.A. Model A119 
and AW119 MKII helicopters. AD 2024-18-01 was prompted by an MCAI 
originated by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States 
of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2023-0035, dated February 
10, 2023 (EASA AD 2023-0035) to correct an unsafe condition identified 
as reports of abnormal rotations on the collective stick torque tube 
assemblies due to erroneous manufacturing.
    AD 2024-18-01 requires repetitive inspections of certain collective 
stick torque tube assemblies for deficiencies and corrective action, as 
applicable. The FAA issued AD 2024-18-01 to address abnormal rotations 
on the collective torque tube assemblies.

Actions Since AD 2024-18-01 Was Issued

    Since the FAA issued AD 2024-18-01, EASA superseded EASA AD 2023-
0035 and issued EASA AD 2026-0045, dated March 4, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-
0045) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that since EASA 
AD 2023-0035 was issued, an improved collective stick torque tube 
assembly was designed, and replacement instructions were issued. The 
unsafe condition, if not addressed, could lead to reduced control of 
the helicopter, which could result in a forced landing, damage to the 
helicopter, and injury to occupants.
    You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at regulations.gov under 
Docket No. FAA-2026-11807.



Material Incorporated by Reference Under 1 CFR Part 51

    The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2026-0045, which specifies procedures for 
repetitive inspections of the collective stick torque tube assembly for 
any relative rotation and, depending on the inspection results, 
replacement of the affected parts with serviceable parts. EASA AD 2026-
0045 also specifies procedures for modification of the helicopter 
through the replacement of affected parts with serviceable parts within 
a specified compliance time. This replacement of an affected part with 
a serviceable part constitutes terminating action for the repetitive 
inspections. EASA AD 2026-0045 also prohibits the installation of 
affected parts.
    This material is reasonably available because the interested 
parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by 
the means identified in the ADDRESSES section.

FAA's Determination

    These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority 
(CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United 
States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of 
Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe 
condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing 
this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described 
previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same 
type design.

Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM

    This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified 
in EASA AD 2026-0045, described previously, as incorporated by 
reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the 
regulatory text of this proposed AD.

Explanation of Required Compliance Information

    In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD 
process, the FAA developed a process to use some CAA ADs as the primary 
source of information for compliance with requirements for 
corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with 
manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate 
EASA AD 2026-0045 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD 
would, therefore, require compliance with EASA AD 2026-0045 in its 
entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences 
identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. 
Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular 
section in EASA AD 2026-0045 does not mean that operators need comply 
only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to 
``all required actions and compliance times,'' compliance with this AD 
requirement is not limited to the section titled ``Required Action(s) 
and Compliance Time(s)'' in EASA AD 2026-0045. Material required by 
EASA AD 2026-0045 for compliance will be available at regulations.gov 
under Docket No. FAA-2026-11807 after the FAA final rule is published.

    The FAA estimates that this AD, if adopted as proposed, would 
affect 60 helicopters of U.S. registry.

AD:

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The FAA has included all known costs in its cost estimate. 
According to the manufacturer, however, some of the costs of this

Authority for This Rulemaking

    Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to 
issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the 
authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, 
describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
    The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in 
Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. 
Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight 
of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for 
practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary 
for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that 
authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to 
exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

Regulatory Findings

    The FAA determined that this proposed AD would not have federalism 
implications under Executive Order 13132. This proposed AD would not 
have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship 
between the national Government and the States, or on the distribution 
of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
    For the reasons discussed above, I certify that the proposed 
regulation:
    (1) Is not a ``significant regulatory action'' under Executive 
Order 12866,
    (2) Would not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska, and
    (3) Would not have a significant economic impact, positive or 
negative, on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria 
of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

of section 207.67 of the Commission's rules. The deadline for filing 
posthearing briefs is 5:15 p.m. on March 29, 2027. In addition, any

the reviews on or before 5:15 p.m. on March 29, 2027. On April 22,

Phase of Countervailing Duty and Antidumping Duty Investigations
